name: Saint Emilia of Caesarea
title: Saint Emilia (Emmelia), Mother of Saint Basil the Great
curatedBio: Emmelia of Caesarea was born in Cappadocia during the late third to early fourth century into a noble Christian family. Following the martyrdom of her father under Licinius, she married Basil the Elder and gave birth to ten children, five of whom are venerated as canonized saints, including Basil the Great and Macrina the Younger. In her later years, guided by her daughter Macrina, she founded a monastic community where nobles and former servants lived as spiritual equals.
deathSummary: Saint Emilia reposed peacefully around 375 after establishing an ascetic monastic retreat and giving her blessing to her monastic children.

image.title: Saint Emilia of Caesarea Sacred Icon

name: Righteous Juliana of Lazarevo
title: Righteous Juliana of Lazarevo (Murom), the Merciful
curatedBio: Righteous Juliana was born in Moscow to noble parents and orphaned in early childhood. Married to George Ossorguin, she lived a life of extraordinary secret asceticism, praying through the night while fulfilling marital and domestic obligations. During the disastrous Russian famine of 1601 to 1603, she sold all her possessions, freed her serfs, and baked bread from wild weeds to feed starving peasants. Her uncomplaining joy and immense compassion became a model of Christian lay holiness.
deathSummary: Saint Juliana reposed peacefully at the age of seventy in 1604, and ten years later her body was found incorrupt, streaming fragrant holy myrrh.

image.title: Righteous Juliana of Lazarevo Sacred Icon

name: Saint Genevieve of Paris
title: Our Holy Mother Genevieve, Patroness of Paris
curatedBio: Born in Nanterre near Paris around 419, Genevieve consecrated her virginity to Christ in childhood upon the counsel of Saint Germanus of Auxerre. Living as an ascetic in Paris, she was revered for prophetic discernment and deep prayer. In 451, as Attila the Hun advanced upon Paris, she urged the citizens to pray and fast, assuring them the city would be spared, which proved true. She subsequently negotiated with Clovis I and Childeric to protect the populace and build church shrines.
deathSummary: Saint Genevieve reposed peacefully around 502 at approximately eighty years of age after decades of spiritual and civic leadership.

image.title: Saint Genevieve of Paris Sacred Icon

name: Saint Elizabeth Ann Seton
title: Saint Elizabeth Ann Seton, Foundress of the Sisters of Charity
curatedBio: Elizabeth Ann Bayley Seton was born in New York City in 1774 into an Episcopalian family. Following the death of her husband William Seton in Italy, she converted to Catholicism in 1805 despite severe familial and social ostracism. Moving to Emmitsburg, Maryland, she established Saint Joseph’s Academy and Free School, pioneering the Catholic parochial school system in the United States. She also founded the Sisters of Charity of Saint Joseph, the first congregation of religious sisters in North America.
deathSummary: Mother Seton died of pulmonary tuberculosis in Emmitsburg, Maryland on January 4, 1821 at the age of forty-six.

image.title: Saint Elizabeth Ann Seton Sacred Icon

name: Saint Syncletica of Alexandria
title: Venerable Mother Syncletica of Alexandria, Desert Amma
curatedBio: Born in Alexandria to wealthy Macedonian parents, Syncletica was renowned for beauty and piety. Rejecting marriage proposals, she distributed her entire inheritance to the poor following her parents’ death. With her blind sister, she moved into a family tomb outside Alexandria, cutting her hair and adopting solitary asceticism. As spiritual seekers flocked to her retreat, she became one of the foremost Desert Mothers, dispensing wisdom preserved in the Apophthegmata Patrum on interior warfare, humility, and contemplative prayer.
deathSummary: After enduring a painful and protracted illness with heroic patience, Mother Syncletica reposed peacefully around 350 at the age of eighty-four.

image.title: Saint Syncletica of Alexandria Sacred Icon

name: Blessed Gertrude van der Oosten
title: Blessed Gertrude van der Oosten, Mystic of Delft
curatedBio: Gertrude was born into a peasant family in Voorgors near Delft. Entering domestic service, she maintained rigorous prayer and contemplative recollection amidst demanding manual labor. Abandoned by her fiancé, she interpreted this trial as a divine calling to devote herself entirely to Christ. She entered the Beguinage at Delft, spending her life in contemplation, writing devotional vernacular hymns, and mystical absorption in the Passion of Christ, eventually bearing the holy stigmata.
deathSummary: Blessed Gertrude reposed peacefully in the Lord on the feast of Epiphany, January 6, 1358 at Delft.

image.title: Blessed Gertrude van der Oosten Sacred Icon

name: Saint Maria Theresia Haze
title: Blessed Maria Theresia Haze, Servant of the Poor
curatedBio: Born in Liège, Belgium in 1782, Maria Theresia experienced hardship during the French Revolution when her family was exiled and stripped of property. Together with her sister, she opened a free school for impoverished young girls in 1824. Recognizing the severe destitution of post-revolutionary society, she founded the Daughters of the Cross in 1833, dedicating her institute to teaching poor children, nursing prisoners and soldiers, and caring for the chronically destitute.
deathSummary: Mother Maria Theresia died peacefully in Liège on January 7, 1876 at the age of ninety-three.

image.title: Saint Maria Theresia Haze Sacred Icon

name: Saint Gudula of Brussels
title: Saint Gudula, Virgin and Patroness of Brussels
curatedBio: Born in Brabant into a prominent Frankish noble family, Gudula was the daughter of Count Witger and Saint Amalberga. Educated at Nivelles Abbey under her cousin Saint Gertrude of Nivelles, she chose to live an ascetic life at her family estate in Moorsel. She spent early mornings walking two miles through darkness to Saint Savior’s Church in Moorsel for prayers. Her emblem, a lantern that rekindled through her prayers whenever snuffed by demons, became an enduring civic and sacred symbol.
deathSummary: Saint Gudula reposed peacefully between 680 and 714 and was buried at Hamme before translation to Brussels Cathedral.

image.title: Saint Gudula of Brussels Sacred Icon

name: Saint Marciana of Mauretania
title: Holy Virgin Martyr Marciana of Mauretania
curatedBio: Marciana was a Christian maiden of noble birth living in Dellys (Rusuccuru) in Roman Mauretania Caesariensis during the persecutions of Emperor Diocletian. Renouncing marriage and secular society, she lived in seclusion outside the city. Zealous for the worship of the one true God, she publicly shattered a statue of Diana in the city square. Arrested and refusing to sacrifice, she was subjected to cruel scourging and imprisoned, where she steadfastly confessed her Christian faith before the magistrate.
deathSummary: Saint Marciana was condemned to the amphitheater in Caesarea of Mauretania, where she was killed by a wild bull and leopard around 303.

image.title: Saint Marciana of Mauretania Sacred Icon

name: Saint Léonie Aviat
title: Saint Léonie Aviat, Co-Foundress of the Oblates of St. Francis de Sales
curatedBio: Léonie Aviat was born in Sézanne, France in 1844 and educated at the Visitation Convent in Troyes. Touched by the harsh exploitation of young women working in textile factories during the industrial revolution, she joined Father Louis Brisson to establish patronages and safe boarding houses for factory workers. In 1868 she co-founded the Oblate Sisters of Saint Francis de Sales, dedicating her community to Christian education, sheltering young laborers, and living Salesian meekness.
deathSummary: Saint Léonie died of bronchopneumonia in Perugia, Italy on January 10, 1914 at the age of sixty-nine.

image.title: Saint Léonie Aviat Sacred Icon

name: Saint Theodosia of Constantinople
title: Holy Virgin Nun Martyr Theodosia of Constantinople
curatedBio: Theodosia was born in Constantinople to pious parents and entered a monastery after distributing her inheritance. In 726, when Emperor Leo the Isaurian decreed the destruction of holy icons, an imperial officer climbed a ladder to smash the celebrated icon of Christ above the Chalke Gate of the imperial palace. Theodosia and a group of women shook the ladder, causing the officer to fall to his death. Arrested by imperial guards, she refused to renounce icon veneration.
deathSummary: She was dragged through the Forum of the Bull where an executioner drove a ram’s horn through her throat around 729.

image.title: Saint Theodosia of Constantinople Sacred Icon

name: Saint Tatiana of Rome
title: Holy Great Martyr Tatiana of Rome, Deaconess
curatedBio: Tatiana was born in Rome to a distinguished Christian consul and became a deaconess of the Roman Church, devoting herself to chastity and assisting the poor and sick. During the reign of Emperor Alexander Severus, she was arrested and brought to the temple of Apollo to sacrifice. Her fervent prayers caused an earthquake that shattered the pagan idol. Subjected to scourging, blinding, and burning coals, angels healed her wounds overnight, defying her persecutors.
deathSummary: Unable to break her confession or harm her with lions in the arena, her persecutors beheaded Tatiana and her father around 226.

image.title: Saint Tatiana of Rome Sacred Icon

name: Saint Veronica of Binasco
title: Blessed Veronica of Binasco, Augustinian Nun and Mystic
curatedBio: Born to humble peasant farmers in Binasco near Milan, Veronica worked in the fields while nurturing an intense longing for religious life. Illiterate, she struggled to learn reading so she could enter a convent. In a vision, the Virgin Mary revealed three spiritual letters: purity of intention, patience without grumbling, and daily meditation on Christ’s Passion. She entered the Augustinian convent of Saint Martha in Milan, living thirty years of mystical prayer and ecstatic contemplation.
deathSummary: Blessed Veronica reposed peacefully at Saint Martha’s convent on January 13, 1497 at the age of fifty-two.

image.title: Saint Veronica of Binasco Sacred Icon

name: Saint Nino of Georgia
title: Saint Nino, Equal-to-the-Apostles, Enlightener of Georgia
curatedBio: Nino was a Cappadocian maiden and relative of Saint George. According to tradition, the Theotokos appeared to her in a dream, entrusting her with a cross fashioned from grapevine branches and sending her to preach the Gospel in Iberia (modern Georgia). Arriving in Mtskheta around 320, Nino healed the sick and preached Christ with miraculous power. She healed Queen Nana and later converted King Mirian III, resulting in Christianity becoming the official religion of Georgia.
deathSummary: Saint Nino reposed peacefully in her hermitage at Bodbe around 335 and was buried where the Bodbe Monastery stands today.

image.title: Saint Nino of Georgia Sacred Icon

name: Saint Ita of Killeedy
title: Saint Ita of Killeedy, Foster-Mother of the Saints of Erin
curatedBio: Born into the noble Déisi of County Waterford around 475, Ita refused wealthy marriage suitors, persuading her father to permit her dedication to Christ. Migrating to County Limerick, she established a convent at the foot of Luachra mountain in Killeedy. She founded a school for young boys, fostering renowned saints including Saint Brendan the Navigator. Known for profound charity, ascetic fasting, and gift of prophecy, she was venerated across Ireland as the second Saint Brigid.
deathSummary: Saint Ita reposed peacefully at her monastery in Killeedy on January 15, 570 at approximately ninety-five years of age.

image.title: Saint Ita of Killeedy Sacred Icon

name: Saint Priscilla of Rome
title: Saint Priscilla of Rome, Matron of the Catacombs
curatedBio: Priscilla was a noble Roman Christian matron of the senatorial Acilian gens, wife of consul Manius Acilius Glabrio, who was martyred under Domitian. A devoted disciple of the Apostles in Rome, she offered her estate on the Via Salaria as a burial refuge for persecuted Christians. This underground cemetery became the Catacombs of Priscilla, renowned as the Queen of Catacombs, preserving the earliest surviving frescoes of the Virgin Mary and the Good Shepherd.
deathSummary: She died peacefully in Rome toward the end of the first century after dedicating her wealth to sheltering Christian martyrs and faithful.

image.title: Saint Priscilla of Rome Sacred Icon

name: Saint Roseline of Villeneuve
title: Saint Roseline of Villeneuve, Carthusian Prioress and Mystic
curatedBio: Born into the aristocratic Villeneuve family at Les Arcs in Provence in 1263, Roseline secretly distributed food to the poor against her father’s wishes, leading to the Miracle of the Roses when her apron filled with blossoms. Refusing prestigious marriage, she entered the Carthusian Order at Bertaud and later became prioress of the Charterhouse of Celle-Roubaud. She lived an austere contemplative life marked by visionary prayer, severe mortification, and extraordinary spiritual counsel.
deathSummary: Saint Roseline died peacefully in her monastery at Celle-Roubaud on January 17, 1329 at sixty-five years of age.

image.title: Saint Roseline of Villeneuve Sacred Icon

name: Saint Prisca of Rome
title: Holy Virgin Martyr Prisca of Rome
curatedBio: According to Roman hagiography, Prisca was a noble thirteen-year-old maiden living in Rome during the persecutions of Emperor Claudius II. Arrested for refusing to sacrifice to Apollo, she confessed Christ with intrepid boldness. Thrown into the arena, lions sent to devour her knelt peacefully at her feet and licked her soles. Kept without food in prison and subjected to the rack, she persevered in prayer until taken along the Ostian Way for final execution.
deathSummary: Saint Prisca was beheaded along the Via Ostiensis around 269, and her body was translated to the church of Santa Prisca on the Aventine Hill.

image.title: Saint Prisca of Rome Sacred Icon

name: Saint Macrina the Elder
title: Saint Macrina the Elder, Confessor of Neocaesarea
curatedBio: Macrina the Elder was born in Pontus and instructed in the Christian faith by Saint Gregory Thaumaturgus. During the severe persecutions of Galerius and Maximinus Daia, she and her husband fled into the forested mountains of Pontus, hiding for seven years in poverty and danger while confessing their allegiance to Christ. Returning after the persecutions, she nurtured her grandchildren, including Basil the Great and Gregory of Nyssa, imparting to them orthodox doctrine and ascetic piety.
deathSummary: Saint Macrina reposed peacefully around 340, praised by Gregory of Nazianzus as the steadfast root of Cappadocia’s saints.

image.title: Saint Macrina the Elder Sacred Icon

name: Saint Maria Cristina of the Immaculate Conception
title: Saint Maria Cristina Brando, Founder of the Victim Expiators of the Eucharist
curatedBio: Adelaide Brando was born in Naples in 1856 into a devout wealthy family. In childhood, she felt a burning devotion to the Eucharistic mystery and made a vow of perpetual virginity. Overcoming persistent frail health and family opposition, she founded the Congregation of the Victim Expiators of the Immaculate Conception in 1884. Her sisters united night-and-day perpetual Eucharistic adoration with dedicated service running orphanages, nursery schools, and trade workshops for impoverished Neapolitan children.
deathSummary: Mother Maria Cristina died peacefully in Casoria, Italy on January 20, 1906 at forty-nine years of age.

image.title: Saint Maria Cristina of the Immaculate Conception Sacred Icon

name: Saint Agnes of Rome
title: Holy Virgin Martyr Agnes of Rome
curatedBio: Agnes was a twelve-year-old Roman maiden from a noble patrician family who consecrated her purity to Christ. When the prefect’s son sought her in marriage, she replied that she was already betrothed to an invisible Heavenly Bridegroom. Enraged, the prefect ordered her dragged naked to a brothel, but angels covered her in radiant light and miraculous hair. Miraculously untouched by flames when condemned to a pyre, she knelt and offered her neck to the executioner’s sword.
deathSummary: Saint Agnes was martyred in Rome around 304 under Diocletian and buried on the Via Nomentana, where the basilica of Sant’Agnese stands.

image.title: Saint Agnes of Rome Sacred Icon

name: Saint Irene of Rome
title: Saint Irene of Rome, Matron and Caregiver of Martyrs
curatedBio: Irene was the pious Christian widow of Saint Castulus, an imperial officer martyred under Diocletian. When Saint Sebastian was tied to a stake on the Palatine Hill, shot with arrows, and left for dead by Roman archers, Irene went in the dead of night to retrieve his corpse for Christian burial. Discovering he was still breathing, she carried him to her home and nursed his severe wounds back to health with unwavering courage and maternal devotion.
deathSummary: Saint Irene reposed peacefully in Rome around 288 after surviving persecution and sheltering underground Christian confessors.

image.title: Saint Irene of Rome Sacred Icon

name: Saint Marianne Cope
title: Saint Marianne of Molokai, Sister of Saint Francis
curatedBio: Born in Germany and raised in Utica, New York, Marianne Cope entered the Sisters of Saint Francis in Syracuse, becoming provincial superior and establishing prominent hospitals. In 1883, responding to a plea from the Kingdom of Hawaii where dozens of religious congregations had refused, Mother Marianne and six sisters traveled to Oahu to care for patients suffering from leprosy. She moved to the remote settlement of Kalaupapa on Molokai, continuing the heroic mission of Saint Damien de Veuster.
deathSummary: Mother Marianne died peacefully of natural causes at Kalaupapa on August 9, 1918 at eighty years of age, having never contracted the disease.

image.title: Saint Marianne Cope Sacred Icon

name: Saint Xenia of Saint Petersburg
title: Blessed Xenia of Saint Petersburg, Fool-for-Christ
curatedBio: Xenia Grigoryevna Petrova was the wife of an imperial army colonel who died suddenly without sacramental preparation. Heartbroken, twenty-six-year-old Xenia gave away her house and estate to the poor and adopted her late husband’s military uniform, taking up the extreme ascetic feat of foolishness for Christ’s sake. For forty-five years she wandered the streets of Saint Petersburg in rags, secretly carrying heavy bricks at night to build the Church of the Smolensk Icon of the Mother of God.
deathSummary: Blessed Xenia reposed peacefully around 1803 at seventy-one years of age, and her chapel in Smolensk Cemetery became a fountain of healings.

image.title: Saint Xenia of Saint Petersburg Sacred Icon

name: Saint Paula of Rome
title: Saint Paula of Rome, Desert Mother and Disciple of Jerome
curatedBio: Paula was born into one of the wealthiest senatorial patrician families of Rome. Following the death of her husband Toxotius, she embraced radical evangelical poverty under the guidance of Saint Marcella and Saint Jerome. Giving away her vast estates in Italy, she traveled on pilgrimage through Egypt and the Holy Land with her daughter Eustochium. Settling in Bethlehem, she founded a monastery and double convent, financing Saint Jerome’s Latin translation of the Bible (the Vulgate).
deathSummary: Saint Paula reposed peacefully in Bethlehem on January 26, 404 at fifty-six years of age and was buried beneath the Church of the Nativity.

image.title: Saint Paula of Rome Sacred Icon

name: Saint Maria, Wife of Saint Xenophon
title: Venerable Maria, Matron and Ascetic of Jerusalem
curatedBio: Maria was a wealthy fifth-century noblewoman of Constantinople and wife of the imperial senator Saint Xenophon. Devoted to Christian piety, they sent their two sons, Arcadius and John, to study law in Beirut. When a tempest wrecked the sons’ ship, Maria and Xenophon believed their children had drowned. Trusting God, they gave away their vast fortune and set out for the Holy Land, where they miraculously discovered both sons living as monks in different Palestinian monasteries.
deathSummary: After living out her final decades in contemplative monastic seclusion near Jerusalem, Saint Maria reposed peacefully in Christ.

image.title: Saint Maria, Wife of Saint Xenophon Sacred Icon

name: Saint Angela Merici
title: Saint Angela Merici, Foundress of the Company of Saint Ursula
curatedBio: Born in Desenzano on Lake Garda in 1474, Angela joined the Third Order of Saint Francis as a young girl. Distressed by the lack of religious instruction for impoverished girls, she gathered companions to teach catechism in their homes. In 1535 at Brescia, she founded the Company of Saint Ursula (the Ursulines), the first secular institute of women dedicated to the education of young women outside cloistered enclosure, revolutionizing female education throughout Europe.
deathSummary: Saint Angela died peacefully in Brescia on January 27, 1540 at sixty-five years of age.

image.title: Saint Angela Merici Sacred Icon

name: Saint Margaret of Hungary
title: Saint Margaret of Hungary, Royal Dominican Ascetic
curatedBio: Daughter of King Béla IV of Hungary and Byzantine princess Maria Laskarina, Margaret was vowed to God before birth for Hungary’s deliverance from the Mongol invasion. Entrusted to the Dominican nuns at Veszprém at age three, she later took solemn vows at the convent on the Island of Hares (Margaret Island) near Buda. Refusing royal marriages arranged by her father, she embraced the humblest monastery duties, severe penance, and unceasing prayer for peace in Hungary.
deathSummary: Exhausted by intense mortification and illness, Saint Margaret reposed on January 18, 1270 at twenty-seven years of age.

image.title: Saint Margaret of Hungary Sacred Icon

name: Saint Bathild
title: Saint Bathild, Queen of the Franks and Liberator of Slaves
curatedBio: Bathild was an Anglo-Saxon noble girl abducted by pirates and sold into slavery in Frankish Gaul. Her wisdom and piety caught the attention of King Clovis II, who married her in 649. As Queen of the Franks and later regent for her son Chlothar III, Bathild outlawed the enslavement of Christians, ransomed innumerable slaves with royal funds, prohibited child sales, and endowed monasteries at Corbie and Chelles, where she eventually retired as a humble nun.
deathSummary: Queen Bathild died peacefully at Chelles Abbey on January 30, 680 following a painful illness borne with serene prayer.

image.title: Saint Bathild Sacred Icon

name: Saint Martina of Rome
title: Holy Virgin Martyr Martina of Rome
curatedBio: Martina was the daughter of a Roman consul who was left an orphan with immense wealth. Distributing her property among poor Christians, she consecrated her virginity to Jesus Christ. Under Emperor Alexander Severus, she was arrested for refusing to worship idols. Led to the temple of Apollo, her prayers caused the statue and part of the temple to collapse. Surviving torture with iron hooks, immersion in boiling grease, and exposure to beasts, she prayed unceasingly.
deathSummary: After her torturers failed to bend her Christian faith, Saint Martina was decapitated outside Rome around 228.

image.title: Saint Martina of Rome Sacred Icon

name: Saint Marcella of Rome
title: Saint Marcella of Rome, Desert Mother of the Aventine
curatedBio: Born into the wealthy Roman senatorial family of the Marcelli, Marcella lost her husband after seven months of marriage and turned her luxurious palace on the Aventine Hill into a monastic community. Under the spiritual instruction of Saint Jerome, she mastered Hebrew and Greek scriptures, resolving complex biblical inquiries. When Alaric the Visigoth sacked Rome in 410, soldiers entered her palace demanding gold; having given everything to the poor, she was severely scourged while shielding her student Principia.
mannerOfDeath: Beaten during the Sack of Rome
deathSummary: Saint Marcella died in the arms of Principia in late August 410 from wounds sustained during the Visigoth Sack of Rome.

image.title: Saint Marcella of Rome Sacred Icon

name: Saint Brigid of Kildare
title: Saint Brigid of Kildare, Equal-to-the-Apostles and Patroness of Ireland
curatedBio: Brigid was born in Faughart around 451, the daughter of a pagan chieftain and a Christian slave mother. Renowned for boundless charity, she gave away food, clothing, and household goods to the indigent. Consecrated as a virgin by Saint Mel, she founded the double monastery of Kildare, a great spiritual center combining communities of men and women under her abbatial jurisdiction. Venerated as the Mary of the Gael, she is honored alongside Patrick and Columba as patron of Ireland.
deathSummary: Saint Brigid reposed peacefully at Kildare Abbey around 525 at seventy-four years of age.

image.title: Saint Brigid of Kildare Sacred Icon

name: Saint Catherine de' Ricci
title: Saint Catherine de' Ricci, Dominican Mystic and Stigmatist
curatedBio: Born in Florence in 1522 into the patrician Ricci family, Catherine entered the Dominican convent of Saint Vincent in Prato at age thirteen. She experienced profound mystical ecstasies and sustained weekly visions of the Passion of Christ, during which she bore the sacred stigmata. A gifted administrator and spiritual counselor, she was appointed prioress at age twenty-five, corresponding extensively with Saint Philip Neri, Saint Charles Borromeo, and prominent Catholic figures throughout Europe.
deathSummary: Saint Catherine reposed peacefully at Prato on February 2, 1590 after a protracted illness borne with holy patience.

image.title: Saint Catherine de' Ricci Sacred Icon

name: Saint Ia of Cornwall
title: Holy Virgin Martyr Ia of Cornwall, Missionary to the Celts
curatedBio: Ia was an Irish noble maiden and sister of Saint Erc who resolved to accompany Saint Fingar and his missionaries to Cornwall. According to legend, when the ship departed without her, she knelt in prayer on the shore and crossed the Celtic Sea upon a large floating leaf of ivy, landing at Hayle in Cornwall ahead of the expedition. Preaching the Christian faith, she converted local Britons and built a hermitage around which the town of St Ives developed.
deathSummary: Saint Ia was beheaded near the Hayle River around 450 under the pagan Cornish ruler Tewdwr Mawr.

image.title: Saint Ia of Cornwall Sacred Icon

name: Saint Joan of France
title: Saint Joan of Valois, Duchess of Berry and Founder of the Annonciades
curatedBio: Daughter of King Louis XI of France, Joan endured physical deformities and harsh rejection from her father. Married for political reasons to the Duke of Orléans, she was repudiated when he ascended the throne as King Louis XII. Retiring to Bourges, she dedicated her royal revenues to charity and founded the monastic Order of the Annunciation of the Blessed Virgin Mary (the Annonciades), whose rule centered on imitating the virtues of Mary recounted in the Gospel.
deathSummary: Saint Joan died peacefully at Bourges on February 4, 1505 at forty years of age.

image.title: Saint Joan of France Sacred Icon

name: Saint Agatha of Sicily
title: Holy Virgin Martyr Agatha of Sicily
curatedBio: Agatha was a noble maiden of Catania, Sicily who dedicated her virginity to Jesus Christ. During the Decian persecution, Roman prefect Quintianus sought her in marriage and, upon her refusal, sent her to a brothel to break her resolve. Remaining steadfast in prayer, she was subjected to cruel torture, including the shearing of her breasts. Consoled in prison by a heavenly vision of Saint Peter who healed her wounds, she persevered in prayer until her final trial.
deathSummary: Saint Agatha was rolled across burning coals mixed with potsherds and martyred at Catania around 251.

image.title: Saint Agatha of Sicily Sacred Icon

name: Saint Dorothy of Caesarea
title: Holy Virgin Martyr Dorothy of Caesarea
curatedBio: Dorothy was a Christian maiden of Caesarea in Cappadocia renowned for wisdom and chastity. Arrested under governor Sapricius during the Diocletian persecution, she refused sacrifice to pagan idols and converted two apostate women sent to dissuade her. As she was led to execution, a skeptical lawyer named Theophilus mocked her Heavenly Bridegroom, asking for fruits from Christ's garden. A miraculous angel child appeared bearing fresh apples and fragrant roses in midwinter, prompting Theophilus's immediate conversion and martyrdom.
deathSummary: Saint Dorothy was beheaded at Caesarea in Cappadocia around 311 after witnessing to Christ.

image.title: Saint Dorothy of Caesarea Sacred Icon

name: Saint Colette of Corbie
title: Saint Colette of Corbie, Reformer of the Poor Clares
curatedBio: Born in Corbie, Picardy in 1381, Colette lived as a solitary recluse walled into a cell near the abbey church for four years. Directed by a vision of Saint Francis of Assisi, she emerged to undertake a comprehensive renewal of the Second Franciscan Order. She established the Colettine Poor Clares, restoring the original radical poverty, barefoot austerity, and unceasing contemplative prayer instituted by Saint Clare, founding seventeen reformed monasteries throughout France, Flanders, and Savoy.
deathSummary: Saint Colette reposed peacefully at her convent in Ghent on March 6, 1447 at sixty-six years of age.

image.title: Saint Colette of Corbie Sacred Icon

name: Saint Josephine Bakhita
title: Saint Josephine Bakhita, Patroness of Human Trafficking Survivors
curatedBio: Born in Darfur, Sudan around 1869, Bakhita was kidnapped by Arab slave traders at age seven, sold five times, and subjected to brutal physical torture and ritual scarring. Brought to Italy by an Italian consular official, she was placed under the custody of the Canossian Sisters in Venice. Winning her legal freedom in an Italian court in 1889, she received baptism taking the name Josephine. She spent fifty years in Schio as a Canossian sister, radiating forgiveness, joy, and humility.
deathSummary: Saint Josephine died peacefully in Schio, Italy on February 8, 1947 after whispering: "Our Lady! Our Lady!"

image.title: Saint Josephine Bakhita Sacred Icon

name: Saint Apollonia of Alexandria
title: Holy Virgin Martyr Apollonia of Alexandria, Patroness of Dentists
curatedBio: Apollonia was an elderly deaconess of the church in Alexandria during a ferocious local pogrom against Christians in 249 described by Bishop Dionysius. A violent mob dragged her through the city, struck her jaws, and violently extracted all her teeth. Threatening to burn her alive in a pyre outside the gates unless she repeated blasphemies, she asked for a moment of freedom, then willingly leapt into the flames to preserve her chaste fidelity to Christ.
deathSummary: Saint Apollonia died a martyr in Alexandria in 249, celebrated for heroic courage in defense of her faith.

image.title: Saint Apollonia of Alexandria Sacred Icon

name: Saint Scholastica
title: Saint Scholastica, Virgin and Twin Sister of Saint Benedict
curatedBio: Scholastica was born in Norcia around 480 into a noble family, the twin sister of Saint Benedict of Nursia. Consecrating herself to God from her youth, she founded a monastery of nuns at Plombariola, five miles south of Monte Cassino. Once a year the siblings met at a farmhouse between their monasteries for prayer and spiritual discourse. According to Saint Gregory the Great, when Benedict prepared to leave during their final meeting, Scholastica’s fervent prayers caused a torrential storm, enabling them to converse all night.
deathSummary: Three days after their final meeting, Saint Scholastica died in her cell around 543, her soul seen by Benedict ascending as a white dove.

image.title: Saint Scholastica Sacred Icon

name: Saint Theodora the Empress
title: Righteous Empress Theodora, Restorer of Holy Icons
curatedBio: Theodora was born in Paphlagonia and married Byzantine Emperor Theophilus, a staunch iconoclast. Throughout her marriage, she secretly venerated icons in her private quarters. Following her husband’s death in 842, serving as regent for her young son Michael III, Theodora summoned the Synod of Constantinople in 843, overthrowing iconoclasm and restoring holy icons to all churches. This triumph of Orthodoxy established the Feast of the Triumph of Orthodoxy, celebrated on the First Sunday of Great Lent.
deathSummary: Saint Theodora retired to the monastery of Gastria where she reposed peacefully in 867; her incorrupt relics lie in Corfu.

image.title: Saint Theodora the Empress Sacred Icon

name: Saint Eulalia of Barcelona
title: Holy Virgin Martyr Eulalia of Barcelona
curatedBio: Eulalia was a thirteen-year-old Christian maiden from Sarrià near Barcelona during the persecutions of Emperor Diocletian. Defying her parents' sheltering, she slipped away into Barcelona and confronted the Roman governor Dacian over the torture of Christians. Stripped and subjected to thirteen distinct tortures corresponding to her years, including scourging, hot irons, and immersion in a flea pit, she persevered in praise. As she breathed her last upon an X-shaped cross, a white dove flew from her lips.
deathSummary: Saint Eulalia was crucified on an X-shaped cross and exposed to death in Barcelona around 304; her tomb is in Barcelona Cathedral.

image.title: Saint Eulalia of Barcelona Sacred Icon

name: Blessed Christina of Spoleto
title: Blessed Christina of Spoleto, Augustinian Penitent
curatedBio: Agostina Camozzi was born in Lake Como in 1435 into a respected family. Following turbulent youthful marriages and grief over the early death of her child, she embraced a profound spiritual conversion. Donning the coarse habit of an Augustinian tertiary, she took the name Christina. Moving to Spoleto, she dedicated the remainder of her life to austere penance, unremitting contemplation of the Crucified Christ, and continuous service to the sick and impoverished in hospitals.
deathSummary: Blessed Christina died peacefully at Spoleto on February 13, 1458 at only twenty-two years of age.

image.title: Blessed Christina of Spoleto Sacred Icon

name: Saint Agostina Livia Pietrantoni
title: Saint Agostina Pietrantoni, Sister of Charity and Martyr of Care
curatedBio: Born in Pozzaglia Sabina, Italy in 1864, Livia entered the Sisters of Charity of Saint Joan Antida Thouret in Rome, taking the religious name Agostina. Assigned to the tuberculosis ward of the Holy Spirit Hospital in Rome—a notoriously hostile, anti-clerical environment—she served violent and infectious patients with heroic meekness and supernatural charity. Despite repeated death threats from an unruly patient whom she nursed, Sister Agostina refused to abandon her hospital duties.
deathSummary: Sister Agostina was stabbed to death on November 13, 1894 by an aggressive patient whom she forgave with her dying breath.

image.title: Saint Agostina Livia Pietrantoni Sacred Icon

name: Saint Georgia of Clermont
title: Saint Georgia of Clermont, Solitary Virgin of Auvergne
curatedBio: Georgia lived as a consecrated virgin and solitary hermit in the countryside near Clermont in Gaul during the late fifth century. Refusing marriage proposals, she withdrew from secular society to spend her life in prayer, fasting, and contemplation. Recorded by Saint Gregory of Tours in his hagiography, when her funeral procession passed from the village to the church, a miraculous flock of white doves descended from the heavens, hovering protectively above her bier until she was laid to rest.
deathSummary: Saint Georgia reposed peacefully around 500 near Clermont-Ferrand in the Auvergne.

image.title: Saint Georgia of Clermont Sacred Icon

name: Saint Juliana of Nicomedia
title: Holy Virgin Martyr Juliana of Nicomedia
curatedBio: Juliana was the daughter of a pagan nobleman in Nicomedia who betrothed her to Roman senator Eleusius. Juliana announced she would only wed him if he became prefect and accepted baptism in Christ. When Eleusius became prefect, she refused to recant her faith. Her father delivered her to judicial torture, where she was scourged, hung by her hair, and thrown into a furnace without harm. Defeating demonic tempters in her cell, she converted hundreds of witnesses before execution.
deathSummary: Saint Juliana was beheaded in Nicomedia around 304 under Emperor Maximian; her relics were later brought to Cumae and Naples.

image.title: Saint Juliana of Nicomedia Sacred Icon

name: Saint Mariamne
title: Saint Mariamne, Equal-to-the-Apostles, Sister of the Apostle Philip
curatedBio: Mariamne was the sister of the holy Apostle Philip. Following Christ's Ascension, she joined Philip and Saint Bartholomew in apostolic missionary journeys through Asia Minor and Greece, preaching the Gospel and enduring severe persecutions. At Hierapolis in Phrygia, when Philip was crucified upside down, Mariamne was stripped and thrown into prison. After Philip gave up his spirit, she and Bartholomew were released due to an earthquake. She continued evangelizing Lycaonia, baptizing multitudes and founding Christian assemblies.
deathSummary: Saint Mariamne reposed peacefully in Lycaonia after many years of apostolic preaching throughout Asia Minor.

image.title: Saint Mariamne Sacred Icon

name: Saint Bernadette Soubirous
title: Saint Bernadette Soubirous, Visionary of Our Lady of Lourdes
curatedBio: Born into poverty in Lourdes, France in 1844, Bernadette was an uneducated, asthmatic fourteen-year-old girl gathering firewood at the Massabielle grotto when the Virgin Mary appeared to her eighteen times in 1858, identifying herself as the Immaculate Conception. The apparitions uncovered a miraculous healing spring that became Christendom's foremost pilgrimage site. Fleeing public adoration, Bernadette entered the Sisters of Charity of Nevers in 1866, embracing hidden suffering, prayer, and infirmary nursing.
deathSummary: Saint Bernadette died of bone tuberculosis in Nevers on April 16, 1879 at thirty-five; her body remains incorrupt.

image.title: Saint Bernadette Soubirous Sacred Icon

name: Saint Philothea of Athens
title: Holy Venerable Nun Martyr Philothea of Athens
curatedBio: Revoula Benizelos was born in Athens in 1522 into a wealthy noble family during Ottoman rule. Following the death of her abusive husband, she took monastic vows as Philothea and converted her ancestral palace into a convent dedicated to Saint Andrew. She established schools for young Greek women, hospitals, and safe shelters for Christian women escaping Ottoman slavery. Her humanitarian bravery provoked Ottoman authorities, who repeatedly raided her monastic institutions.
deathSummary: Ottoman soldiers stormed her chapel during an all-night vigil, brutally beating her; she reposed from her wounds on February 19, 1589.

image.title: Saint Philothea of Athens Sacred Icon

name: Saint Jacinta Marto
title: Saint Jacinta Marto, Child Visionary of Fátima
curatedBio: Born in Aljustrel, Portugal in 1910, Jacinta was a seven-year-old shepherd girl who, alongside her brother Francisco and cousin Lúcia, witnessed six apparitions of the Virgin Mary at the Cova da Iria in 1917. Deeply affected by visions of purgatory and the suffering of sinners, Jacinta practiced heroically mature penance, offering daily sacrifices, giving her lunch to poor children, and praying the Rosary incessantly for peace and the conversion of Russia.
deathSummary: Jacinta died of pleurisy following the Spanish flu epidemic in Lisbon on February 20, 1920 at nine years of age.

image.title: Saint Jacinta Marto Sacred Icon

name: Blessed Maria Enrichetta Dominici
title: Blessed Maria Enrichetta Dominici, Servant of the Sisters of Saint Anne
curatedBio: Caterina Dominici was born in Carmagnola near Turin in 1829 into a farming family. Entering the Sisters of Saint Anne and Providence in Turin in 1850, she took the name Maria Enrichetta. Elected Superior General at age thirty-two, she governed the congregation for thirty-three years with profound wisdom, expanding its educational and charitable institutes across Italy and sending the first sisters to open missions in Secunderabad, India.
deathSummary: Blessed Maria Enrichetta died peacefully in Turin on February 21, 1894 at sixty-four years of age.

image.title: Blessed Maria Enrichetta Dominici Sacred Icon

name: Saint Margaret of Cortona
title: Saint Margaret of Cortona, Franciscan Penitent
curatedBio: Born in Laviano, Tuscany in 1247, Margaret spent nine years as the mistress of a young nobleman in Montepulciano. When her lover was murdered, she was led to his corpse by his hound, inspiring total repentance. Publicly seeking forgiveness in Cortona, she entered the Third Order of Saint Francis, living in extreme ascetic poverty and dedicating her days to nursing the sick. She founded a hospital at Cortona and a congregation of tertiary sisters known as the Poverelle.
deathSummary: Saint Margaret died peacefully at Cortona on February 22, 1297 at fifty years of age; her body remains incorrupt.

image.title: Saint Margaret of Cortona Sacred Icon

name: Saint Milburga of Wenlock
title: Saint Milburga, Anglo-Saxon Abbess of Wenlock
curatedBio: Milburga was the daughter of King Merewalh of the Magonsæte and Saint Ermenburga, sister of Saint Mildred of Minster. Choosing religious virginity, she founded a double monastery at Much Wenlock in Shropshire around 680, serving as its first abbess. Celebrated for miraculous gifts, including power over wild birds that damaged crops and healing the blind, she ruled her abbey with maternal love and monastic discipline, making Wenlock a center of early English monastic learning.
deathSummary: Saint Milburga reposed peacefully at Much Wenlock on February 23, 722 after receiving the Holy Mysteries.

image.title: Saint Milburga of Wenlock Sacred Icon

name: Saint Bertha of Kent
title: Saint Bertha of Kent, Christian Queen of the Anglo-Saxons
curatedBio: Bertha was a Christian Merovingian Frankish princess, daughter of King Charibert I of Paris. When she married the pagan King Æthelberht of Kent, she brought with her the Frankish bishop Liudhard to maintain Christian worship at Saint Martin’s Church in Canterbury. Her exemplary piety, virtue, and gentle influence paved the way for King Æthelberht to welcome Saint Augustine of Canterbury’s Gregorian mission in 597, leading directly to the Christianization of the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms.
deathSummary: Queen Bertha reposed peacefully in Canterbury around 606 and was entombed in the abbey church of Saint Peter and Saint Paul.

image.title: Saint Bertha of Kent Sacred Icon

name: Saint Walpurga of Heidenheim
title: Saint Walpurga, Anglo-Saxon Missionary and Abbess in Germania
curatedBio: Born in Wessex around 710, Walpurga was the daughter of Saint Richard the Pilgrim and sister of Saints Willibald and Winibald. Educated at Wimborne Abbey under Saint Tetta, she accompanied Saint Lioba on the missionary expedition to Germania summoned by Saint Boniface. Following her brother Winibald’s death in 761, Walpurga became abbess of the double monastery of Heidenheim in Bavaria. A miraculous medicinal oil known as Walburgisöl streamed from her relics at Eichstätt for centuries.
deathSummary: Saint Walpurga reposed peacefully at Heidenheim on February 25, 779 at sixty-eight years of age.

image.title: Saint Walpurga of Heidenheim Sacred Icon

name: Saint Paula Montal Fornés
title: Saint Paula Montal Fornés, Foundress of the Pious School Sisters
curatedBio: Born in Arenys de Mar near Barcelona in 1799, Paula recognized that the regeneration of civil and Christian society depended upon educating young girls, who were then excluded from schooling. In 1829 at Figueres, she opened a free academy for girls, founding the Daughters of Mary, Sisters of the Pious Schools (the Escolapias). Overcoming political revolutions and civil unrest in nineteenth-century Spain, she established seven schools, dedicating her religious institute to educating and spiritually forming young women.
deathSummary: Saint Paula died peacefully at Olesa de Montserrat on February 26, 1889 at eighty-nine years of age.

image.title: Saint Paula Montal Fornés Sacred Icon

name: Saint Anne Line
title: Holy Martyr Anne Line, Shelterer of Priests
curatedBio: Anne Higham was born in Essex into a strict Calvinist family but embraced the Catholic faith alongside her brother and husband, for which all three were disinherited. After her husband was exiled to Flanders where he died in poverty, Anne placed herself under the direction of Jesuit priest John Gerard, taking charge of a secret refuge house in London where underground priests were concealed, fed, and vested for Mass during the Elizabethan persecutions.
deathSummary: Arrested after Candlemas Mass in 1601, Saint Anne was condemned for harboring priests and hanged at Tyburn on February 27, 1601.

image.title: Saint Anne Line Sacred Icon

name: Saint Angela of Foligno
title: Saint Angela of Foligno, Mistress of Theologians and Franciscan Mystic
curatedBio: Born in Foligno, Umbria in 1248, Angela lived a worldly and comfortable life until a series of natural disasters and spiritual unrest moved her to seek confession in 1285. Following the premature death of her mother, husband, and sons, she sold all her possessions and entered the Third Order of Saint Francis. Dictating her mystical colloquies with the Holy Trinity and Passion of Christ to her confessor Brother Arnaldo, she was acclaimed as the "Mistress of Theologians".
deathSummary: Saint Angela reposed peacefully at Foligno on January 4, 1309 at sixty-one years of age; her feast is also celebrated on February 28.

image.title: Saint Angela of Foligno Sacred Icon

name: Saint Eudokia of Heliopolis
title: Holy Righteous Nun Martyr Eudokia of Heliopolis
curatedBio: Eudokia was a wealthy Samaritan courtesan living in Heliopolis (Baalbek), Phoenicia during the reign of Emperor Trajan. Hearing the monk Germanus read biblical prophecies concerning the Last Judgment, she was struck with deep compunction and received baptism from Bishop Theodote. Distributing her immense wealth to the poor and freeing her slaves, she entered a monastery near Baalbek, living thirty years of austere repentance, contemplation, and working miraculous healings.
deathSummary: Saint Eudokia was beheaded by order of the Roman governor Vincent around 126 after refusing to sacrifice to idols.

image.title: Saint Eudokia of Heliopolis Sacred Icon

name: Saint Agnes of Bohemia
title: Saint Agnes of Bohemia, Princess and Poor Clare Abbess
curatedBio: Agnes was the daughter of King Ottokar I of Bohemia. Refusing imperial marriage alliances arranged by European monarchs, including Holy Roman Emperor Frederick II, she devoted her life to Christ. In Prague in 1234, she built a hospital for the poor and a monastery of the Poor Clares, entering the cloister herself. She maintained a famous, affectionate spiritual correspondence with Saint Clare of Assisi, who addressed her as "half of her soul".
deathSummary: Saint Agnes died peacefully in Prague on March 2, 1282 at seventy years of age.

image.title: Saint Agnes of Bohemia Sacred Icon

name: Saint Katharine Drexel
title: Saint Katharine Drexel, Heiress and Foundress of Xavier University
curatedBio: Katharine Drexel was born in Philadelphia in 1858 into immense banking wealth. Deeply moved by the plight of Native Americans and African Americans facing racial oppression, she used her personal inheritance to establish missions and schools throughout the United States. In 1891 she founded the Sisters of the Blessed Sacrament, dedicating her life and fortune to establishing Xavier University of Louisiana—the first Catholic historically black university—and sixty missionary schools nationwide.
deathSummary: Mother Katharine died peacefully in Cornwells Heights, Pennsylvania on March 3, 1955 at ninety-six years of age.

image.title: Saint Katharine Drexel Sacred Icon

name: Blessed Placide Viel
title: Blessed Placide Viel, Superior of the Sisters of Christian Schools
curatedBio: Eulalie Viel was born in Quettehou, Normandy in 1815 into a humble peasant family. Entering the Sisters of the Christian Schools of Mercy under Saint Marie-Madeleine Postel, she took the religious name Placide. Appointed Superior General at age thirty, she governed the congregation for thirty-one years, navigating religious conflicts and the Franco-Prussian War while establishing dozens of charity schools, orphanages, and hospitals across France and England.
deathSummary: Blessed Placide died peacefully at Saint-Sauveur-le-Vicomte on March 4, 1877 at sixty-one years of age.

image.title: Blessed Placide Viel Sacred Icon

name: Saint Olivia of Brescia
title: Saint Olivia of Brescia, Holy Virgin Martyr
curatedBio: Olivia was a noble Christian virgin of Brescia in Lombardy during the reign of Emperor Hadrian. Known for her devout life of prayer and continuous assistance to underground Christians, she was arrested during imperial crackdowns. Confessing Christ with fearless resolve before pagan magistrates, she rejected all entreaties to sacrifice to Jupiter. Enduring scourging and imprisonment with joyful prayer, she gave up her spirit under the executioner's sword.
deathSummary: Saint Olivia was beheaded in Brescia around 138; her relics are venerated in the Church of Saint Afra.

image.title: Saint Olivia of Brescia Sacred Icon

name: Saint Rose of Viterbo
title: Saint Rose of Viterbo, Preacher and Franciscan Penitent
curatedBio: Born in Viterbo in 1233, Rose entered the Third Order of Saint Francis as a young girl. Gifted with fiery mystical eloquence, at age twelve she walked through the public streets of Viterbo bearing a crucifix, boldly preaching repentance and defending the Papacy against the forces of Holy Roman Emperor Frederick II. Exiled by imperial officials, she predicted the Emperor’s imminent death, which occurred precisely as foretold, allowing her triumphant return.
deathSummary: Saint Rose died peacefully at Viterbo on March 6, 1251 at only eighteen years of age; her body remains incorrupt.

image.title: Saint Rose of Viterbo Sacred Icon

name: Saints Perpetua and Felicity
title: Holy Martyrs Perpetua and Felicity of Carthage
curatedBio: Vivia Perpetua was a twenty-two-year-old Roman noblewoman nursing her infant son, and Felicity was an enslaved Christian woman who gave birth in prison. Arrested in Carthage under Emperor Septimius Severus for converting to Christianity, Perpetua recorded their imprisonment in an extraordinary firsthand prison diary. Stripped and exposed to a rabid heifer in the Roman amphitheater, the two women held hands and exchanged the kiss of peace before suffering execution with serenely triumphant faith.
deathSummary: Saints Perpetua and Felicity were martyred in the amphitheater at Carthage on March 7, 203.

image.title: Saints Perpetua and Felicity Sacred Icon

name: Saint Frances of Rome
title: Saint Frances of Rome, Matron and Foundress of the Olivetan Oblates
curatedBio: Frances was born in Rome in 1384 into an aristocratic family. Married to Lorenzo Ponziani, she lived forty years of exemplary marital fidelity while transforming her palace into a dispensary of food and medicine for victims of war and plague. Blessed with constant conscious vision of her Guardian Angel walking beside her, she established the Oblates of Saint Benedict at Tor de' Specchi, where noble Roman widows served the city's poorest outcasts.
deathSummary: Saint Frances died peacefully in Rome on March 9, 1440 at fifty-six; her feast is widely kept March 8 and 9.

image.title: Saint Frances of Rome Sacred Icon

name: Saint Catherine of Bologna
title: Saint Catherine of Bologna, Poor Clare Mystic and Sacred Artist
curatedBio: Catherine de' Vigri was born in Bologna in 1413 and educated as a court lady to the Princess of Ferrara. Renouncing courtly luxury, she entered the Poor Clares, serving as baker and infirmarian while excelling as a sacred painter, illuminator, and author of mystical treatises, including The Seven Spiritual Weapons. In 1456 she founded the monastery of Corpus Domini in Bologna, guiding her sisters with contemplative humility and supernatural wisdom.
deathSummary: Saint Catherine died peacefully in Bologna on March 9, 1463 at forty-nine; her uncorrupted body remains seated in her chapel.

image.title: Saint Catherine of Bologna Sacred Icon

name: Saint Anastasia the Patrician
title: Venerable Mother Anastasia the Patrician of Alexandria
curatedBio: Anastasia was a noble court lady of Constantinople and trusted confidante of Emperor Justinian I. When Empress Theodora grew jealous of her, Anastasia fled to Alexandria and founded a convent. Following Theodora’s death, Justinian sought her return, prompting her to disguise herself as a male monk named Anastasios under Saint Daniel of Scetis. She lived twenty-eight years in solitary confinement in a desert cave, praying unceasingly until Daniel revealed her true sanctity upon her deathbed.
deathSummary: Saint Anastasia reposed peacefully in the Scetis Desert around 576 after decades of solitary contemplation.

image.title: Saint Anastasia the Patrician Sacred Icon

name: Saint Theodora of Arta
title: Saint Theodora, Basilissa of Epirus and Monastic of Arta
curatedBio: Theodora Petraliphina was born into a prominent Byzantine noble family and married Michael II Komnenos Doukas, Despot of Epirus. Driven into exile in the Pindus mountains by her unfaithful husband, she endured five years of extreme poverty with her infant son. When Michael repented, she returned, reconciling the kingdom and founding the Monastery of Saint George in Arta. Following her husband's death, she took monastic vows, spending her remaining years in prayer and charity.
deathSummary: Saint Theodora reposed peacefully at Arta around 1280; her relics are enshrined in the Church of Saint Theodora in Arta.

image.title: Saint Theodora of Arta Sacred Icon

name: Saint Fina of San Gimignano
title: Saint Fina (Serafina), Virgin Ascetic of San Gimignano
curatedBio: Fina dei Ciardi was born in San Gimignano, Tuscany in 1238. Stricken in childhood with a debilitating paralytic illness that caused excruciating sores, she chose to lie on an oak plank in her home rather than a soft bed for five years, uniting her suffering with Christ’s Passion. Known for cheerful serenity and continuous prayer for her neighbors, she received a vision of Saint Gregory the Great, who foretold her eternal repose eight days before her passing.
deathSummary: Saint Fina died on March 12, 1253 at fifteen years of age; upon her death, fragrant white violets miraculously sprouted from her wooden plank.

image.title: Saint Fina of San Gimignano Sacred Icon

name: Saint Euphrasia of Constantinople
title: Venerable Mother Euphrasia of Constantinople, Nun of the Thebaid
curatedBio: Euphrasia was born in Constantinople around 380, the daughter of a pious imperial senator and relative of Emperor Theodosius I. Following her father’s death, she moved to Egypt with her mother and entered a strict convent in the Thebaid at age seven. When she reached adulthood, Emperor Arcadius asked her to wed a wealthy senator; she wrote back requesting that all her ancestral wealth be distributed to churches and the poor, living fifty years of extreme humility, fasting, and monastic labor.
deathSummary: Saint Euphrasia reposed peacefully in her Egyptian convent around 420 at thirty years of age.

image.title: Saint Euphrasia of Constantinople Sacred Icon

name: Saint Matilda of Ringelheim
title: Saint Matilda, Queen of Germany and Patroness of Large Families
curatedBio: Matilda was born in Westphalia around 895 into Saxon nobility and educated at Herford Abbey. In 909 she married Henry the Fowler, Duke of Saxony, who became King of East Francia. Renowned for generosity to the destitute and visiting prisoners, she was criticized by her sons Otto I and Henry for her lavish almsgiving. Following her husband's death in 936, she founded monasteries at Quedlinburg, Nordhausen, and Enger, retiring to Quedlinburg to live alongside the nuns in prayer.
deathSummary: Queen Matilda died peacefully at Quedlinburg Abbey on March 14, 968 at seventy-three years of age.

image.title: Saint Matilda of Ringelheim Sacred Icon

name: Saint Louise de Marillac
title: Saint Louise de Marillac, Co-Foundress of the Daughters of Charity
curatedBio: Born in Paris in 1591, Louise endured an unsettled youth and widowed motherhood before coming under the spiritual direction of Saint Vincent de Paul. In 1633, responding to the widespread destitution of seventeenth-century France, she gathered peasant women to nurse the sick and educate poor children, establishing the Daughters of Charity—the first non-cloistered religious congregation of women. Her sisters worked in hospitals, battlefields, prisons, and orphanages throughout Europe.
deathSummary: Saint Louise died peacefully in Paris on March 15, 1660 at sixty-eight years of age; her body remains incorrupt.

image.title: Saint Louise de Marillac Sacred Icon

name: Saint Eusebia of Hamage
title: Saint Eusebia, Anglo-Saxon and Frankish Abbess of Hamage
curatedBio: Eusebia was the daughter of Saint Adalbald of Ostrevent and Saint Rictrude of Marchiennes. Raised in an atmosphere of extraordinary sanctity alongside three saintly siblings, upon the death of her father she entered the convent of Hamage founded by her great-grandmother Saint Gertrude. Elected abbess at the tender age of twelve, she governed her community with precocious wisdom and austerity, defending monastic customs against interference and fostering rigorous Celtic-influenced Benedictine prayer.
deathSummary: Saint Eusebia reposed peacefully at Hamage on March 16, 660 at twenty-three years of age.

image.title: Saint Eusebia of Hamage Sacred Icon

name: Saint Gertrude of Nivelles
title: Saint Gertrude of Nivelles, Abbess and Patroness of Gardeners and Travelers
curatedBio: Gertrude was born around 628, the daughter of Pippin of Landen, Mayor of the Palace of Austrasia, and Saint Itta. At age ten, she boldly refused marriage to the son of a Frankish duke, stating she would have no bridegroom but Jesus Christ. Together with her mother, she founded the double monastery of Nivelles in Brabant, becoming abbess at age twenty. She was celebrated for acquiring Irish and Roman biblical manuscripts, hospitable care for pilgrims, and prophetic prayer.
deathSummary: Saint Gertrude reposed peacefully at Nivelles on March 17, 659 at thirty-three years of age.

image.title: Saint Gertrude of Nivelles Sacred Icon

name: Blessed Sibyllina Biscossi
title: Blessed Sibyllina Biscossi, Blind Dominican Recluse of Pavia
curatedBio: Sibyllina was born in Pavia, Italy in 1287 and orphaned in infancy. Struck completely blind at age twelve, she was taken in by the Dominican tertiary sisters. Resolving to live solely for God, she had a tiny recluse cell constructed against the wall of the Dominican Church of Saint Thomas in Pavia. For sixty-five years, she lived walled inside this enclosure in unceasing prayer, penance, and counseling multitudes of citizens who sought her window for spiritual guidance.
deathSummary: Blessed Sibyllina died peacefully in her cell at Pavia on March 19, 1367 at eighty years of age.

image.title: Blessed Sibyllina Biscossi Sacred Icon

name: Saint Mary of Egypt
title: Venerable Mother Mary of Egypt, Desert Penitent
curatedBio: Born in Egypt around 344, Mary lived seventeen years as a public prostitute in Alexandria. Joining a pilgrimage to Jerusalem out of curious lust, an invisible force prevented her from crossing the threshold of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre. Broken with compunction before an icon of the Theotokos, she crossed the Jordan River into the desolate desert, living forty-seven years in absolute solitude, nakedness, and prayer, discovered only by the priest Saint Zosimas before her holy repose.
deathSummary: Saint Mary of Egypt reposed peacefully around 421; a wild lion helped Saint Zosimas dig her desert grave.

image.title: Saint Mary of Egypt Sacred Icon

name: Saint Photina the Samaritan Woman
title: Holy Great Martyr Photina (Svetlana), Equal-to-the-Apostles
curatedBio: Photina was the Samaritan woman who conversed with Jesus Christ at Jacob's Well, receiving the revelation of the Living Water. Converted and baptized after Pentecost alongside her five sisters and two sons, she preached the Gospel throughout Asia Minor and Carthage. Brought before Emperor Nero in Rome, she and her sons refused to deny Christ. Enduring brutal tortures, she converted Nero's daughter Domnina and a hundred servants before her final martyrdom.
deathSummary: Saint Photina was thrown down a deep well in Rome around 66 after triumphing over all persecutions.

image.title: Saint Photina the Samaritan Woman Sacred Icon

name: Saint Benedetta Cambiagio Frassinello
title: Saint Benedetta Cambiagio Frassinello, Foundress of the Benedictine Sisters
curatedBio: Born in Langasco near Genoa in 1791, Benedetta entered marriage with Giovanni Frassinello. After two years of marriage, both felt called to consecrated celibacy and entered religious life. Working with the bishop of Pavia, Benedetta established schools for destitute young girls in Ronco Scrivia to rescue them from moral degradation and prostitution. In 1838 she founded the Benedictine Sisters of Providence, dedicating her institute to educating, feeding, and safeguarding impoverished young women.
deathSummary: Saint Benedetta died peacefully in Ronco Scrivia on March 21, 1858 at sixty-six years of age.

image.title: Saint Benedetta Cambiagio Frassinello Sacred Icon

name: Saint Lea of Rome
title: Saint Lea of Rome, Roman Ascetic Widow and Desert Mother
curatedBio: Lea was a wealthy noble Roman patrician widow who renounced social rank and worldly opulence following her husband’s death. Joining the ascetic circle of Saint Marcella on the Aventine Hill, she placed herself under the spiritual direction of Saint Jerome. Becoming superior of a monastic community of consecrated virgins, she clothed herself in sackcloth, spent whole nights in vigil, and performed the humblest domestic chores. Jerome praised her as a master of humility and contemplative silence.
deathSummary: Saint Lea reposed peacefully in Rome on March 22, 384, celebrated by Jerome as passing directly into eternal paradise.

image.title: Saint Lea of Rome Sacred Icon

name: Saint Rafqa Pietra Choboq Ar-Rayès
title: Saint Rafqa of Himlaya, Lebanese Maronite Nun and Mystic
curatedBio: Born in Himlaya, Lebanon in 1832, Boutroussieh entered the Mariamette Sisters before transferring to the cloistered Baladite Order of the Maronite Church at Saint Joseph Monastery in Jrabta. In 1885, she prayed to share in the suffering of Christ’s Passion. Shortly thereafter, she developed painful blindness and total paralysis of her limbs, which she endured for twenty-nine years with joyous gratitude, continuing to knit socks and praise the Lord from her wooden plank.
deathSummary: Saint Rafqa died peacefully in Jrabta, Lebanon on March 23, 1914 at eighty-one years of age; her tomb is renowned for healings.

image.title: Saint Rafqa Pietra Choboq Ar-Rayès Sacred Icon

name: Saint Catherine of Sweden
title: Saint Catherine of Vadstena, Daughter of Saint Bridget of Sweden
curatedBio: Catherine was born around 1332, the fourth child of Saint Bridget of Sweden. Married to a pious nobleman, both took vows of perpetual chastity. In 1349, she joined her mother on pilgrimage to Rome, sharing her ascetic life, charity, and struggles for Church renewal for twenty-three years. Following Bridget’s death, Catherine brought her mother’s holy relics back to Sweden and became abbess of the Brigittine motherhouse at Vadstena Abbey, leading the congregation with maternal grace.
deathSummary: Saint Catherine died peacefully at Vadstena Abbey on March 24, 1381 at forty-nine years of age.

image.title: Saint Catherine of Sweden Sacred Icon

name: Saint Margaret Clitherow
title: Holy Martyr Margaret Clitherow, The Pearl of York
curatedBio: Margaret Middleton was born in York around 1556 and married John Clitherow, a prosperous butcher. Converting to the Catholic faith in 1574, she turned her home into a secret safehouse, concealing fugitive Catholic priests and hosting clandestine celebrations of the Holy Mass during the Elizabethan persecutions. Arrested in 1586, she refused to plead before the court to protect her children from being forced to testify under torture against their own mother.
deathSummary: Saint Margaret was pressed to death on the Tollbooth bridge in York on March 25, 1586, dying with her arms outstretched in the form of a cross.

image.title: Saint Margaret Clitherow Sacred Icon

name: Saint Margaret of England
title: Saint Margaret of England, Cistercian Nun and Recluse
curatedBio: Margaret was born in England in the twelfth century, the sister of Saint Thomas of Beverley. Accompanying her mother on pilgrimage to the Holy Land, she was trapped in Jerusalem during the siege of Saladin in 1187, where she heroically carried water to the Christian defenders upon the city ramparts. Ransomed from captivity, she traveled across Europe on pilgrimage before retiring as a Cistercian recluse at the abbey of Notre-Dame-des-Prés near Troyes, France.
deathSummary: Saint Margaret reposed peacefully in her hermitage near Troyes on March 26, 1192 after decades of contemplative prayer.

image.title: Saint Margaret of England Sacred Icon

name: Saint Augusta of Treviso
title: Holy Virgin Martyr Augusta of Treviso
curatedBio: Augusta was the daughter of an unyielding pagan German ruler named Madrucco who held dominion in the hills of Serravalle (modern Vittorio Veneto) in the fifth century. Secretly instructed in the Christian faith and baptized, Augusta devoted herself to prayer and secretly distributed bread to persecuted Christian prisoners. When her father discovered her faith, he threw her into a furnace and had her broken on a wheel; surviving unharmed, she was led to execution.
deathSummary: Saint Augusta was beheaded by order of her own father at Serravalle around 400; her shrine stands on Mount Augusta.

image.title: Saint Augusta of Treviso Sacred Icon

name: Saint Guntilda of Thuringia
title: Saint Guntilda, Holy Virgin and Recluse of Thuringia
curatedBio: Guntilda was an Anglo-Saxon noblewoman who answered the call of Saint Boniface to assist in the evangelization of Germanic tribes in the eighth century. Renowned for profound asceticism, biblical scholarship, and humility, she served as a monastic teacher and later lived as an anchorite recluse in Thuringia. She dedicated her solitude to intercessory prayer for missionary bishops and the conversion of the pagan Saxons, guiding generations of young Germanic nuns in holy scripture.
deathSummary: Saint Guntilda reposed peacefully in Thuringia around 748 after decades of contemplative prayer and missionary sacrifice.

image.title: Saint Guntilda of Thuringia Sacred Icon

name: Saint Gladys of Wales
title: Saint Gladys (Gwladys), Hermit and Matron of Wales
curatedBio: Gladys was the eldest daughter of King Brychan of Brycheiniog and wife of Saint Gwynllyw (Woolos). Following the guidance of their eldest son, Saint Cadoc, Gladys and Gwynllyw underwent a profound religious conversion, renouncing royalty and warfare. They lived as ascetic hermits on the River Ebbw, bathing in cold water and subsisting on wild herbs. Gladys later founded her own solitary hermitage at Pencarnau, spending her final decades in unceasing prayer.
deathSummary: Saint Gladys reposed peacefully at her hermitage in Gwent around 500; her church stands in Newport.

image.title: Saint Gladys of Wales Sacred Icon

name: Saint Osburga of Coventry
title: Saint Osburga of Coventry, First Abbess of Coventry
curatedBio: Osburga was an Anglo-Saxon princess who founded a monastery of holy virgins at Coventry in Warwickshire during the reign of King Canute around 1016. Celebrated for austere mortification, continuous vigil, and profound maternal compassion for the impoverished inhabitants of the Midlands, she served as Coventry’s first abbess. Her monastery was destroyed during Danish invasions, but her tomb became Coventry’s primary pilgrimage shrine, where miraculous healings were recorded for centuries.
deathSummary: Saint Osburga reposed peacefully at Coventry around 1018; her feast was celebrated on March 30 throughout medieval England.

image.title: Saint Osburga of Coventry Sacred Icon

name: Saint Balbina of Rome
title: Holy Virgin Martyr Balbina of Rome
curatedBio: Balbina was the daughter of Saint Quirinus, a Roman tribune martyred under Emperor Hadrian. Stricken in youth with severe scrofulous disease of the throat, she was brought to Pope Saint Alexander I in prison; upon kissing the Pope’s chains, she was miraculously healed. Baptized alongside her father, Balbina consecrated her virginity to Jesus Christ and devoted her wealth to burying Christian martyrs. Arrested under Emperor Antoninus Pius, she confessed Christ and was put to death.
deathSummary: Saint Balbina was martyred in Rome around 130 and buried on the Appian Way; her ancient titular church stands on the Aventine Hill.

image.title: Saint Balbina of Rome Sacred Icon

name: Saint Mary of Egypt
title: Venerable Mother Mary of Egypt, Desert Penitent and Wonderworker
curatedBio: Mary lived seventeen years in Alexandria as a public courtesan before traveling to Jerusalem. Barred by a divine barrier from entering the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, she wept before an icon of the Virgin Mary, received absolution, and crossed the Jordan into the desert. For forty-seven years she lived in complete wilderness isolation, triumphing over demonic passions through relentless prayer and subsisting on miraculous grace until her meeting with Father Zosimas.
deathSummary: Saint Mary reposed peacefully in the desert around 421; Father Zosimas discovered her holy body with an inscription in the sand.

image.title: Saint Mary of Egypt Sacred Icon

name: Saint Theodosia of Tyre
title: Holy Virgin Martyr Theodosia of Tyre
curatedBio: Theodosia was an eighteen-year-old Christian maiden of Tyre in Phoenicia during the Diocletian persecutions. Visiting Christian prisoners condemned to the copper mines of Palestine, she comforted them and asked to be remembered in their prayers. Arrested and dragged before the Roman governor Urbanus at Caesarea Maritima, she refused to sacrifice to idols. The governor ordered her sides torn with iron claws to the bone and thrown into the Mediterranean Sea.
deathSummary: Saint Theodosia was tied to a heavy stone and cast into the sea at Caesarea Maritima on April 2, 307.

image.title: Saint Theodosia of Tyre Sacred Icon

name: Saint Burgundofara
title: Saint Burgundofara (Fara), Frankish Foundress and Abbess of Faremoutiers
curatedBio: Burgundofara was born into a prominent Frankish noble family and consecrated to God in childhood by the Irish missionary Saint Columbanus. When her father later attempted to force her into political marriage, she was stricken with a violent fever and blindness, which vanished when her father relented. Around 620, she founded the double monastery of Faremoutiers, introducing the strict Columbanian Rule and governing the abbey for forty years as a haven of monastic scholarship and charity.
deathSummary: Saint Burgundofara died peacefully at Faremoutiers Abbey on April 3, 657 at approximately sixty years of age.

image.title: Saint Burgundofara Sacred Icon

name: Saint Pherbutha of Persia
title: Holy Virgin Martyr Pherbutha (Ferbuta) of Seleucia
curatedBio: Pherbutha was the sister of Saint Simeon Barsabae, Bishop of Seleucia-Ctesiphon, who was martyred by Persian King Shapur II in 341. Serving as a consecrated virgin, she was arrested alongside her widowed sister and servant following false accusations from Zoroastrian Magi that they had poisoned Queen Shapur. Offered freedom if she agreed to wed the Zoroastrian chief priest, Pherbutha replied that she was consecrated to Christ alone.
mannerOfDeath: Sawn in two with a wooden saw
deathSummary: Saint Pherbutha was tied to stakes and sawn in two at Seleucia in 342 under King Shapur II.

image.title: Saint Pherbutha of Persia Sacred Icon

name: Saint Juliana of Cornillon
title: Saint Juliana of Cornillon, Premonstratensian Mystic of the Eucharist
curatedBio: Born near Liège, Belgium in 1193 and orphaned at age five, Juliana was raised by the Augustinian canonesses at Mont-Cornillon leper hospital. From age sixteen she received repeated visions of the full moon with a black stripe, interpreted by Christ as the absence of a liturgical feast dedicated solely to the Blessed Sacrament. Her persistent theological advocacy and collaboration with Jacques Pantaléon (later Pope Urban IV) led to the universal institution of the Solemnity of Corpus Christi in 1264.
deathSummary: Saint Juliana died peacefully in a recluse cell at Fosses-la-Ville on April 5, 1258 at sixty-five years of age.

image.title: Saint Juliana of Cornillon Sacred Icon

name: Saint Catherine of Genoa
title: Saint Catherine of Genoa, Mystic of Divine Love and Purgatory
curatedBio: Caterina Fieschi was born in Genoa in 1447 into a distinguished patrician family. Married at sixteen to a dissolute nobleman, she endured ten years of emotional devastation before an overwhelming mystical encounter during confession in 1473 transformed her life. Together with her converted husband, she moved into the Pammatone Hospital in Genoa, serving terminal plague patients for twenty-two years as hospital directress. Her sublime mystical writings, notably The Treatise on Purgatory, profoundly influenced Catholic spiritual theology.
deathSummary: Saint Catherine died peacefully in Genoa on September 15, 1510 at sixty-three years of age; her body remains incorrupt.

image.title: Saint Catherine of Genoa Sacred Icon

name: Blessed Ursulina of Parma
title: Blessed Ursulina of Parma, Messenger of Peace to Avignon
curatedBio: Ursulina was born in Parma in 1375 into a devout family. At age fifteen, she received interior mystical revelations instructing her to travel to Avignon and Rome to implore Antipope Clement VII and Pope Boniface IX to end the Great Western Schism. Traveling on foot across the Alps with her mother, she addressed the rival pontiffs with remarkable diplomatic courage and evangelical fervor, seeking the unity of Christ’s Church before retiring to Parma in contemplative charity.
deathSummary: Blessed Ursulina died peacefully in Verona on April 7, 1410 at thirty-five years of age.

image.title: Blessed Ursulina of Parma Sacred Icon

name: Saint Julie Billiart
title: Saint Julie Billiart, Foundress of the Sisters of Notre Dame de Namur
curatedBio: Marie Rose Julie Billiart was born in Cuvilly, France in 1751. Following a shooting attack on her father's shop, the severe trauma left her completely paralyzed for twenty-two years. From her bed, she taught catechism to village children and sheltered hunted priests during the French Revolution. In 1804 at Amiens, she was miraculously healed of paralysis and founded the Sisters of Notre Dame de Namur, dedicating her congregation to the free Christian education of poor girls.
deathSummary: Saint Julie died peacefully in Namur, Belgium on April 8, 1816 at sixty-four years of age.

image.title: Saint Julie Billiart Sacred Icon

name: Saint Casilda of Toledo
title: Saint Casilda of Toledo, Virgin Recluse of Burgos
curatedBio: Casilda was the daughter of the Muslim ruler Al-Mamun of Toledo in eleventh-century Spain. Moved by compassion for Christian prisoners held in her father’s dungeons, she secretly carried bread to them wrapped in her robes. When confronted by her father’s guards, the bread miraculously turned into a bouquet of fragrant roses. Following a miraculous healing of severe hemorrhage in the holy waters of San Vicente near Briviesca, she was baptized and lived as a solitary hermit.
deathSummary: Saint Casilda reposed peacefully in her hermitage near Briviesca around 1050 at an advanced age.

image.title: Saint Casilda of Toledo Sacred Icon

name: Saint Magdalene of Canossa
title: Saint Magdalene of Canossa, Foundress of the Canossian Daughters of Charity
curatedBio: Born in Verona in 1774 into the illustrious noble house of Canossa, Magdalene experienced childhood abandonment and serious illness before resolving to serve Christ in the poor. Shocked by the moral degradation and poverty following the Napoleonic Wars in northern Italy, she abandoned her ancestral palace in 1808. She moved into the poorest district of Verona, establishing free charity schools for girls, nursing the abandoned sick, and founding the Canossian Daughters of Charity.
deathSummary: Saint Magdalene died peacefully in Verona on Good Friday, April 10, 1835 at sixty-one years of age.

image.title: Saint Magdalene of Canossa Sacred Icon

name: Saint Gemma Galgani
title: Saint Gemma Galgani, The Flower of Lucca and Passionist Mystic
curatedBio: Gemma was born near Lucca, Italy in 1878 and lost her mother in childhood. Afflicted with spinal tuberculosis, she was miraculously healed in 1899 following a novena to Saint Gabriel of Our Lady of Sorrows. Gifted with intense mystical colloquies, she sustained the sacred stigmata on her hands, feet, and side every Thursday through Friday, bearing the visible wounds of Christ’s Passion with childlike humility while living as a quiet laywoman in the Giannini household.
deathSummary: Saint Gemma died of tuberculosis in Lucca on Holy Saturday, April 11, 1903 at twenty-five years of age.

image.title: Saint Gemma Galgani Sacred Icon

name: Saint Vissia of Fermo
title: Holy Virgin Martyr Vissia of Fermo
curatedBio: Vissia was a noble Christian virgin living in the Picenum region of Italy during the persecutions under Emperor Decius. Dedicated to perpetual chastity and prayer, she was denounced to Roman magistrate Falconius for refusing to offer incense to pagan gods. When threats and promises failed to break her faith, she was scourged, racked, and led out of the city walls where she commended her soul to Jesus Christ before suffering decapitation.
deathSummary: Saint Vissia was beheaded at Fermo around 250; her relics are venerated in the Cathedral of Fermo.

image.title: Saint Vissia of Fermo Sacred Icon

name: Saint Margaret of Castello
title: Saint Margaret of Castello, Blind and Crippled Dominican Penitent
curatedBio: Born near Florence in 1287, Margaret was born blind, hunchbacked, and lame. Horrified by her deformities, her noble parents locked her in a vault near a church for fourteen years. Taken to Città di Castello to seek a miraculous cure that failed, her parents abandoned her on the streets. Taken in by impoverished townsfolk, she became a Dominican tertiary, spending her life in ecstatic prayer, visiting prisoners, and counseling the sick with supernatural joy and compassion.
deathSummary: Saint Margaret died peacefully in Città di Castello on April 13, 1320 at thirty-three; her body remains incorrupt.

image.title: Saint Margaret of Castello Sacred Icon

name: Saint Lydwina of Schiedam
title: Saint Lydwina of Schiedam, Patroness of Ice Skaters and Chronic Illness
curatedBio: Born in Schiedam near Rotterdam in 1380, Lydwina was injured in an ice skating fall at age fifteen, breaking a rib. The injury turned gangrenous and developed into total, agonizing paralysis, confining her to her bed for thirty-eight years. Instructed by her priest to meditate upon the Passion of Christ, she embraced her bed as an altar of redemptive suffering. She was gifted with mystical ecstasies and sustained solely by the Holy Eucharist during her final seven years.
