deathSummary: Saint Lydwina died peacefully on Easter Tuesday, April 14, 1433 at fifty-three years of age.

image.title: Saint Lydwina of Schiedam Sacred Icon

name: Saint Hunna of Alsace
title: Saint Hunna, The Holy Washerwoman of Alsace
curatedBio: Hunna was the noble wife of Huno of Hunawihr in Alsace during the seventh century. Devoted to Christian charity, she personally washed the clothing and linens of her impoverished peasants and lepers, earning the affectionate title of "the Holy Washerwoman". When her son Deodatus was born, she consecrated him to God, and he later became a monk and bishop. Her unpretentious holiness demonstrated that sanctity is achieved through the humblest duties performed with supernatural love.
deathSummary: Saint Hunna reposed peacefully at Hunawihr around 679; her tomb was a beloved pilgrimage shrine in Alsace.

image.title: Saint Hunna of Alsace Sacred Icon

name: Saint Encratis of Zaragoza
title: Holy Virgin Martyr Encratis (Engracia) of Zaragoza
curatedBio: Encratis was a noble Lusitanian maiden traveling through Hispania Tarraconensis to Roussillon to marry a Christian prince around 304. Arriving in Zaragoza during the Diocletian persecutions, she witnessed the brutal torture of Christian citizens under governor Dacian. Moved by righteous indignation, she publicly rebuked the governor for shedding innocent blood. Arrested immediately, she was scourged, tied to horses, and mutilated with iron combs, surviving excruciating tortures with intrepid fortitude.
mannerOfDeath: Iron nail driven into her forehead
deathSummary: Saint Encratis was martyred at Zaragoza around 304 when an iron nail was driven through her forehead.

image.title: Saint Encratis of Zaragoza Sacred Icon

name: Saint Kateri Tekakwitha
title: Saint Kateri Tekakwitha, Lily of the Mohawks
curatedBio: Tekakwitha was born in 1656 at Ossernenon (Auriesville, New York) to a Mohawk chief and Christian Algonquin mother. Orphaned at age four by smallpox that scarred her face and impaired her vision, she was raised by her anti-Christian uncle. Converted by Jesuit missionaries, she received baptism in 1676 as Catherine (Kateri). Facing intense persecution from her tribe, she fled two hundred miles on foot to the Catholic mission at Kahnawake near Montreal, living five years of extraordinary mortification and virginal prayer.
deathSummary: Saint Kateri died at Kahnawake on April 17, 1680 at twenty-four; moments after her death, her smallpox scars miraculously vanished.

image.title: Saint Kateri Tekakwitha Sacred Icon

name: Saint Anthousa of Constantinople
title: Saint Anthousa of Constantinople, Imperial Nun and Defender of Icons
curatedBio: Anthousa was the daughter of Byzantine iconoclast Emperor Constantine V Copronymus. Despite her father’s bitter persecution of icon venerators and pressure on her to marry, Anthousa embraced monastic virginity, being tonsured by Patriarch Tarasios. Using her imperial wealth, she founded the double monastery of Saint Euphemia at the Golden Horn, financing orphanages and shelters for widows, and boldly defended the veneration of holy images leading up to the Seventh Ecumenical Council.
deathSummary: Saint Anthousa reposed peacefully at Constantinople around 809 at fifty-two years of age.

image.title: Saint Anthousa of Constantinople Sacred Icon

name: Saint Emma of Lesum
title: Saint Emma of Lesum, Countess and Benefactress of Bremen
curatedBio: Emma was a Saxon noblewoman of the Immedinger family and sister of Bishop Meinwerk of Paderborn. Married to Count Liudger of Saxony, following his early death in 1011, she dedicated her immense widow's wealth to the Church and the alleviation of poverty. She endowed Bremen Cathedral with expansive estates and funded the construction of churches throughout Lower Saxony, spending her final three decades in solitary prayer and personally caring for sick peasants.
deathSummary: Countess Emma died peacefully in Bremen on April 19, 1038; her tomb in Bremen Cathedral was venerated for centuries.

image.title: Saint Emma of Lesum Sacred Icon

name: Saint Agnes of Montepulciano
title: Saint Agnes of Montepulciano, Dominican Prioress and Wonderworker
curatedBio: Born in Gracciano near Montepulciano in 1268, Agnes entered a Franciscan convent at age nine. At age fifteen, the citizens of Proceno requested her to establish a monastery, where she was appointed abbess by papal dispensation. In 1306, instructed by a vision of Saint Dominic, she built a monastery of Dominican nuns in Montepulciano. Celebrated for prophetic knowledge and deep contemplative prayer, during which white manna miraculously fell upon her while praying, she governed her sisters with profound sanctity.
deathSummary: Saint Agnes died peacefully in Montepulciano on April 20, 1317 at forty-nine; Saint Catherine of Siena visited her incorrupt body.

image.title: Saint Agnes of Montepulciano Sacred Icon

name: Saint Alexandra of Rome
title: Holy Great Martyr Empress Alexandra of Rome
curatedBio: Alexandra was the imperial consort of Roman Emperor Diocletian. Witnessing the extraordinary miracles and supernatural courage of the Great Martyr George while he was tortured on the wheel and surviving unharmed, Alexandra stepped out of the imperial pavilion, fell at George’s feet, and openly confessed Jesus Christ as the true God. Enraged by her public apostasy from Roman paganism, Diocletian condemned his own empress to death by decapitation.
mannerOfDeath: Condemned to decapitation; reposed before the sword
deathSummary: Sentenced to execution alongside Saint George, Saint Alexandra prayed peacefully on the way to the scaffold and gave up her spirit around 303.

image.title: Saint Alexandra of Rome Sacred Icon

name: Saint Senorina of Basto
title: Saint Senorina of Basto, Benedictine Abbess and Wonderworker of Portugal
curatedBio: Senorina was born in Vieira do Minho around 924 into the Galician-Portuguese nobility, a relative of Saint Rudesind. Educated by her aunt Godina at the monastery of Saint John of Vieira, Senorina took Benedictine vows and was appointed abbess at age thirty-six. She moved the community to Basto, where she governed with exemplary humility. Recorded in early Portuguese hagiography, her prayers miraculously multiplied grain during regional famines and silenced noisy frogs whose croaking disturbed the monastic Office.
deathSummary: Saint Senorina died peacefully at Basto on April 22, 982 at fifty-eight years of age; her tomb is in Basto.

image.title: Saint Senorina of Basto Sacred Icon

name: Saint Polychronia
title: Saint Polychronia, Mother of the Holy Great Martyr George
curatedBio: Polychronia was a devout Christian noblewoman of Lydda (Diospolis) in Palestine. Married to the imperial Roman senator Gerontios of Cappadocia, she raised her son George in strict Christian piety following her husband's early martyrdom. When George boldly confessed Christ before Diocletian, Polychronia traveled to Nicomedia to encourage him in his sufferings. Openly affirming her own Christian faith before the emperor, she was arrested, severely scourged, and crowned with martyrdom.
deathSummary: Saint Polychronia was martyred in Nicomedia around 303 shortly before the execution of her son Saint George.

image.title: Saint Polychronia Sacred Icon

name: Saint Mary Euphrasia Pelletier
title: Saint Mary Euphrasia Pelletier, Foundress of the Good Shepherd Sisters
curatedBio: Rose Virginie Pelletier was born on Noirmoutier island, France in 1796 during the anti-clerical French Revolution. In 1814 she joined the Order of Our Lady of Charity of the Refuge in Tours, taking the name Mary Euphrasia. Recognizing that rescuing traumatized women and young girls required centralized governance, in 1835 she established the Congregation of Our Lady of Charity of the Good Shepherd in Angers, founding one hundred and ten convents worldwide during her lifetime.
deathSummary: Saint Mary Euphrasia died of cancer in Angers on April 24, 1868 at seventy-one years of age.

image.title: Saint Mary Euphrasia Pelletier Sacred Icon

name: Saint Franca of Piacenza
title: Saint Franca Visdomini, Cistercian Abbess and Contemplative
curatedBio: Franca was born in Piacenza in 1175 into the noble Visdomini family. Placed in the Benedictine convent of Saint Siro at age seven, she took vows at fourteen and was elected abbess at twenty-four. Striving for deeper silence and stricter mortification, she led her community into the Cistercian Order, founding the monastery of Pittolo. She spent her nights in choir reciting the Psalter with outstretched arms, counseling the citizens of Lombardy with spiritual wisdom.
deathSummary: Saint Franca died peacefully at Pittolo on April 25, 1218 at forty-three years of age.

image.title: Saint Franca of Piacenza Sacred Icon

name: Blessed Alda of Siena
title: Blessed Alda (Aldobrandesca) of Siena, Humiliate Penitent
curatedBio: Alda was born in Siena in 1249 into the noble Bellabanti family. Following the early death of her husband, she gave away her entire wealth to the poor and joined the Third Order of the Humiliati. She spent her remaining years nursing the sick in the municipal hospital of Siena, caring for destitute patients with infectious wounds and enduring mystical ecstasies and demonic attacks with patient contemplation of Christ’s wounds.
deathSummary: Blessed Alda died peacefully in Siena on April 26, 1309 at sixty years of age.

image.title: Blessed Alda of Siena Sacred Icon

name: Saint Zita of Lucca
title: Saint Zita of Lucca, Patroness of Domestic Servants
curatedBio: Born in Monsagrati near Lucca in 1212 into a poor peasant family, Zita became a domestic servant in the Fatinelli household at age twelve, serving the same family for forty-eight years. Despite initial ridicule and cruelty from fellow servants, she greeted every task as service to Christ, rising before dawn to attend daily Mass and secretly feeding the hungry with her own rations. Her master once found her kitchen full of angels baking bread while she was rapt in prayer.
deathSummary: Saint Zita died peacefully in Lucca on April 27, 1272 at sixty years of age; her body remains incorrupt in the Basilica of San Frediano.

image.title: Saint Zita of Lucca Sacred Icon

name: Saint Gianna Beretta Molla
title: Saint Gianna Beretta Molla, Physician, Mother, and Martyr of Maternal Love
curatedBio: Gianna was born near Milan in 1922, earning doctorates in medicine and surgery and opening a clinic in Mesero dedicated to mothers and infants. Married to Pietro Molla, she balanced medical service with joyous family life. During her fourth pregnancy in 1961, doctors discovered a large uterine fibroma. Given options that would have aborted her child, Gianna unequivocally instructed the surgeons to save the unborn child’s life regardless of the risk to her own.
deathSummary: Saint Gianna gave birth to healthy daughter Gianna Emanuela and died seven days later on April 28, 1962 at thirty-nine years of age.

image.title: Saint Gianna Beretta Molla Sacred Icon

name: Saint Catherine of Siena
title: Saint Catherine of Siena, Doctor of the Church and Patroness of Europe
curatedBio: Caterina Benincasa was born in Siena in 1347, the twenty-fifth child of a cloth dyer. Consecrating her virginity to Christ at age seven, she entered the Dominican Mantellate tertiary sisters. Experiencing mystical marriage to Christ, she cared for plague victims, converted condemned criminals on the scaffold, and dictated sublime spiritual treatises in The Dialogue. Her prophetic letters to Pope Gregory XI persuaded him to leave Avignon and return the papacy to Rome in 1377.
deathSummary: Saint Catherine died in Rome on April 29, 1380 at thirty-three; she was proclaimed Doctor of the Church in 1970.

image.title: Saint Catherine of Siena Sacred Icon

name: Saint Marie of the Incarnation
title: Saint Marie of the Incarnation, Ursuline Mystic and Mother of the Canadian Church
curatedBio: Marie Guyart was born in Tours, France in 1599. Widowed at nineteen with an infant son, she entered the Ursuline monastery of Tours after experiencing mystical union with the Blessed Trinity. In 1639, answering a missionary calling, she sailed to New France, founding the Ursuline convent in Quebec—the first school for girls in North America. She mastered Huron, Algonquin, and Iroquois, composing dictionaries and catechisms while educating Indigenous and French girls.
deathSummary: Saint Marie died peacefully in Quebec on April 30, 1672 at seventy-two years of age.

image.title: Saint Marie of the Incarnation Sacred Icon

name: Saint Isidora the Simple
title: Blessed Isidora the Fool-for-Christ of Tabennisi
curatedBio: Isidora was a fourth-century nun at the Tabennisi monastery in the Egyptian Thebaid under Saint Pachomius. Adopting the ascetic feat of foolishness for Christ’s sake, she wore a dishcloth bound around her head and served the humblest kitchen chores, sweeping floors and washing cooking pots without ever sitting at the communal table. When Saint Pitirim was told by an angel to seek the greatest saint of the monastery, he fell at Isidora’s feet, revealing her secret angelic sanctity to the astonished sisters.
deathSummary: Fleeing human praise, Blessed Isidora vanished into the desert around 365, spending her final days in complete solitary contemplation.

image.title: Saint Isidora the Simple Sacred Icon

name: Saint Matrona of Moscow
title: Blessed Matrona of Moscow, Blind and Paralyzed Wonderworker
curatedBio: Matrona Dmitrievna Nikonova was born in Sebino, Russia in 1881. Born blind without eyes and losing the use of her legs at age seventeen, she possessed extraordinary prophetic discernment and spiritual vision from childhood. Fleeing Bolshevik persecution in Moscow, she lived in secret apartments, receiving dozens of distressed citizens daily and praying through the night. Foretelling the Soviet victory in World War II, she healed illnesses and brought spiritual consolation to thousands during state atheism.
deathSummary: Blessed Matrona reposed peacefully in Moscow on May 2, 1952; her relics at Pokrovsky Monastery draw millions of pilgrims.

image.title: Saint Matrona of Moscow Sacred Icon

name: Saint Maura of the Thebaid
title: Holy Martyr Maura of the Thebaid
curatedBio: Maura was a young Egyptian Christian woman married for only twenty days to the reader Saint Timothy. During the Diocletian persecutions around 286, when Timothy was arrested and blinded for refusing to deliver up the holy liturgical books, the Roman governor Arrianus summoned Maura, urging her to persuade her husband to sacrifice. Instead, inspired by Timothy’s holy fortitude, Maura boldly confessed Christ alongside him, having her hair torn out and fingers crushed with iron tongs.
deathSummary: Saint Maura and Saint Timothy were crucified facing each other for nine days before giving up their spirits around 286.

image.title: Saint Maura of the Thebaid Sacred Icon

name: Saint Pelagia of Tarsus
title: Holy Virgin Martyr Pelagia of Tarsus
curatedBio: Pelagia was a noble maiden of Tarsus in Cilicia distinguished for beauty and wealth. When Emperor Diocletian’s adopted son sought her in marriage, Pelagia replied that she had consecrated her virginity to Jesus Christ, the King of Heaven. Secretly instructed and baptized by Bishop Linus of Tarsus, she distributed her fine garments to the poor. Stricken with despair, the Emperor’s son fell on his sword. Brought before Diocletian, Pelagia was condemned to a heated red-hot bronze ox.
mannerOfDeath: Burned in a red-hot bronze ox
deathSummary: Making the sign of the cross, Saint Pelagia entered the red-hot bronze ox at Rome around 290, surrendering her soul like pure incense.

image.title: Saint Pelagia of Tarsus Sacred Icon

name: Saint Irene of Thessalonica
title: Holy Great Martyr Irene of Thessalonica, Equal-to-the-Apostles
curatedBio: Penelope was the daughter of a pagan prince named Licinius in Thrace. Taught the Christian faith by an angel and the elder Apellian, she was baptized taking the name Irene (Peace). Overturning her father’s idols, she converted both her parents to Christ. Dragged before successive Persian and Roman rulers, she survived being thrown into a pit of vipers, tied to millstones, and sawn asunder without harm. Preaching across Thrace, she converted over ten thousand pagans through word and miracle.
deathSummary: Saint Irene was beheaded at Ephesus around 304 after an extraordinary apostolic ministry across the Balkans.

image.title: Saint Irene of Thessalonica Sacred Icon

name: Saint Benedicta of Rome
title: Saint Benedicta of Rome, Holy Virgin and Monastic
curatedBio: Benedicta was a consecrated virgin living in a monastic community in Rome during the sixth century under Saint Galla. Recorded by Pope Saint Gregory the Great in his Dialogues, Benedicta received a heavenly vision of Saint Peter thirty days before her death, who assured her that her prayers and virginity were acceptable before the Lord. Stricken with a gentle fever, she gathered her monastic sisters, praising God and departing peacefully to her Heavenly Bridegroom.
deathSummary: Saint Benedicta reposed peacefully in Rome around 546; her life was commemorated by Saint Gregory the Great.

image.title: Saint Benedicta of Rome Sacred Icon

name: Saint Flavia Domitilla
title: Holy Virgin Martyr Flavia Domitilla, Imperial Roman Martyr
curatedBio: Flavia Domitilla was a Roman noblewoman of the imperial Flavian dynasty, niece of Roman consul Titus Flavius Clemens. Converted to Christianity by Saints Nereus and Achilleus, she consecrated her virginity to Jesus Christ, refusing marriage to the pagan nobleman Aurelian. Exiled by Emperor Domitian to the desolate island of Pandateria (Ventotene) for confessing Christianity, she was later brought to Terracina. When she refused once more to sacrifice to idols, her bedchamber was set ablaze.
deathSummary: Saint Domitilla was burned to death in Terracina around 95 under Emperor Trajan alongside her foster sisters.

image.title: Saint Flavia Domitilla Sacred Icon

name: Saint Pelagia of Antioch
title: Holy Virgin Martyr Pelagia of Antioch, Disciple of Saint Lucian
curatedBio: Pelagia was a fifteen-year-old Christian maiden of Antioch during the persecutions of Emperor Diocletian around 303. When Roman soldiers surrounded her home to arrest her and subject her to judicial violation in a brothel, Pelagia asked permission to enter her upper room to change into suitable attire. Dressed in her finest white garments, she prayed to preserve her virginal purity intact for Christ and threw herself from the roof of the house, offering her life directly to God.
mannerOfDeath: Leapt from roof to preserve virginity
deathSummary: Saint Pelagia died in Antioch around 303; praised by Saint John Chrysostom and Saint Ambrose for heroic chastity.

image.title: Saint Pelagia of Antioch Sacred Icon

name: Saint Maria Theresa Gerhardinger
title: Blessed Maria Theresa Gerhardinger, Foundress of the School Sisters of Notre Dame
curatedBio: Caroline Gerhardinger was born in Regensburg, Bavaria in 1797. Deeply distressed by the closure of religious schools during the secularization of Bavaria, she became a certified teacher at age twelve. Encouraged by Bishop Georg Michael Wittmann, in 1833 she founded the School Sisters of Notre Dame, dedicated to providing rigorous free Christian education to poor girls. Her congregation expanded across Europe and North America, educating tens of thousands of immigrant children.
deathSummary: Blessed Maria Theresa died peacefully in Munich on May 9, 1879 at eighty-one years of age.

image.title: Saint Maria Theresa Gerhardinger Sacred Icon

name: Saint Solange of Bourges
title: Holy Virgin Martyr Solange of Bourges, Patroness of Berry
curatedBio: Solange was born around 860 into a humble peasant family in Villemont near Bourges. Renowned for beauty, piety, and love of solitary prayer while tending her father's sheep, she made a secret vow of virginity to Jesus Christ. When Bernard, the son of the Count of Poitiers, encountered her in the pastures and attempted to carry her away on horseback, she struggled free and threw herself into a stream. Enraged by her refusal, Bernard drew his sword.
deathSummary: Saint Solange was beheaded at Saint-Solange in Berry on May 10, 880; her shrine is a major pilgrimage center of central France.

image.title: Saint Solange of Bourges Sacred Icon

name: Saint Rictrude of Marchiennes
title: Saint Rictrude of Marchiennes, Frankish Abbess
curatedBio: Rictrude was born in Gascony around 614 and married Saint Adalbald of Ostrevent, bearing four children who are all venerated as canonized saints: Maurontius, Clotsinda, Eusebia, and Adalsinda. Following the murder of her husband by pagan relatives in 652, Rictrude resisted royal pressure from King Clovis II to remarry, taking the veil from Saint Amand at Marchiennes Abbey. She governed the double monastery for forty years with maternal tenderness and strict adherence to the Columbanian Rule.
deathSummary: Saint Rictrude died peacefully at Marchiennes Abbey on May 12, 688 at seventy-four years of age.

image.title: Saint Rictrude of Marchiennes Sacred Icon

name: Saint Glykeria of Heraclea
title: Holy Virgin Martyr Glykeria of Heraclea
curatedBio: Glykeria was the daughter of a Roman senator living in Trajanopolis in Thrace during the reign of Antoninus Pius. Tracing the sign of the cross upon her forehead, she entered the pagan temple of Jupiter during an imperial festival; her prayer caused the statue of Jupiter to crash into dust. Dragged to prison and subjected to the rack, she was saved by angels who provided bread. Cast to wild lions at Heraclea, a lioness approached and rested peacefully at her feet.
mannerOfDeath: Exposed to wild beasts; yielded spirit peacefully
deathSummary: A second lion approached without mauling her; Saint Glykeria prayed to Christ and yielded her spirit peacefully around 177.

image.title: Saint Glykeria of Heraclea Sacred Icon

name: Saint Agnes of Poitiers
title: Saint Agnes of Poitiers, First Abbess of Holy Cross
curatedBio: Agnes was raised in the royal Frankish court of Queen Saint Radegund. In 559, when Radegund founded the Abbey of the Holy Cross in Poitiers, she selected Agnes to be its first abbess. Agnes journeyed to Arles to study the monastic rule of Saint Caesarius, adopting its austere discipline of communal poverty, silent reading, and copying of holy manuscripts. Celebrated for poetic and theological erudition, she was praised by the Christian poet Saint Venantius Fortunatus.
deathSummary: Saint Agnes died peacefully at Poitiers on May 13, 588; her tomb is in the Church of Saint Radegund.

image.title: Saint Agnes of Poitiers Sacred Icon

name: Saint Maria Mazzarello
title: Saint Maria Domenica Mazzarello, Co-Foundress of the Salesian Sisters
curatedBio: Born in Mornese, Piedmont in 1837 into a peasant family, Maria worked in the vineyards while nurturing deep Eucharistic piety. After contracting typhoid while nursing sick relatives, her physical stamina was permanently shattered. Turning to dressmaking, she gathered local village girls to teach them needlework, prayer, and literacy. In 1872, collaborating with Saint John Bosco, she founded the Daughters of Mary Help of Christians (the Salesian Sisters), leading the congregation with joyful maternal simplicity.
deathSummary: Saint Maria died peacefully in Nizza Monferrato on May 14, 1881 at forty-four years of age.

image.title: Saint Maria Mazzarello Sacred Icon

name: Saint Dymphna of Geel
title: Holy Virgin Martyr Dymphna of Geel, Patroness of Mental Health
curatedBio: Dymphna was a seventh-century Irish Christian princess, the daughter of a pagan Celtic king named Damon and a Christian mother. When her mother died, the grief-maddened king resolved to marry his own daughter because of her resemblance to his wife. Horrified, fourteen-year-old Dymphna fled Ireland across the sea with her priest Father Gerebernus, settling at Geel in Flanders where she opened a hospice for the poor. When her father tracked them down, he ordered Gerebernus slain.
deathSummary: When Dymphna refused his advances, her father drew his sword and beheaded her at Geel around 650; Geel became a world-renowned therapeutic haven.

image.title: Saint Dymphna of Geel Sacred Icon

name: Saint Maxima of Fréjus
title: Saint Maxima of Fréjus, Holy Virgin of Provence
curatedBio: Maxima was a Christian virgin living in Provence during the eighth century who consecrated her life to God, refusing all worldly alliances. She founded a monastery of nuns in the forest of Callian near Grasse, governing her sisters with ascetic rigor and evangelical charity. Celebrated in southern Gaul for protecting villages from raiding pirates and healing the afflicted through prayer, her memory gave rise to the coastal town of Sainte-Maxime on the French Riviera.
deathSummary: Saint Maxima reposed peacefully in her monastery at Callian around 750; her relics are venerated in Sainte-Maxime.

image.title: Saint Maxima of Fréjus Sacred Icon

name: Saint Restituta of Carthage
title: Holy Virgin Martyr Restituta of Carthage, Patroness of Ischia
curatedBio: Restituta was a noble Christian maiden of Carthage in Roman Africa during the persecutions under Diocletian. Refusing to sacrifice to pagan deities, she was subjected to cruel tortures and placed in a boat filled with pitch, resin, and tow set ablaze and set adrift in the Mediterranean Sea. Miraculously untouched by the flames, Restituta commended her soul to God as the boat drifted across the sea, washing ashore at the Bay of San Montano on the island of Ischia.
mannerOfDeath: Exposed to flames in a boat at sea
deathSummary: Saint Restituta martyred around 304; her boat drifted ashore at Ischia where fragrant white lilies miraculously blossomed.

image.title: Saint Restituta of Carthage Sacred Icon

name: Saint Sunniva of Selje
title: Saint Sunniva, Irish Princess and Patroness of Western Norway
curatedBio: Sunniva was a tenth-century Irish Christian princess who fled her homeland in unruddered boats with her companions to escape a pagan Viking king who demanded her in marriage. Trusting divine providence, the boats drifted across the North Sea, landing on the uninhabited island of Selja off the western coast of Norway. Living in seaside caves in prayer and subsisting on fish, when pagan local jarls arrived to slaughter them, Sunniva prayed for protection; massive falling boulders sealed the cave entrance.
mannerOfDeath: Crushed and sealed inside seaside cave
deathSummary: Saint Sunniva and her companions died sealed in the cave on Selja around 996; King Olav Tryggvason discovered her incorrupt body in 996.

image.title: Saint Sunniva of Selje Sacred Icon

name: Saint Maria Bernarda Bütler
title: Saint Maria Bernarda Bütler, Franciscan Missionary to Latin America
curatedBio: Verena Bütler was born in Auw, Switzerland in 1848 into a farming family. Entering the Franciscan convent of Mary Help of Sinners in Altstätten, she was appointed novice mistress and superior. In 1888, responding to missionary pleas from South America, Mother Bernarda led six sisters to Ecuador, founding the Franciscan Missionary Sisters of Mary Help of Sinners. Driven into exile by anti-clerical persecution in 1895, she relocated to Cartagena, Colombia, serving impoverished patients and homeless children for thirty years.
deathSummary: Saint Maria Bernarda died peacefully in Cartagena, Colombia on May 19, 1924 at seventy-five years of age.

image.title: Saint Maria Bernarda Bütler Sacred Icon

name: Saint Lydwina of Schiedam
title: Saint Lydwina of Schiedam, Mystic of Patient Suffering
curatedBio: Confined to her bed from age fifteen after a severe ice-skating accident that paralyzed her body, Lydwina lived in Schiedam for thirty-eight years in intense physical agony. Transforming her bed into a spiritual center for all of Holland, she received celestial visions of heaven and purgatory, sustained solely by the Holy Sacrament. Pilgrims, theologians, and townspeople flocked to her humble bedside to receive spiritual counsel, witnessing her unwavering, joyful peace amidst excruciating bodily suffering.
deathSummary: Saint Lydwina died peacefully on Easter Tuesday, 1433 at fifty-three; her relics were enshrined in Saint John's Church in Schiedam.

image.title: Saint Lydwina of Schiedam Sacred Icon

name: Saint Helena
title: Holy Empress Helena, Equal-to-the-Apostles, Discoverer of the True Cross
curatedBio: Flavia Julia Helena was born around 248 in Drepanum, Bithynia, the mother of Emperor Constantine the Great. Baptized a Christian in her sixties, she used her imperial position to clothe the poor, liberate prisoners, and fund churches. In 326, at age eighty, she embarked on an archaeological pilgrimage to Jerusalem. Excavating beneath the pagan temple of Venus on Golgotha, she discovered the Holy Sepulchre and the True Cross of Christ, building basilicas at Bethlehem and the Mount of Olives.
deathSummary: Saint Helena reposed peacefully around 330 in Nicomedia in the arms of her son Constantine; she was entombed in Rome.

image.title: Saint Helena Sacred Icon

name: Saint Rita of Cascia
title: Saint Rita of Cascia, Patroness of Impossible Causes and the Heartbroken
curatedBio: Margherita Lotti was born in Roccaporena, Umbria in 1381. Married to a harsh and violent man, she endured eighteen years of abuse with prayerful meekness, eventually converting her husband before he was murdered in a vendetta. Following the deaths of her two sons, she reconciled the feuding families and entered the Augustinian convent in Cascia. In 1442, meditating upon Christ’s Crown of Thorns, a thorn from the crucifix miraculously struck her forehead, leaving an open wound that lasted fifteen years.
deathSummary: Saint Rita died peacefully in Cascia on May 22, 1457 at seventy-six years of age; her body remains incorrupt.

image.title: Saint Rita of Cascia Sacred Icon

name: Saint Euphrosyne of Polotsk
title: Venerable Mother Euphrosyne of Polotsk, Patroness of Belarus
curatedBio: Predslava was born around 1104, the granddaughter of Prince Vseslav of Polotsk. Refusing all royal suitors, at age twelve she entered the convent of the Holy Savior in Polotsk, taking the name Euphrosyne. A gifted scholar, she spent her days copying liturgical manuscripts, using the proceeds to feed the poor. She founded monasteries for men and women, schools for young girls, and commissioned the renowned Cross of Saint Euphrosyne. In old age, she undertook a pilgrimage to the Holy Land.
deathSummary: Saint Euphrosyne reposed peacefully in Jerusalem on May 23, 1173 and was buried at the monastery of Saint Theodosius.

image.title: Saint Euphrosyne of Polotsk Sacred Icon

name: Saint Joanna the Myrrhbearer
title: Saint Joanna the Myrrhbearer, Wife of Chuza
curatedBio: Joanna was the aristocratic wife of Chuza, royal steward to King Herod Antipas. Healed by Jesus Christ of a debilitating infirmity, she abandoned court luxury to accompany the Savior throughout Galilee, providing for Him and the Apostles out of her personal financial resources. Standing steadfastly beneath the Cross at Calvary during the Crucifixion, Joanna went with Mary Magdalene on Easter dawn to anoint the body of Jesus, becoming one of the first heralds to proclaim His Resurrection to the Apostles.
deathSummary: Saint Joanna reposed peacefully in the first century after decades of apostolic service to the early Christian Church.

image.title: Saint Joanna the Myrrhbearer Sacred Icon

name: Saint Madeleine Sophie Barat
title: Saint Madeleine Sophie Barat, Foundress of the Society of the Sacred Heart
curatedBio: Born in Joigny, France in 1779 during a catastrophic town fire, Madeleine Sophie was educated in classical Greek, Latin, and philosophy by her brother, a Catholic priest who was imprisoned during the Reign of Terror. Recognizing that European society required profound spiritual regeneration following the French Revolution, in 1800 she founded the Society of the Sacred Heart. She governed the congregation for sixty-three years, establishing one hundred and five academies dedicated to the intellectual education of young women worldwide.
deathSummary: Saint Madeleine Sophie died peacefully in Paris on Ascension Thursday, May 25, 1865 at eighty-five years of age.

image.title: Saint Madeleine Sophie Barat Sacred Icon

name: Saint Mariana de Jesús de Paredes
title: Saint Mariana of Jesus de Paredes, Lily of Quito
curatedBio: Mariana was born in Quito, Ecuador in 1618 into the Spanish aristocracy and orphaned in early childhood. Under the guidance of the Jesuits, she took vows of perpetual virginity and lived as a solitary recluse in a quiet room of her sister's home. Sleeping on a wooden cross for only three hours nightly, she subsisted primarily on the Holy Eucharist. In 1645, when earthquakes and devastating plague struck Quito, Mariana offered her life publicly in church as a sacrificial victim for the city.
deathSummary: Immediately after her offering, the plague ceased; Mariana fell ill and died on May 26, 1645 at twenty-six years of age.

image.title: Saint Mariana de Jesús de Paredes Sacred Icon

name: Saint Melangell of Wales
title: Saint Melangell, Welsh Solitary Abbess and Patroness of Small Animals
curatedBio: Melangell was an Irish princess who fled across the sea to Wales around 590 to escape a forced marriage. Living as a solitary hermit in the remote Pennant Melangell valley for fifteen years, she slept on bare rock and prayed in wilderness silence. One day, Prince Brochwel of Powys was hunting a hare; the hare fled beneath Melangell’s robe, and the hunting hounds fell back howling, refusing to harm it. Deeply moved, the prince gave her the surrounding valley as an inviolable sanctuary.
deathSummary: Saint Melangell died peacefully in her valley around 641; her stone Romanesque shrine stands in Pennant Melangell Church.

image.title: Saint Melangell of Wales Sacred Icon

name: Saint Margaret Pole
title: Blessed Margaret Pole, Countess of Salisbury and Royal English Martyr
curatedBio: Margaret Plantagenet was born at Farleigh Castle in 1473, the daughter of the Duke of Clarence and niece of Kings Edward IV and Richard III. Created Countess of Salisbury and appointed governess to Princess Mary Tudor, she was one of the wealthiest noblewomen in Renaissance England. When her son Cardinal Reginald Pole wrote against King Henry VIII’s self-assumed ecclesiastical supremacy, the tyrant had the sixty-seven-year-old Countess imprisoned in the Tower of London without trial for two years.
mannerOfDeath: Decapitation at the Tower of London
deathSummary: Blessed Margaret was beheaded on Tower Green on May 28, 1541, dying with words: "Blessed are they who suffer persecution for righteousness' sake."

image.title: Saint Margaret Pole Sacred Icon

name: Saint Theodosia of Constantinople
title: Holy Virgin Nun Martyr Theodosia of Constantinople, Icon Defender
curatedBio: Theodosia was born in Constantinople and entered the monastery of Saint Anastasia. In 726, when Emperor Leo the Isaurian ordered the public destruction of holy icons, an imperial guard ascended a ladder to shatter the revered bronze icon of Christ above the Chalke Gate of the imperial palace. Theodosia and a company of courageous women shook the ladder to defend the sacred icon, causing the soldier to plunge to his death. Arrested, she refused to deny the veneration of Christ’s holy image.
mannerOfDeath: Ram's horn driven through her throat
deathSummary: An executioner drove a ram's horn through Saint Theodosia's throat in the Forum of the Bull around 729.

image.title: Saint Theodosia of Constantinople Sacred Icon

name: Saint Joan of Arc
title: Saint Joan of Arc, The Maid of Orléans, Patroness of France
curatedBio: Born in Domrémy, France in 1412 into a peasant family, Joan was twelve when she began hearing the celestial voices of Saint Michael the Archangel, Saint Catherine of Alexandria, and Saint Margaret of Antioch. Guided by these heavenly voices, seventeen-year-old Joan went to Charles VII, dressed in armor, and lifted the siege of Orléans in nine days, leading the Dauphin to his coronation at Reims. Captured by the Burgundians in 1430, she was sold to the English and subjected to a corrupt ecclesiastical trial.
deathSummary: Saint Joan was burned at the stake in Rouen on May 30, 1431 at nineteen, gazing upon a raised crucifix and crying out "Jesus!"

image.title: Saint Joan of Arc Sacred Icon

name: Saint Petronilla of Rome
title: Holy Virgin Martyr Petronilla of Rome
curatedBio: Petronilla was a first-century Roman virgin maiden, celebrated in ancient Roman martyrologies as the spiritual daughter of Saint Peter the Apostle. Stricken with a chronic paralytic illness, Peter healed her to demonstrate God's miraculous power, after which she returned willingly to her bed of suffering in patient thanksgiving. When Roman nobleman Flaccus sought her in marriage, Petronilla asked for three days to consider; spending the three days in fasting and prayer, she received the Holy Mysteries and reposed in immaculate virginity.
deathSummary: Saint Petronilla died peacefully in Rome at the conclusion of three days of prayer; her ancient sarcophagus was in Saint Peter's Basilica.

image.title: Saint Petronilla of Rome Sacred Icon

name: Saint Charita of Rome
title: Holy Martyr Charita of Rome, Disciple of Saint Justin Martyr
curatedBio: Charita was a devout Christian woman living in Rome during the reign of Emperor Marcus Aurelius. A devoted disciple of the Christian philosopher Saint Justin Martyr, she attended his philosophical school in Rome, studying the defense of the Christian faith. When Justin and his students were arrested by the Roman prefect Rusticus in 165 for refusing to offer incense to pagan idols, Charita boldly confessed her faith in Jesus Christ, refusing to apostatize under threat of death.
deathSummary: Saint Charita was scourged and beheaded in Rome around 165 alongside Saint Justin Martyr and their companions.

image.title: Saint Charita of Rome Sacred Icon

name: Saint Blandina of Lyon
title: Holy Virgin Martyr Blandina of Lyon, Patroness of Lyon
curatedBio: Blandina was an enslaved Christian maiden living in Lugdunum (modern Lyon, France) during the ferocious persecutions under Emperor Marcus Aurelius in 177. Despite her frail physical stature, Blandina endured days of torture that exhausted relays of executioners, continually crying out: "I am a Christian, and among us no evil is done!" Bound to a stake in the amphitheater as meat for wild beasts that refused to touch her, she inspired her fellow martyrs with superhuman fortitude.
mannerOfDeath: Enclosed in a net and gored by a wild bull
deathSummary: After scourging, roasting upon an iron chair, and goring by a bull, Saint Blandina was dispatched by the sword in Lyon in 177.

image.title: Saint Blandina of Lyon Sacred Icon

name: Saint Clotilde
title: Saint Clotilde, Queen of the Franks and Patroness of Brides
curatedBio: Clotilde was a Burgundian Christian princess born around 475. In 493 she married King Clovis I of the Salian Franks, who remained a pagan. Through her gentle persuasion, patient prayer, and moral witness, Clovis promised during the desperate Battle of Tolbiac in 496 to accept baptism if granted victory. Clovis was baptized alongside three thousand Frankish warriors on Christmas Day 496, establishing France as the "Eldest Daughter of the Church".
deathSummary: Queen Clotilde died peacefully in Tours on June 3, 545 at Saint Martin's Basilica; she was buried in Paris.

image.title: Saint Clotilde Sacred Icon

name: Saint Saturnina of Arras
title: Holy Virgin Martyr Saturnina of Arras
curatedBio: Saturnina was an eighth-century noble maiden of Germany who fled across the Rhine to avoid a forced marriage to an unyielding pagan suitor. Settling in the region of Arras in northern Gaul, she lived as a consecrated virgin, dedicating her days to prayer and instructing peasant children in the Gospel. Her relentless suitor pursued her across Gaul, discovering her kneeling in prayer in a forest near Sains-lès-Marquion, where he drew his sword in fury.
deathSummary: Saint Saturnina was beheaded at Sains-lès-Marquion around 750; her relics are venerated in the Cathedral of Tournai.

image.title: Saint Saturnina of Arras Sacred Icon

name: Saint Valeria of Caesarea
title: Holy Martyr Valeria of Caesarea in Palestine
curatedBio: Valeria was a Christian woman living in Caesarea Maritima in Palestine during the persecutions of Emperor Diocletian around 304. Alongside her Christian companions Cyria and Zenaida, she withdrew to a quiet house outside the city walls, dedicating herself to fasting, vigils, and persistent intercessory prayer for the preservation of the persecuted Church. Denounced to Roman governor Galerius for gathering Christians in prayer, Valeria refused to sacrifice to idols, persevering through cruel scourging.
deathSummary: Saint Valeria was tortured and crowned with martyrdom at Caesarea in Palestine around 304.

image.title: Saint Valeria of Caesarea Sacred Icon

name: Saint Candida of Rome
title: Holy Virgin Martyr Candida of Rome
curatedBio: Candida was an early Christian maiden of Rome living during the persecutions under Emperor Diocletian. Consecrating her virginity to Jesus Christ, she was arrested on the Ostian Way for visiting and burying the bodies of martyred Christians. Brought before the Roman magistrate, she boldly proclaimed her allegiance to the Savior and refused to sacrifice to pagan idols. Stripped and severely beaten with rods, she was led to the Portuensian Way where she was crowned with martyrdom.
mannerOfDeath: Beaten to death with leaded scourges
deathSummary: Saint Candida was martyred outside Rome around 304 and buried in the Catacombs of Saint Felix on the Via Portuense.

image.title: Saint Candida of Rome Sacred Icon

name: Saint Maria Teresa Soubiran
title: Blessed Maria Teresa Soubiran, Foundress of the Sisters of Marie Auxiliatrice
curatedBio: Sophie Soubiran was born in Castelnaudary, France in 1820. In 1854 she founded the Sisters of Marie Auxiliatrice, uniting perpetual adoration of the Blessed Sacrament with compassionate social work for destitute, overworked young factory women in Paris. In an extraordinary trial of sanctity, a manipulative assistant falsely accused Mother Soubiran, expelling her from her own congregation in 1874. She lived her final fifteen years in silent humility as an anonymous sister in Paris.
deathSummary: Blessed Maria Teresa died peacefully in Paris on June 7, 1889 at sixty-nine; her innocence was fully restored post-mortem.

image.title: Saint Maria Teresa Soubiran Sacred Icon

name: Saint Melania the Elder
title: Saint Melania the Elder, Roman Patrician and Desert Mother of Jerusalem
curatedBio: Melania was born in Spain around 350 into the Roman senatorial aristocracy. Widowed at twenty-two after losing her husband and two sons, she placed her remaining son in Roman guardianship, sold her vast estates, and sailed to Egypt to visit the Desert Fathers of Nitria. When Arian persecutions struck the Egyptian monasteries, Melania personally financed the exiled monks in Palestine. In 375, she founded a double monastery on the Mount of Olives in Jerusalem, guiding fifty nuns in prayer and scholarly translation.
deathSummary: Saint Melania reposed peacefully in Jerusalem around 410 at sixty years of age.

image.title: Saint Melania the Elder Sacred Icon

name: Saint Pelagia of Antioch
title: Holy Virgin Martyr Pelagia of Antioch, Crowned with Glory
curatedBio: Pelagia was a fifteen-year-old Christian maiden living in Antioch during the Diocletian persecutions. When soldiers surrounded her home to drag her to trial and violation in a brothel, she asked permission to go upstairs to dress. Clothed in bridal white, she prayed to preserve her virginal dedication to Christ intact, then threw herself from the parapet into the courtyard below. Praised by Saint John Chrysostom in two sermons, her death was hailed as an act of holy martyrdom.
mannerOfDeath: Leapt from roof to preserve virginity
deathSummary: Saint Pelagia yielded her pure spirit to God in Antioch around 303; her feast was observed universally across early Christendom.

image.title: Saint Pelagia of Antioch Sacred Icon

name: Saint Margaret of Scotland
title: Saint Margaret of Scotland, Queen and Benefactress of the Poor
curatedBio: Born in Hungary around 1045 into the English royal house of Wessex, Margaret fled England following the Norman Conquest and married King Malcolm III of Scotland in 1070. As Queen of Scots, she brought religious, liturgical, and cultural renewal to Scotland, reforming church synods and founding Dunfermline Abbey. Celebrated for extraordinary personal charity, she washed the feet of six poor beggars every morning and secretly emptied the royal treasury to feed starving highland peasants.
deathSummary: Queen Margaret died in Edinburgh Castle on November 16, 1093 at forty-eight; her feast is kept on June 10.

image.title: Saint Margaret of Scotland Sacred Icon

name: Saint Paula Frassinetti
title: Saint Paula Frassinetti, Foundress of the Sisters of Saint Dorothy
curatedBio: Paula was born in Genoa in 1809. In 1834 at Quinto near Genoa, she gathered six companions to establish a free primary school for impoverished girls, founding the Sisters of Saint Dorothy. Enduring extreme poverty, internal dissent, and anti-clerical hostility in nineteenth-century Italy, she relocated the motherhouse to Saint Onofrio on the Janiculum Hill in Rome in 1844, expanding the congregation across Europe and establishing flourishing educational missions in Brazil.
deathSummary: Saint Paula died of pneumonia in Rome on June 11, 1884 at seventy-four; her body remains incorrupt at Sant'Onofrio.

image.title: Saint Paula Frassinetti Sacred Icon

name: Saint Cunigunde of Poland
title: Saint Kinga (Cunigunde) of Poland, Queen and Poor Clare Abbess
curatedBio: Kinga was born in 1224, the daughter of King Béla IV of Hungary and niece of Saint Elizabeth of Hungary. Married to Boleslaus V the Chaste, High Duke of Poland, both spouses took a mutual vow of perpetual chastity before the Bishop of Kraków. Using her dowry to ransom prisoners and rebuild Polish towns destroyed by the Mongol invasions, she founded the salt mines of Wieliczka and the Poor Clare monastery of Stary Sącz, where she retired as a nun upon her husband’s death.
deathSummary: Saint Kinga died peacefully at Stary Sącz on July 24, 1292 at sixty-eight years of age.

image.title: Saint Cunigunde of Poland Sacred Icon

name: Saint Aquilina of Byblos
title: Holy Virgin Martyr Aquilina of Byblos
curatedBio: Aquilina was a twelve-year-old Christian girl living in Byblos (Phoenicia) during the Diocletian persecutions. Converted by Bishop Euthalius, she was denounced to Roman magistrate Volusian for teaching Christianity to her young school companions. Brought before the tribunal, she refused to worship idols. The magistrate ordered red-hot needles driven through her ears and temples, burning her brain; miraculously revived by an angel in prison, she knelt in thanksgiving before her final crown.
deathSummary: Saint Aquilina was beheaded at Byblos on June 13, 293 at twelve years of age; sweet-scented myrrh flowed from her relics.

image.title: Saint Aquilina of Byblos Sacred Icon

name: Blessed Castora Gabrielli
title: Blessed Castora Gabrielli, Franciscan Penitent of Gubbio
curatedBio: Castora was born in Gubbio, Umbria into the noble Gabrielli family. Married to the nobleman Santuccio Sanfonerio, she suffered twenty-five years of verbal violence, domestic cruelty, and contempt from her unfaithful husband with heroic meekness and unceasing prayer. Following his death, she distributed her wealth to the indigent and entered the Third Order of Saint Francis, spending her remaining years in mystical contemplation and serving the sick in the hospitals of Gubbio.
deathSummary: Blessed Castora died peacefully in Gubbio on June 14, 1391; her relics are venerated in the Church of San Francesco.

image.title: Blessed Castora Gabrielli Sacred Icon

name: Saint Germaine Cousin
title: Saint Germaine Cousin, The Little Shepherdess of Pibrac
curatedBio: Born in Pibrac near Toulouse in 1579, Germaine was born with a deformed right hand and suffered from severe scrofula. Abused and starved by her cruel stepmother, she was forced to sleep in the stable on straw and tend sheep in the forest. Despite severe privation, she shared her meager crusts with beggars, led village children in prayer, and attended daily Mass. Miraculously, sheep left under the protection of her staff were never attacked by wolves in the forest.
deathSummary: Saint Germaine died peacefully on her straw bed in the stable on June 15, 1601 at twenty-two; her body was found incorrupt in 1644.

image.title: Saint Germaine Cousin Sacred Icon

name: Saint Julitta of Tarsus
title: Holy Martyr Julitta and her Child Cyricus of Tarsus
curatedBio: Julitta was a wealthy Christian noblewoman living in Iconium (Asia Minor) during the Diocletian persecutions. Fleeing with her three-year-old son Cyricus to Tarsus, she was arrested by governor Alexander. Refusing to sacrifice to idols, Julitta was scourged. As she was beaten, little Cyricus struggled in the governor's arms, crying out: "I am a Christian too!" and scratching the tyrant’s face. Enraged, the governor threw the toddler down the stone steps, killing him instantly.
deathSummary: Thanking God that her child had preceded her to paradise, Saint Julitta was beheaded at Tarsus on June 16, 304.

image.title: Saint Julitta of Tarsus Sacred Icon

name: Saint Emily de Vialar
title: Saint Emily de Vialar, Foundress of the Sisters of Saint Joseph of the Apparition
curatedBio: Anne Marguerite Émilie de Vialar was born in Gaillac, France in 1797 into the provincial nobility. Following her mother's early death, she spent fifteen years caring for the poor and sick in her hometown. In 1832, inheriting a substantial fortune from her grandfather, she purchased a house in Gaillac and founded the Sisters of Saint Joseph of the Apparition. In 1835 she sailed to Algiers, establishing schools and hospitals across North Africa, Greece, and the Ottoman Empire.
deathSummary: Saint Emily died peacefully in Marseille on August 24, 1856 at fifty-eight years of age; her feast is kept on June 17.

image.title: Saint Emily de Vialar Sacred Icon

name: Saint Elizabeth of Schönau
title: Saint Elizabeth of Schönau, Benedictine Mystic and Visionary
curatedBio: Born near Bonn in 1129, Elizabeth entered the double monastery of Schönau Abbey at age twelve, making profession as a Benedictine nun in 1147. From age twenty-three she experienced profound ecstatic visions of the heavenly court, the Virgin Mary, and the martyrdom of Saint Ursula and her companions. A spiritual confidante and correspondent of Saint Hildegard of Bingen, Elizabeth recorded her visionary theological dialogues in three celebrated Latin books, Liber Visionum, guiding medieval monastic reform.
deathSummary: Saint Elizabeth died peacefully at Schönau Abbey on June 18, 1164 at thirty-five years of age.

image.title: Saint Elizabeth of Schönau Sacred Icon

name: Saint Juliana Falconieri
title: Saint Juliana Falconieri, Foundress of the Servite Religious Sisters
curatedBio: Born in Florence in 1270 into the noble Falconieri family, Juliana refused all marriage proposals arranged by her family, receiving the habit of the Servants of Mary (Servites) from her uncle, Saint Alexis Falconieri. In 1304, she founded the Mantellate (Servite Tertiary Sisters), dedicating her life to nursing the sick, reconciling feuding factions in Florence, and practicing intense mortification. On her deathbed, unable to ingest food, the Holy Host placed upon her chest miraculously vanished into her flesh.
deathSummary: Saint Juliana died peacefully in Florence on June 19, 1341 at seventy-one; a cross-shaped mark remained upon her chest.

image.title: Saint Juliana Falconieri Sacred Icon

name: Saint Florence of Poitiers
title: Saint Florence of Poitiers, Virgin Hermit and Disciple of Saint Hilary
curatedBio: Florence was a fourth-century young pagan maiden living in Phrygia (Asia Minor). When Saint Hilary of Poitiers was exiled to Phrygia by Emperor Constantius II for defending the Nicene faith against Arianism, Florence heard him preach Christ and was converted and baptized. When Hilary was recalled to Gaul in 360, Florence followed him to Poitiers, where Hilary established her in a solitary hermitage near Comblé (Celle-l’Evescault). She spent her life in prayer, fasting, and contemplation.
deathSummary: Saint Florence reposed peacefully in her hermitage at Comblé around 366 at twenty-nine years of age.

image.title: Saint Florence of Poitiers Sacred Icon

name: Saint Demetria of Rome
title: Holy Virgin Martyr Demetria of Rome
curatedBio: Demetria was the daughter of Saint Flavian and Saint Dafrosa, and the sister of Saint Bibiana. During the persecutions of Roman Emperor Julian the Apostate in 362, when her noble parents were martyred for their Christian confession, Demetria and Bibiana were stripped of their ancestral estate and confined in their home without food. Hauled before the Roman governor Apronianus, Demetria boldly proclaimed her faith in Jesus Christ, falling dead at the tribunal from exhaustion and supernatural peace.
mannerOfDeath: Died during tribunal confession under Julian the Apostate
deathSummary: Saint Demetria yielded her spirit to God at the Roman tribunal on June 21, 362; her body was buried near the Church of Santa Bibiana.

image.title: Saint Demetria of Rome Sacred Icon

name: Saint Alena of Forest
title: Holy Virgin Martyr Alena of Forest (Brussels)
curatedBio: Alena was a seventh-century noble maiden born in Dilbeek near Brussels to a pagan Frankish lord named Levold. Secretly drawn to the Christian faith, she slipped out of her father's castle across the river to attend night vigils at the Christian church in Forest. When her father discovered her secret Christian devotion, he dispatched guards to drag her home. Resisting their force while clinging to a tree trunk, the guards brutally severed her arm.
mannerOfDeath: Arm severed by soldiers during arrest
deathSummary: Saint Alena bled to death from her severed arm at Forest around 640; an angel carried her severed limb to the church altar.

image.title: Saint Alena of Forest Sacred Icon

name: Saint Audrey of Ely
title: Saint Audrey (Æthelthryth), Anglo-Saxon Queen and Abbess of Ely
curatedBio: Æthelthryth was born in Exning, Suffolk around 636, the daughter of King Anna of East Anglia. Married for political reasons first to Tondberht and later to King Ecgfrith of Northumbria, she preserved her perpetual virginity throughout twelve years of royal marriage. Receiving the veil from Saint Wilfrid in 672, she founded the great double monastery of Ely on an island in the fens, governing her community with austere humility and wearing only coarse wool.
deathSummary: Saint Audrey died at Ely on June 23, 679; sixteen years later her body was found incorrupt; her name originated the word "tawdry".

image.title: Saint Audrey of Ely Sacred Icon

name: Saint Elizabeth
title: Righteous Elizabeth, Mother of Saint John the Baptist
curatedBio: Elizabeth was of the lineage of Aaron, the righteous wife of the priest Zechariah, living in the hill country of Judea. Barren and advanced in years, the Archangel Gabriel announced to Zechariah that she would bear the Forerunner of the Lord. When the Virgin Mary visited her, Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit and cried out: "Blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb!" During Herod’s slaughter of the innocents, a mountain miraculously opened to shelter Elizabeth and John.
deathSummary: Saint Elizabeth reposed peacefully in the Judean wilderness forty days after Zechariah’s martyrdom in the Temple.

image.title: Saint Elizabeth Sacred Icon

name: Saint Febronia of Nisibis
title: Holy Virgin Martyr Febronia of Nisibis
curatedBio: Febronia was an exceptionally beautiful and scholarly nun in a monastery of fifty virgins in Nisibis, Mesopotamia under her aunt Abbess Bryene. When Roman soldiers under Selenus and Lysimachus surrounded the city to execute Christians during the Diocletian persecutions, the sisters fled, but Febronia remained behind caring for the bedridden. Arrested and offered royal wealth if she apostatized, eighteen-year-old Febronia refused. Stripped, racked, and having her teeth and breasts severed, she prayed unceasingly.
deathSummary: Saint Febronia was beheaded at Nisibis around 304; the commander Lysimachus was so stricken that he converted and became a monk.

image.title: Saint Febronia of Nisibis Sacred Icon

name: Saint Perseveranda
title: Saint Perseveranda (Pecinna), Holy Virgin of Poitou
curatedBio: Perseveranda was an early Christian maiden born in Poitou in western Gaul. Consecrating her virginity to Jesus Christ, she lived an austere communal life of prayer alongside her holy sisters in the diocese of Poitiers. Celebrated for persevering fidelity during periods of barbarian unrest and civil strife in late antique Gaul, she instructed generations of Christian women in scripture and holy chastity, giving rise to the shrine of Sainte-Pézenne near Niort.
deathSummary: Saint Perseveranda reposed peacefully in Poitou around 726; her tomb is in Sainte-Pézenne.

image.title: Saint Perseveranda Sacred Icon

name: Saint Joanna the Myrrhbearer
title: Righteous Joanna the Myrrhbearer, Witness of the Resurrection
curatedBio: Wife of Chuza, steward to King Herod Antipas, Joanna was healed of sickness by Jesus Christ and became His devoted disciple. Supporting the apostolic company out of her personal means throughout Judea, she stood with Mary beneath the Cross during the Crucifixion and returned on the third day to anoint Christ’s body, receiving from the angels the proclamation of the Resurrection. She served the early Church in Jerusalem as a motherly pillar of charity.
deathSummary: Saint Joanna reposed peacefully in the first century; celebrated on June 27 and the Sunday of the Myrrhbearers.

image.title: Saint Joanna the Myrrhbearer Sacred Icon

name: Saint Potamiaena of Alexandria
title: Holy Virgin Martyr Potamiaena of Alexandria
curatedBio: Potamiaena was a Christian maiden of extraordinary beauty and wisdom living in Alexandria during the persecution under Roman prefect Aquila around 205. Subjected to judicial torture because of her chaste refusal of sexual violation, she was threatened with immersion in a cauldron of boiling pitch unless she blasphemed Christ. Asking that the pitch be poured over her drop by drop so her tormentors might witness her patience, the officer Basilides was so moved by her fortitude that he converted to Christ.
deathSummary: Saint Potamiaena was martyred in boiling pitch at Alexandria around 205 alongside her mother Saint Marcella.

image.title: Saint Potamiaena of Alexandria Sacred Icon

name: Saint Mary, Mother of John Mark
title: Saint Mary of Jerusalem, Mother of Saint Mark the Evangelist
curatedBio: Mary was a devout Christian matron living in Jerusalem, a relative of Saint Barnabas and mother of Saint Mark the Evangelist. Her spacious home in Jerusalem served as a primary gathering place and house church for the infant Christian community. When the Apostle Peter was miraculously liberated from prison by an angel in Acts 12, he went directly to Mary’s house, where the Apostles and disciples were gathered in fervent prayer for his deliverance.
deathSummary: Saint Mary reposed peacefully in Jerusalem in the first century after dedicating her house and wealth to the Apostles.

image.title: Saint Mary, Mother of John Mark Sacred Icon

name: Saint Lucina of Rome
title: Saint Lucina of Rome, Matron and Caregiver of Martyrs
curatedBio: Lucina was a wealthy Roman Christian matron of the noble Anician gens who placed her life and fortune at the service of the persecuted Church in the first century. Instructed by the Apostles Peter and Paul, she visited imprisoned Christians in the Mamertine Prison, provided nourishment to confessors, and retrieved the bodies of martyred saints for sacred burial in her private vineyard catacombs on the Appian and Ostian Ways, where Saint Paul was initially interred.
deathSummary: Saint Lucina reposed peacefully in Rome after surviving imperial persecution and sheltering the apostolic faithful.

image.title: Saint Lucina of Rome Sacred Icon

name: Righteous Esther
title: Righteous Queen Esther, Deliverer of her People
curatedBio: Esther was an orphan maiden of the tribe of Benjamin raised in Susa by her cousin Mordecai during the Babylonian captivity. Chosen as queen by Persian King Ahasuerus (Xerxes I), she concealed her Jewish identity until royal minister Haman plotted the extermination of all Jews in the empire. Urged by Mordecai and calling her people to three days of fasting and prayer, Esther boldly risked her life by entering the king's presence unsummoned, thwarting the genocidal plot and delivering her nation.
deathSummary: Queen Esther reposed peacefully in Persia in the fifth century BC; her tomb in Hamadan, Iran is venerated to this day.

image.title: Righteous Esther Sacred Icon

name: Saint Monegundis of Chartres
title: Saint Monegundis, Solitary Recluse of Tours
curatedBio: Monegundis was born into a prominent family in Chartres in the sixth century. Following the tragic death of her two young daughters from fever, she sank into profound mourning before receiving divine illumination to dedicate her grief entirely to God. With her husband's consent, she built a solitary anchorite cell in Chartres, living on barley bread and water. Later moving to Tours near the tomb of Saint Martin, she established a monastery where she healed the blind and sick.
deathSummary: Saint Monegundis reposed peacefully in Tours around 570; her life was recorded by Saint Gregory of Tours.

image.title: Saint Monegundis of Chartres Sacred Icon

name: Saint Anatolia of Rome
title: Holy Virgin Martyr Anatolia of Rome
curatedBio: Anatolia was a noble Christian maiden of Rome during the Decian persecution around 250. When her aristocratic pagan suitor Titus Aurelius was rejected because of her virginal dedication to Christ, he denounced her to the Roman magistrate. Confined to an estate in Picenum and subjected to venomous serpents that refused to bite her, she converted the executioner Audax. Condemned to death by sword, Anatolia knelt in serene prayer, sealing her bridal fidelity to Jesus Christ.
deathSummary: Saint Anatolia was beheaded in Picenum around 250; her relics are venerated in the Abbey of Farfa.

image.title: Saint Anatolia of Rome Sacred Icon

name: Saint Elizabeth of Portugal
title: Saint Elizabeth of Aragon, Queen of Portugal and Peacemaker
curatedBio: Born in Zaragoza in 1271, Elizabeth was the daughter of King Peter III of Aragon and great-niece of Saint Elizabeth of Hungary. Married at twelve to King Denis of Portugal, she lived forty years of heroic patience amidst her husband's infidelity, raising his illegitimate children alongside her own. Renowned as the Peacemaker, on multiple occasions she rode unarmed onto the battlefield between feuding kings and armies, halting wars through prayer and moral authority.
deathSummary: Saint Elizabeth died peacefully in Estremoz on July 4, 1336 at sixty-five; her body was found incorrupt at Coimbra.

image.title: Saint Elizabeth of Portugal Sacred Icon

name: Saint Zoe of Rome
title: Holy Martyr Zoe of Rome, Wife of Saint Nicostratus
curatedBio: Zoe was the wife of Nicostratus, high jailer of Rome under Emperor Diocletian. Stricken mute for six years by a severe affliction of the throat, when Saint Sebastian visited Christian prisoners in her home, Zoe fell at Sebastian’s feet in silent supplication. Sebastian made the sign of the cross over her mouth, and her speech was immediately restored, praising God. Baptized alongside her husband and thirty-three household members, she was arrested while praying at Saint Peter's tomb.
mannerOfDeath: Hanged by her hair over a fire of foul dung
deathSummary: Saint Zoe was hanged by her hair over suffocating smoke and drowned in the Tiber River around 286.

image.title: Saint Zoe of Rome Sacred Icon

name: Saint Maria Goretti
title: Saint Maria Goretti, Virgin Martyr of Purity and Forgiveness
curatedBio: Maria was born in Corinaldo, Italy in 1890 into an impoverished sharecropping family that moved to the malaria-ridden marshes of Ferriere di Conca. Following her father's death, eleven-year-old Maria cooked, washed, and looked after her younger siblings while her mother labored in the fields. On July 5, 1902, twenty-year-old Alessandro Serenelli attempted to rape her; Maria resisted fiercely, warning him that he was committing a mortal sin. Alessandro stabbed her fourteen times with an awl.
deathSummary: Before dying on July 6, 1902 at eleven, Maria forgave Alessandro, praying that he would join her in paradise; her forgiveness led to his complete repentance.

image.title: Saint Maria Goretti Sacred Icon

name: Saint Kyriake of Nicomedia
title: Holy Great Martyr Kyriake (Dominica) of Nicomedia
curatedBio: Kyriake was born in Nicomedia to devout Christian parents who had prayed for a child, naming her Kyriake because she was born on the Lord's Day (Kyriake in Greek, Dominica in Latin). When the Diocletian persecutions began, her parents were exiled and Kyriake was brought before Caesar Maximian. Scourged, hung by her hair, and cast to hungry wild beasts that knelt and licked her feet, she converted hundreds of witnesses before an angel announced her heavenly crown.
mannerOfDeath: Yielded her spirit in prayer before decapitation
deathSummary: As the executioner raised his sword, Saint Kyriake knelt in prayer and yielded her soul directly to God around 303 in Nicomedia.

image.title: Saint Kyriake of Nicomedia Sacred Icon

name: Saint Landrada of Munsterbilzen
title: Saint Landrada, Frankish Abbess of Munsterbilzen
curatedBio: Landrada was a seventh-century noble Austrasian maiden who renounced secular wealth and courtly marriage to live as a solitary ascetic in the forest of Belisia (modern Bilzen, Belgium). Under the spiritual direction of Saint Lambert of Maastricht, she founded the monastery of Munsterbilzen around 670, attracting daughters of Frankish nobility to lives of prayer, liturgical choral chant, and care for the indigent.
deathSummary: Saint Landrada died peacefully at Munsterbilzen Abbey on July 8, 690; her tomb became a celebrated pilgrimage center.

image.title: Saint Landrada of Munsterbilzen Sacred Icon

name: Saint Veronica Giuliani
title: Saint Veronica Giuliani, Capuchin Mystic and Stigmatist
curatedBio: Ursula Giuliani was born in Mercatello sul Metauro, Italy in 1660. Entering the Capuchin Poor Clares in Città di Castello at age seventeen, she took the name Veronica. In 1697 she received the sacred stigmata on her hands, feet, and side, followed by an imprint of the Crown of Thorns upon her head. Subjected to humiliating ecclesiastical inquisitions and stripped of office to test her obedience, her heroic humility convinced her superiors. Her ten-volume spiritual diary remains a classic of mystical literature.
deathSummary: Saint Veronica died peacefully in Città di Castello on July 9, 1727 at sixty-six years of age; an autopsy revealed symbols of Christ's Passion imprinted on her heart.

image.title: Saint Veronica Giuliani Sacred Icon

name: Saint Felicity of Rome
title: Holy Martyr Felicity of Rome and her Seven Sons
curatedBio: Felicity was a noble Roman Christian widow living during the reign of Emperor Antoninus Pius. After her husband's death, she consecrated her life to fasting, vigils, and distributing her estate to the poor while raising her seven sons: Januarius, Felix, Philip, Silvanus, Alexander, Vitalis, and Martial. Denounced by pagan priests for converting Roman patricians, Felicity was commanded to sacrifice. Refusing, she watched each of her seven sons martyred before her eyes, encouraging them to win eternal glory.
deathSummary: Saint Felicity was beheaded in Rome around 165 four months after witnessing the martyrdom of her seven sons.

image.title: Saint Felicity of Rome Sacred Icon

name: Saint Olga of Kiev
title: Holy Princess Olga of Kiev, Equal-to-the-Apostles, Grand Duchess of Rus
curatedBio: Olga was born in Pskov around 890 and married Grand Prince Igor I of Kiev. Following Igor’s murder by the Drevlians in 945, Olga served as regent for her young son Sviatoslav I, ruling Kievan Rus with remarkable political and administrative brilliance. Traveling to Constantinople in 957, she received holy baptism from Patriarch Polyeuktos with Emperor Constantine VII as godfather, taking the name Helena. She preached Christ throughout Rus, preparing the spiritual ground for the Christianization of Rus under her grandson Saint Vladimir.
deathSummary: Saint Olga reposed peacefully in Kiev on July 11, 969 at approximately seventy-nine years of age; her incorrupt relics rested in the Tithe Church.

image.title: Saint Olga of Kiev Sacred Icon

name: Saint Veronica
title: Saint Veronica, The Woman with the Issue of Blood
curatedBio: According to Christian tradition, Veronica was the woman suffering from a twelve-year hemorrhage recorded in the Gospels who touched the hem of Jesus’s garment and was immediately healed. As Christ carried His heavy Cross along the Via Dolorosa to Mount Calvary, Veronica stepped out from the weeping crowd, took her linen veil, and tenderly wiped the blood and sweat from His holy face. Miraculously, the true image (Vera Icon) of Christ's sacred countenance was permanently imprinted upon her cloth.
deathSummary: Saint Veronica reposed peacefully in Rome in the first century; her sacred veil has been venerated at Saint Peter's Basilica for centuries.

image.title: Saint Veronica Sacred Icon

name: Saint Clelia Barbieri
title: Saint Clelia Barbieri, Youngest Foundress in Church History
curatedBio: Born in San Giovanni in Persiceto near Bologna in 1847 into extreme poverty, Clelia spun hemp and assisted her parish priest by teaching catechism from age fourteen. In 1868, at only twenty-one, she united with three companions to establish the Little Sisters of the Mother of Sorrows (Minime dell'Addolorata), dedicating their community to caring for the abandoned elderly, educating poor children, and nursing the sick in rural Italian villages.
deathSummary: Saint Clelia died of tuberculosis on July 13, 1870 at twenty-three; her miraculous voice is heard singing alongside her sisters' choir to this day.

image.title: Saint Clelia Barbieri Sacred Icon

name: Saint Kateri Tekakwitha
title: Saint Kateri Tekakwitha, Lily of the Mohawks
curatedBio: Tekakwitha was born in 1656 at Ossernenon in Mohawk country. Orphaned at age four by smallpox that impaired her eyesight and scarred her face, she lived a life of quiet recollection. Baptized by Jesuit missionary Father Jacques de Lamberville in 1676, she made a vow of perpetual virginity—unheard of among her people. Fleeing tribal hostility, she walked two hundred miles to Kahnawake near Montreal, where she spent her final years in prayer, penance, and caring for elderly sick villagers.
deathSummary: Saint Kateri died at Kahnawake on Holy Wednesday, April 17, 1680 at twenty-four; celebrated on July 14 in the United States.

image.title: Saint Kateri Tekakwitha Sacred Icon

name: Saint Edith of Polesworth
title: Saint Edith of Polesworth, Anglo-Saxon Queen and Abbess
curatedBio: Edith was the daughter of King Edward the Elder and sister of King Æthelstan of England. In 925 she married the Viking ruler King Sihtric Cáech of York, who agreed to receive Christian baptism. Following Sihtric's early death in 927, Edith returned to the Midlands, taking the veil and founding the Benedictine nunnery of Polesworth Abbey in Warwickshire. She lived thirty years of exemplary prayer, study of scripture, and generous distribution of royal revenues to poor Mercian peasants.
deathSummary: Saint Edith reposed peacefully at Polesworth Abbey around 960; her shrine in Warwickshire was a major pilgrimage site.

image.title: Saint Edith of Polesworth Sacred Icon

name: Saint Marie-Madeleine Postel
title: Saint Marie-Madeleine Postel, Foundress of the Sisters of Christian Schools of Mercy
curatedBio: Julie Postel was born in Barfleur, Normandy in 1756. During the violent anti-clerical persecutions of the French Revolution, she boldly sheltered non-juring priests in her home, kept the Blessed Sacrament concealed in a wardrobe, and conducted secret clandestine prayer services for Catholic villagers. In 1807, at age fifty-one, she founded the Sisters of the Christian Schools of Mercy, rebuilding the ruined Benedictine Abbey of Saint-Sauveur-le-Vicomte with her own hands and opening free schools for girls.
deathSummary: Saint Marie-Madeleine died peacefully at Saint-Sauveur-le-Vicomte on July 16, 1846 at eighty-nine years of age.

image.title: Saint Marie-Madeleine Postel Sacred Icon

name: Saint Marina of Antioch
title: Holy Great Martyr Marina (Margaret) of Antioch
curatedBio: Marina was born in Pisidian Antioch, the daughter of a pagan priest named Aedesius. Taught the Christian faith by her Christian foster mother, Marina consecrated her virginity to Jesus Christ at age fifteen. Roman governor Olybrius was enchanted by her beauty and sought to marry her, but Marina declared: "I am a servant of Jesus Christ." Thrown into a dungeon, she saw a terrifying dragon symbolizing Satan, which she trampled underfoot with the sign of the cross.
deathSummary: After surviving torture by fire and water, Saint Marina was beheaded at Antioch around 304 under Diocletian.

image.title: Saint Marina of Antioch Sacred Icon

name: Saint Elizabeth the New Martyr
title: Holy New Martyr Grand Duchess Elizabeth Feodorovna of Russia
curatedBio: Princess Elisabeth of Hesse and by Rhine was the granddaughter of Queen Victoria and married Grand Duke Sergei Alexandrovich of Russia, converting to Orthodoxy. Following her husband's assassination in 1905, Elizabeth visited his murderer in prison to forgive him. Selling her royal jewelry, she founded the Martha and Mary Convent of Mercy in Moscow, serving as abbess and nursing Moscow’s poorest sick citizens. Arrested by the Bolsheviks in 1918, she was transported to Alapayevsk in the Urals.
mannerOfDeath: Thrown alive into an iron mine shaft with grenades
deathSummary: Thrown into a pit on July 18, 1918, Saint Elizabeth bandaged the wounds of dying companions and sang the Cherubic Hymn until her death.

image.title: Saint Elizabeth the New Martyr Sacred Icon

name: Saint Macrina the Younger
title: Saint Macrina the Younger, Spiritual Matriarch of the Cappadocian Fathers
curatedBio: Macrina was born in Caesarea in Cappadocia in 327, the eldest daughter of Saint Basil the Elder and Saint Emilia. Renouncing marriage after her fiancé died, she turned the family estate at Annesi on the Iris River into a coenobitic monastic community where aristocrats and former slaves lived in absolute equality. Macrina spiritually guided her younger brothers Basil the Great, Gregory of Nyssa, and Peter of Sebaste. Gregory recorded her sublime deathbed dialogue on the soul in his treatise De Anima.
deathSummary: Saint Macrina reposed peacefully in her monastery at Annesi on July 19, 379; her brother Gregory buried her beside her holy parents.

image.title: Saint Macrina the Younger Sacred Icon

name: Saint Margaret of Antioch
title: Saint Margaret the Virgin, Patroness of Expectant Mothers
curatedBio: Margaret was a Christian maiden of Antioch who refused the marriage suit of Roman prefect Olybrius during the Diocletian persecutions. Thrown into a dungeon, she triumphed over demonic visions and was scourged and branded with torches. Popular devotion throughout medieval Europe revered her as one of the Fourteen Holy Helpers and one of the heavenly voices that spoke to Saint Joan of Arc, invoking her intercession especially for women during childbirth.
deathSummary: Saint Margaret was beheaded at Antioch around 304; her feast has been kept on July 20 across Western Europe for a millennium.

image.title: Saint Margaret of Antioch Sacred Icon

name: Saint Praxedes of Rome
title: Saint Praxedes of Rome, Holy Virgin and Shelterer of Martyrs
curatedBio: Praxedes was a noble Roman Christian virgin of the first and second centuries, the daughter of Saint Pudens and sister of Saint Pudentiana. Following her father's martyrdom, Praxedes and her sister distributed their ancestral patrimony to the poor and converted their family palace into an underground church. Praxedes spent her days sheltering hunted Christians from imperial guards, visiting those imprisoned in the Mamertine Prison, and collecting the blood of decapitated martyrs with sponges to bury with honor.
deathSummary: Saint Praxedes reposed peacefully in Rome around 165; her titular basilica of Santa Prassede preserves early Christian mosaics.

image.title: Saint Praxedes of Rome Sacred Icon

name: Saint Mary Magdalene
title: Saint Mary Magdalene, Equal-to-the-Apostles, Apostola Apostolorum
curatedBio: Mary of Magdala was delivered by Jesus Christ from seven demons, becoming His most faithful follower throughout His public ministry. Supporting Christ out of her resources, Mary stood beside the Mother of God at the foot of the Cross during the Crucifixion and wept outside the empty tomb on Easter morning. Risen Christ appeared to her first, commanding her: "Go to my brethren and say to them, I ascend unto my Father." For this, Saint Thomas Aquinas named her the Apostle to the Apostles.
deathSummary: According to Eastern tradition, Saint Mary Magdalene accompanied Saint John to Ephesus where she reposed peacefully around 68.

image.title: Saint Mary Magdalene Sacred Icon

name: Saint Bridget of Sweden
title: Saint Bridget of Sweden, Foundress of the Brigittines and Patroness of Europe
curatedBio: Birgitta Birgersdotter was born in Finsta, Sweden in 1303 into high nobility. Married to Ulf Gudmarsson and mother of eight children, including Saint Catherine of Sweden, after her husband’s death she embraced austere poverty. In 1344 she founded the Order of the Most Holy Savior (the Brigittines) at Vadstena Abbey. Gifted with extraordinary mystical revelations of the Passion of Christ and the Nativity, she lived in Rome from 1350, fearlessly rebuking papal corruption and urging the Avignon papacy to return to Rome.
deathSummary: Saint Bridget died in Rome on July 23, 1373 at seventy years of age; her relics were brought to Vadstena Abbey.

image.title: Saint Bridget of Sweden Sacred Icon

name: Saint Christina the Astonishing
title: Saint Christina the Astonishing, Mystic of Sint-Truiden
curatedBio: Christina was born in Brustem, Belgium in 1150 and orphaned at age fifteen. At age twenty-one, she suffered a massive seizure and was pronounced dead. During her funeral Mass in the church of Sint-Truiden, Christina suddenly sat up on her bier and levitated to the church rafters. She related that she had witnessed heaven, hell, and purgatory, and was offered the choice to enter heaven or return to earth to suffer penance for the salvation of souls and the relief of purgatory.
deathSummary: Saint Christina died peacefully in the convent of Saint Catherine in Sint-Truiden on July 24, 1224 at seventy-four years of age.

image.title: Saint Christina the Astonishing Sacred Icon

name: Saint Olympias the Deaconess
title: Holy Righteous Olympias the Deaconess of Constantinople
