curatedBio: Olympias was born in Constantinople around 368 into the imperial nobility, the orphaned heiress of immense ancestral fortunes. Widowed at nineteen after twenty months of marriage to the prefect Nebridius, she refused marriage to Emperor Theodosius I’s kinsman, consecrating her wealth and life to Christ. Ordained deaconess by Patriarch Nektarios, she built a monastery next to Hagia Sophia, feeding hundreds of poor daily and serving as the steadfast defender of Saint John Chrysostom during his exile.
deathSummary: Saint Olympias reposed peacefully in exile in Nicomedia around 408 at forty years of age; her relics were brought to Constantinople.

image.title: Saint Olympias the Deaconess Sacred Icon

name: Saint Anne
title: Righteous Saint Anne, Mother of the Blessed Virgin Mary
curatedBio: Anne was of the royal tribe of David, the daughter of Matthan the priest and wife of Righteous Joachim of Nazareth. Enduring fifty years of childlessness and the bitter reproaches of her contemporaries in Israel, Anne poured out her grief in her garden beneath a laurel tree, weeping before God. An angel of the Lord appeared, announcing that she would conceive a daughter who would be blessed across all generations. Anne gave birth to Mary, dedicating her at three years old to the Temple.
deathSummary: Righteous Saint Anne reposed peacefully in Jerusalem at the age of seventy-nine, having fulfilled her divine role in salvation history.

image.title: Saint Anne Sacred Icon

name: Saint Anthusa of Mantinea
title: Venerable Mother Anthusa of Mantinea, Abbess and Confessor
curatedBio: Anthusa was an eighth-century Byzantine ascetic who withdrew from worldly society to a desolate mountain near Lake Mantinea in Paphlagonia. Founding a double monastery where she governed ninety sisters with austere prayer, during the iconoclast persecution under Emperor Constantine V Copronymus she was dragged before imperial inquisitors for venerating holy icons. Miraculously predicting that the Emperor’s wife would safely give birth to twins (future Emperor Leo IV and Anthusa), the grateful empress spared her life.
deathSummary: Saint Anthusa reposed peacefully in her monastery at Mantinea around 759 at seventy-five years of age.

image.title: Saint Anthusa of Mantinea Sacred Icon

name: Saint Alphonsa of India
title: Saint Alphonsa of the Immaculate Conception, First Indian Woman Saint
curatedBio: Anna Muttathupadathu was born in Kudamaloor, Kerala, India in 1910 into the Syro-Malabar Catholic Church. Orphaned in infancy, she deliberately burned her feet in an ash pit at age thirteen to prevent an arranged marriage so she could dedicate her life entirely to Jesus Christ. Entering the Franciscan Clarist Congregation at Bharananganam, she took the name Alphonsa. Confined to bed for decades by painful pneumonia, malaria, and ulcers, she united her suffering with Christ’s Passion with serene joy.
deathSummary: Saint Alphonsa died peacefully in Bharananganam on July 28, 1946 at thirty-five; her tomb is Kerala’s foremost pilgrimage shrine.

image.title: Saint Alphonsa of India Sacred Icon

name: Saint Martha of Bethany
title: Righteous Saint Martha of Bethany, Sister of Lazarus and Mary
curatedBio: Martha was the hospitable sister of Lazarus and Mary living in Bethany near Jerusalem. Frequently welcoming Jesus Christ into her home, when Lazarus died she ran to meet the Savior, uttering her momentous confession of faith: "Yes, Lord: I have believed that thou art the Christ, the Son of God, who should come into the world." Present when Christ raised Lazarus from the four-day tomb, according to Western tradition Martha traveled to Gaul, taming the mythical Tarasque monster through prayer.
deathSummary: Saint Martha reposed peacefully at Tarascon in Provence around 84; her tomb is in the Collegiate Church of Sainte-Marthe.

image.title: Saint Martha of Bethany Sacred Icon

name: Saint Julitta of Caesarea
title: Holy Martyr Julitta of Caesarea in Cappadocia
curatedBio: Julitta was a wealthy Christian noblewoman living in Caesarea in Cappadocia during the reign of Emperor Diocletian. When a corrupt pagan magistrate seized her ancestral lands, Julitta brought a lawsuit in court. The magistrate stated that Christians had no civil rights under the imperial edicts unless they sacrificed to the Roman gods. Offered the return of her properties if she apostatized, Julitta boldly replied: "Perish life, and perish riches, rather than that I should deny my Lord Jesus Christ!"
deathSummary: Saint Julitta was thrown into a bonfire in Caesarea around 303; praised by Saint Basil the Great in a panegyric.

image.title: Saint Julitta of Caesarea Sacred Icon

name: Saint Helena of Skövde
title: Saint Helena of Skövde, Noble Matron and Martyr of Sweden
curatedBio: Elin was born around 1101 into the Swedish aristocracy of Västergötland. Following her husband's early death, she gave her wealth to the poor, built the church of Skövde, and traveled on pilgrimage to Rome and Jerusalem. Upon her return, when her abusive son-in-law was murdered by his own mistreated servants, his vengeful family falsely blamed Helena and assassinated her while she was walking to the consecration of a church at Götene. Miraculous springs burst from the site of her death.
deathSummary: Saint Helena was assassinated near Götene on July 31, 1160; she became Sweden’s foremost female patron saint.

image.title: Saint Helena of Skövde Sacred Icon

name: Righteous Solomonia
title: Holy Mother Solomonia, Martyr of the Old Covenant
curatedBio: Solomonia was the heroic mother of the seven holy Maccabean youth—Habim, Antonin, Gurias, Eleazar, Eusebonas, Alim, and Marcellus—who suffered martyrdom under Seleucid King Antiochus IV Epiphanes in 166 BC. When Antiochus demanded they apostatize and eat swine flesh forbidden by divine law, Solomonia exhorted each son to endure horrific torments for the eternal God rather than preserve temporary earthly life. After witnessing the martyrdom of all seven of her sons with unflinching faith, Solomonia offered thanksgiving to God and leaped into the flames.
deathSummary: Saint Solomonia suffered martyrdom in Antioch around 166 BC after triumphantly watching her seven sons die for the Law of Moses.

image.title: Righteous Solomonia Sacred Icon

name: Saint Theodota of Nicaea
title: Holy Martyr Theodota and her Three Sons
curatedBio: Theodota was a pious Christian noblewoman from Nicaea in Bithynia during the persecutions of Emperor Diocletian around 304. Left a widow with three young sons, she instructed them tirelessly in Christian virtues. When she rejected the advances of the prefect Simplicius and refused to worship pagan idols, Simplicius ordered her and her children delivered to the governor of Bithynia. Refusing to yield even when her eldest son Evodius was scourged before her eyes, Theodota and her three children were cast into a blazing furnace, surrendering their souls together.
deathSummary: Saint Theodota and her three young sons were martyred inside a fiery furnace in Nicaea around 304.

image.title: Saint Theodota of Nicaea Sacred Icon

name: Saint Lydia of Philippi
title: Saint Lydia the Purpuraria, First European Convert
curatedBio: Lydia was a prosperous merchant of Thyatira who traded in luxury purple-dyed fabrics in the Roman colony of Philippi in Macedonia. As recorded in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 16:14-15), she was a worshipper of God who gathered with other women for Sabbath prayer outside the city gates by the Gangites River. When the Apostle Paul arrived and preached Christ, the Lord opened Lydia's heart; she was baptized alongside her entire household and generously compelled Paul, Silas, and Luke to make her home their apostolic headquarters.
deathSummary: Saint Lydia lived out her days in holiness as a pillar of the early Philippian church, reposing peacefully in the first century.

image.title: Saint Lydia of Philippi Sacred Icon

name: Saint Ia of Persia
title: Holy Virgin Martyr Ia of Persia
curatedBio: Ia was a devout Christian maiden of the Sasanian Persian Empire during the severe persecutions under Shah Shapur II around 362. Known for her exemplary piety, charity, and bold defense of the Gospel, she was arrested by Zoroastrian magi along with nine thousand fellow Christians. Confined in a dark prison, she was subjected to cruel tortures when she categorically refused to worship the sun and fire. Ia encouraged her fellow prisoners to remain steadfast in Christ until she was finally led forth and beheaded.
deathSummary: Saint Ia was beheaded in Persia around 362 after enduring severe tortures for refusing to adore the sacred fire.

image.title: Saint Ia of Persia Sacred Icon

name: Saint Nonna of Nazianzus
title: Righteous Nonna, Mother of Saint Gregory the Theologian
curatedBio: Nonna was raised in a pious Christian family in Cappadocia and was given in marriage to Gregory of Nazianzus the Elder, a member of the Hypsistarian sect. Through fervent prayer, unceasing patience, and holy example, Nonna converted her husband to orthodox Christianity; he was subsequently consecrated Bishop of Nazianzus. Nonna consecrated all three of her children to God: Saint Gregory the Theologian (one of the Three Holy Hierarchs), Saint Caesarius the Physician, and Saint Gorgonia. While praying at the Holy Table in church, she surrendered her soul peacefully into the hands of Christ.
deathSummary: Saint Nonna reposed peacefully while in prayer at the church altar in Nazianzus in 374.

image.title: Saint Nonna of Nazianzus Sacred Icon

name: Saint Christina of Bolsena
title: Holy Great Martyr Christina of Tyre and Bolsena
curatedBio: Christina was the daughter of a wealthy pagan Roman magistrate named Urbanus in Bolsena (or Tyre) in the third century. Locked in a tower surrounded by ornate idols of gold and silver, Christina contemplated the beauty of creation, embraced faith in the one true God, and shattered her father's idols, distributing the precious metal fragments to the destitute. Enraged, her father and subsequent Roman magistrates subjected her to hooks, wheel tortures, boiling oil, and serpents. Untouched by the beasts, she was finally pierced through with arrows and lances.
deathSummary: Saint Christina was martyred by spear and arrows in Bolsena around 304 under Diocletian.

image.title: Saint Christina of Bolsena Sacred Icon

name: Saint Theodora of Sihla
title: Venerable Mother Theodora of Sihla, Solitary of Moldavia
curatedBio: Theodora was born in Vânători-Neamț, Moldavia, in the seventeenth century. After a short marriage entered out of filial obedience, she and her husband mutually decided to embrace monasticism. Theodora entered the Varzaresti skete, but after Ottoman raids ravaged the convent, she retreated deep into the untamed wilderness of the Sihla mountains. Living in a secluded stone cave for thirty years in prayer, fasting, and contemplation, she was nourished miraculously by birds carrying breadcrumbs from the nearby monastery. Before reposing, she received the Holy Mysteries from hieromonks who discovered her shining cell.
deathSummary: Saint Theodora reposed peacefully in her wilderness cave at Sihla in the early eighteenth century.

image.title: Saint Theodora of Sihla Sacred Icon

name: Saint Mary MacKillop
title: Saint Mary of the Cross MacKillop, Patroness of Australia
curatedBio: Mary Helen MacKillop was born in Melbourne, Australia, the eldest of eight children of Scottish immigrant parents. Dedicated to serving the poor, isolated, and marginalized rural children of the Australian Outback, she co-founded the Sisters of Saint Joseph of the Sacred Heart alongside Father Julian Tenison Woods in 1866. Despite enduring profound ecclesiastical opposition, false accusations, and a temporary excommunication for exposing clerical abuse, MacKillop demonstrated unwavering forgiveness and perseverance, establishing dozens of free Catholic schools, orphanages, and shelters across Australia and New Zealand.
deathSummary: Saint Mary MacKillop reposed peacefully in North Sydney on August 8, 1909; canonized by Pope Benedict XVI in 2010.

image.title: Saint Mary MacKillop Sacred Icon

name: Saint Teresa Benedicta of the Cross
title: Saint Teresa Benedicta of the Cross (Edith Stein), Virgin and Martyr
curatedBio: Edith Stein was born into an observant Jewish family in Breslau, Germany. After studying phenomenology under Edmund Husserl, she became an acclaimed philosopher and academic. Her reading of the autobiography of Saint Teresa of Ávila prompted her conversion to the Catholic Church in 1922. In 1933, she entered the Discalced Carmelite monastery in Cologne, taking the religious name Teresa Benedicta of the Cross. Transferred to the Netherlands to escape Nazi persecution, she was arrested by the Gestapo in retaliation for the Dutch bishops' condemnation of antisemitism and deported to Auschwitz-Birkenau.
deathSummary: Saint Teresa Benedicta was murdered in the gas chambers of Auschwitz-Birkenau on August 9, 1942; canonized in 1998 as a co-patroness of Europe.

image.title: Saint Teresa Benedicta of the Cross Sacred Icon

name: Saint Asteria of Bergamo
title: Holy Virgin Martyr Asteria of Bergamo
curatedBio: Asteria was a Christian maiden of Bergamo in Lombardy during the severe Diocletian persecutions at the start of the fourth century. Alongside her sister Saint Grata, Asteria was moved with holy compassion to recover the severed body and head of Saint Alexander, the Roman soldier martyr of the Theban Legion, granting him an honorable Christian burial. Denounced to the imperial authorities for burying the martyr and steadfastly refusing to sacrifice to Roman idols, Asteria was subjected to cruel interrogations and crowned with martyrdom by the sword.
deathSummary: Saint Asteria was beheaded in Bergamo around 307 under Emperor Diocletian.

image.title: Saint Asteria of Bergamo Sacred Icon

name: Saint Clare of Assisi
title: Saint Clare of Assisi, Foundress of the Poor Clares
curatedBio: Clare Offreduccio was born to a noble aristocratic family in Assisi, Italy. Captivated by the apostolic preaching of Saint Francis of Assisi, she fled her family home on Palm Sunday in 1212 to receive the tonsure from Francis at the Portiuncula. She established the Second Order of Saint Francis (the Poor Clares) at San Damiano, where she lived fifty years of strict enclosure, fasting, and joyful poverty. In 1240, holding aloft the Blessed Sacrament in a monstrance from the convent window, Clare miraculously repelled attacking Saracen mercenaries.
deathSummary: Saint Clare reposed peacefully at San Damiano on August 11, 1253, two days after Pope Innocent IV approved her Rule.

image.title: Saint Clare of Assisi Sacred Icon

name: Saint Jane Frances de Chantal
title: Saint Jane Frances de Chantal, Co-Foundress of the Visitation
curatedBio: Jane Frances Frémyot was born in Dijon, France, the daughter of the president of the Burgundian Parliament. At twenty she married the Baron de Chantal, bearing six children and managing the feudal estate with boundless charity toward local peasants. Following her husband's untimely death in a hunting accident, she met Saint Francis de Sales in 1604, who became her spiritual director. In 1610, they founded the Order of the Visitation of Holy Mary, designed for women of weak health or older age who were excluded from austere monastic orders.
deathSummary: Saint Jane Frances de Chantal reposed peacefully at the Visitation convent in Moulins on December 13, 1641; celebrated on August 12.

image.title: Saint Jane Frances de Chantal Sacred Icon

name: Saint Radegund of Poitiers
title: Saint Radegund, Queen of the Franks and Abbess of Poitiers
curatedBio: Radegund was a Thuringian royal princess captured in childhood during the Frankish conquest and forced into marriage with Merovingian King Chlothar I. Renowned for her deep ascetic devotion and tireless care for lepers and the destitute, she fled the royal court after Chlothar murdered her brother. Consecrated as a deaconess by Saint Medard of Noyon, Radegund founded the Abbey of the Holy Cross at Poitiers in 552. She obtained a fragment of the True Cross from Byzantine Emperor Justin II, for which Venantius Fortunatus composed the immortal hymn Vexilla Regis.
deathSummary: Saint Radegund reposed in peace at Poitiers on August 13, 587; buried in the church she established.

image.title: Saint Radegund of Poitiers Sacred Icon

name: Saint Anthusa of Seleucia
title: Holy Martyr Anthusa of Seleucia and her Companions
curatedBio: Anthusa was a noble Christian woman who lived in Seleucia during the persecutions under Emperor Valerian around 258. Having embraced Christ through the preaching of Bishop Saint Athanasius, she was baptized alongside two faithful servants, Charisius and Neophytus. When local magistrates arrested them for their confession, Anthusa refused to offer incense to pagan deities, encouraging her servants to welcome eternal life. Bound and subjected to harsh beatings, Anthusa was condemned and beheaded, sealing her apostolic testimony with her blood.
deathSummary: Saint Anthusa was beheaded for Christ in Seleucia around 258 under Valerian.

image.title: Saint Anthusa of Seleucia Sacred Icon

name: The Most Holy Theotokos
title: Dormition and Falling Asleep of the Most Holy Theotokos
curatedBio: The Blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of Jesus Christ the Incarnate Son of God, is venerated as the highest of all saints and pure vessel of divine incarnation. Commended by Christ upon the Cross into the protective care of Saint John the Beloved Apostle, Mary lived in Jerusalem and Ephesus, offering prayer and counsel to the early Apostles. Forewarned by Archangel Gabriel of her impending departure, she reposed peacefully surrounded by the Apostles miraculously assembled from across the world, her body subsequently translated incorrupt into heavenly glory.
deathSummary: The Mother of God fell asleep peacefully in Jerusalem around 48 AD; celebrated universally on August 15.

image.title: The Most Holy Theotokos Sacred Icon

name: Saint Beatrice da Silva
title: Saint Beatrice da Silva Meneses, Foundress of the Conceptionists
curatedBio: Beatrice da Silva was born in Ceuta into Portuguese nobility, the sister of Saint Amadeus of Portugal. A lady-in-waiting to Queen Isabel of Castile, her remarkable beauty provoked intense jealousy in the queen, who imprisoned Beatrice in a sealed trunk for three days without food. During this confinement, Beatrice received a vision of the Virgin Mary instructing her to found a new religious order. Withdrawing to the Cistercian convent in Toledo, she later founded the Order of the Immaculate Conception (the Conceptionists), wearing white tunics with blue mantles.
deathSummary: Saint Beatrice reposed peacefully in Toledo on August 16, 1492; canonized by Pope Paul VI in 1976.

image.title: Saint Beatrice da Silva Sacred Icon

name: Saint Clare of Montefalco
title: Saint Clare of the Cross of Montefalco, Augustinian Abbess
curatedBio: Clare of Montefalco entered a local Franciscan hermitage at the age of six before joining her sister in founding an Augustinian monastery in Montefalco, Umbria. Chosen as abbess in 1291, she was renowned for extreme penance, prophetic insight, and intense mystical contemplation of the Passion of Jesus Christ. Clare frequently experienced long ecstasies during which she testified that Christ had implanted His Cross deeply into her heart. Following her death, sisters inspecting her heart discovered fibrous markings resembling the crucifix, nails, crown of thorns, and scourge.
deathSummary: Saint Clare of Montefalco reposed peacefully in Montefalco on August 17, 1308; canonized by Pope Leo XIII in 1881.

image.title: Saint Clare of Montefalco Sacred Icon

name: Saint Helena Augusta
title: Holy Empress Helena, Equal to the Apostles
curatedBio: Flavia Julia Helena was born in Drepanum (Bithynia) into modest circumstances before marrying Roman general Constantius Chlorus and giving birth to Constantine the Great. Following Constantine's conversion and the Edict of Milan, Empress Helena embraced Christianity, using imperial wealth to build basilicas across the Holy Land and feed the poor. In 326, in her eightieth year, she traveled on pilgrimage to Jerusalem, initiating excavations on Golgotha that uncovered the Tomb of Christ and the True Cross of the Crucifixion.
deathSummary: Saint Helena reposed in Nicomedia around 330 in the arms of her son Constantine; enshrined in Rome.

image.title: Saint Helena Augusta Sacred Icon

name: Righteous Sarah the Matriarch
title: Righteous Sarah, Wife of Abraham and Mother of Nations
curatedBio: Sarah was the beloved wife and companion of the Patriarch Abraham, traveling with him from Ur of the Chaldees to the promised land of Canaan in obedience to God's covenant. Though barren into her old age, God promised Abraham that nations and kings would descend from her, changing her name from Sarai to Sarah ('Princess'). At ninety, Sarah conceived and gave birth to Isaac, fulfilling the divine promise. Commended in the New Testament as an exemplar of faith, obedience, and maternal virtue, she lived one hundred and twenty-seven years.
deathSummary: Righteous Sarah reposed peacefully in Kiryat Arba (Hebron) at the age of 127; buried in the Cave of Machpelah.

image.title: Righteous Sarah the Matriarch Sacred Icon

name: Saint Maria De Mattias
title: Saint Maria De Mattias, Foundress of the Adorers of the Blood of Christ
curatedBio: Maria De Mattias was born in Vallecorsa in the Papal States during a period of violent brigandage and political turbulence. Inspired by Saint Gaspar del Bufalo's missions, Maria consecrated herself to God and founded the Congregation of the Adorers of the Blood of Christ in Acuto in 1834. Overcoming deep cultural prejudices against female teachers, she opened over seventy schools to educate young girls and catechize peasants across central Italy, transforming violent communities through the saving power of the Precious Blood.
deathSummary: Saint Maria De Mattias reposed peacefully in Rome on August 20, 1866; canonized by Pope John Paul II in 2003.

image.title: Saint Maria De Mattias Sacred Icon

name: Saint Bassa of Edessa
title: Holy Martyr Bassa and her Sons Theognis, Agapius, and Pistus
curatedBio: Bassa was a noble Christian woman of Larissa in Thessaly married to a pagan priest named Valerius during the reign of Emperor Maximian Galerius around 304. Bassa secretly raised her three young sons—Theognis, Agapius, and Pistus—in the Christian faith. When her husband discovered their faith, he denounced them to the proconsul. The children were interrogated and put to death before their mother's eyes, each encouraged by Bassa to remain faithful to Christ. Exiled to Cyzicus and thrown into the sea, Bassa was miraculously preserved before being beheaded.
deathSummary: Saint Bassa was beheaded on the island of Cyzicus around 304 after seeing her three sons martyred.

image.title: Saint Bassa of Edessa Sacred Icon

name: Saint Anthusa of Constantinople
title: Saint Anthusa the Confessor, Abbess of Mantineon
curatedBio: Anthusa was born in Constantinople and dedicated her life to monastic asceticism, establishing the Monastery of Mantineon in the Black Sea region. During the fierce iconoclastic persecution under Emperor Constantine V Copronymus, Anthusa boldly confessed the veneration of holy icons. Summoned before the emperor and ordered to desecrate the icons, she refused with holy courage. She was subjected to tortures and threatened with exile until Empress Irene's miraculous prophecy regarding the birth of twin children saved Anthusa from execution, allowing her to govern her flock in holiness.
deathSummary: Saint Anthusa reposed peacefully in her monastery around 759 at an advanced old age.

image.title: Saint Anthusa of Constantinople Sacred Icon

name: Saint Rose of Lima
title: Saint Rose of Lima, First Canonized Saint of the Americas
curatedBio: Isabel Flores de Oliva, called Rose for her radiant countenance, was born in Lima, Peru, to Spanish colonists. Inspired by Saint Catherine of Siena, she took a perpetual vow of virginity, cut off her hair, and practiced severe fasting. Entering the Third Order of Saint Dominic, she lived in a small wooden hermitage built in her parents' garden, producing intricate embroidery to support her household and caring for indigenous, destitute, and sick citizens. Renowned for mystical visions, she became the first person born in the Western Hemisphere to be canonized.
deathSummary: Saint Rose of Lima reposed peacefully in Lima on August 24, 1617, at age thirty-one; feast celebrated August 23.

image.title: Saint Rose of Lima Sacred Icon

name: Saint Joan Elisabeth Bichier des Ages
title: Saint Joan Elisabeth Bichier des Ages, Foundress
curatedBio: Joan Elisabeth was born into a noble French family at the Château des Ages in Le Blanc. Following the upheaval of the French Revolution, which claimed the family estate and forced her into poverty, she met Saint André-Hubert Fournet. Together in 1807, they established the Congregation of the Daughters of the Cross (Sisters of Saint Andrew) in Poitou, dedicated to teaching destitute rural children and caring for the impoverished sick and elderly. Her motherly humility and profound trust in Divine Providence led the community to spread across France.
deathSummary: Saint Joan Elisabeth reposed peacefully at La Puye on August 26, 1838; celebrated in the liturgy on August 24/26.

image.title: Saint Joan Elisabeth Bichier des Ages Sacred Icon

name: Saint Patricia of Naples
title: Saint Patricia of Naples, Virgin and Patroness of Naples
curatedBio: Patricia was a noble maiden of Constantinople, believed to be of imperial lineage related to Emperor Constans II. To avoid a forced imperial marriage, she renounced worldly titles and fled to Rome, where Pope Liberius consecrated her as a virgin dedicated to Christ. After the death of her father, Patricia returned briefly to Constantinople to liquidate her patrimony and distribute all proceeds to the poor. Embarking on a pilgrimage to Jerusalem, a fierce storm shipwrecked her on the island of Megaride near Naples, where she established a convent.
deathSummary: Saint Patricia reposed peacefully in Naples around 665; her relics in San Gregorio Armeno are renowned for miraculous liquefaction.

image.title: Saint Patricia of Naples Sacred Icon

name: Saint Natalia of Nicomedia
title: Holy Martyr Natalia of Nicomedia
curatedBio: Natalia was a noble Christian woman who lived in Nicomedia during the persecutions of Emperor Maximian Galerius around 306. Her husband Adrian was head of the imperial praetorium who was converted upon witnessing the immense joy and fortitude of tortured Christians. When Adrian was cast into prison, Natalia disguised herself and secretly entered his cell, washing his wounds and encouraging him to hold fast to the eternal crown. After Adrian was martyred by having his limbs shattered upon an anvil, Natalia kept his severed hand and died in peace.
mannerOfDeath: Exhaustion and grief after witnessing martyrdom
deathSummary: Saint Natalia reposed peacefully in Argyropolis near Constantinople around 306 after the martyrdom of her husband Saint Adrian.

image.title: Saint Natalia of Nicomedia Sacred Icon

name: Saint Monica of Hippo
title: Saint Monica, Model of Christian Mothers
curatedBio: Monica was a Berber Christian woman born in Tagaste, Numidia (modern Algeria). Given in marriage to Patricius, an ill-tempered pagan Roman official, she converted him and his contentious mother through gentle humility, patience, and continual prayer. Her greatest anguish was her eldest son Augustine, whose dissolute lifestyle and Manichaean heresy caused her seventeen years of weeping. Advised by Saint Ambrose that 'the child of those tears shall never perish,' Monica witnessed Augustine's baptism in Milan in 387, shortly before falling peacefully ill at Ostia Tiberina.
deathSummary: Saint Monica reposed peacefully at Ostia near Rome in 387 in the company of Saint Augustine.

image.title: Saint Monica of Hippo Sacred Icon

name: Saint Joaquina de Vedruna
title: Saint Joaquina de Vedruna de Mas, Foundress
curatedBio: Joaquina de Vedruna was born into Catalan nobility in Barcelona. In 1799 she married Teodoro de Mas, bearing nine children. During the Napoleonic invasion of Spain, her husband fought in the resistance while Joaquina fled with their children. Following his death in 1816, she resolved to dedicate her widowhood to God. In 1826, guided by Capuchin Father Esteban de Olot, she established the Carmelite Sisters of Charity (Vedruna) in Vic, dedicating the congregation to free education for impoverished girls and medical nursing for the sick.
deathSummary: Saint Joaquina reposed peacefully in Barcelona during a cholera epidemic on August 28, 1854; canonized in 1959.

image.title: Saint Joaquina de Vedruna Sacred Icon

name: Saint Sabina of Rome
title: Holy Martyr Sabina of Rome
curatedBio: Sabina was a wealthy patrician Roman widow, daughter of Herod Metallarius and wife of the senator Valentinus in Vindena, Umbria. Introduced to the Gospel by her Syrian slave maiden Saint Serapia, Sabina embraced Christ and assisted Serapia in distributing food and alms to persecuted Christians. When Serapia was arrested and beaten to death under Emperor Hadrian around 126, Sabina gave her body a sacred burial. Soon summoned before the prefect Elpidius, Sabina refused to sacrifice to Jupiter and was martyred by the sword on the Aventine Hill.
deathSummary: Saint Sabina was beheaded on the Aventine Hill in Rome around 126; the Basilica of Santa Sabina stands on the site of her villa.

image.title: Saint Sabina of Rome Sacred Icon

name: Saint Margaret Ward
title: Saint Margaret Ward, The Pearl of Tyburn, Martyr
curatedBio: Margaret Ward was born in Congleton, Cheshire, into English gentry. During the Elizabethan persecutions of Catholic priests, she learned that Father William Watson was confined in horrific squalor in Bridewell Prison. Gaining access by visiting him with baskets of provisions, she smuggled in a sturdy rope, facilitating his escape down the prison walls. When the boatman hired to convey him confessed under duress, Margaret was arrested. Flogged repeatedly and offered her liberty if she attended Protestant services and asked the Queen's pardon, she refused and was hanged at Tyburn.
deathSummary: Saint Margaret Ward was hanged at Tyburn on August 30, 1588; canonized as one of the Forty Martyrs of England and Wales.

image.title: Saint Margaret Ward Sacred Icon

name: Saint Isabel of France
title: Blessed Isabel of France, Virgin and Princess of France
curatedBio: Isabel was the daughter of King Louis VIII of France and Queen Blanche of Castile, and younger sister to Saint Louis IX. From early youth, she showed profound devotion to prayer and voluntary poverty, refusing marriage proposals from Emperor Conrad IV to consecrate her virginity to God. With the support of Saint Louis, she established the Franciscan Monastery of the Humility of the Blessed Virgin at Longchamp near Paris in 1260. She authored an austere Rule approved by Pope Urban IV and spent her final years in prayer and service.
deathSummary: Saint Isabel reposed peacefully at Longchamp Abbey on February 23, 1270; venerated on August 31.

image.title: Saint Isabel of France Sacred Icon

name: Saint Verena of Zurzach
title: Saint Verena of Zurzach, Hermitess and Healer of the Rhine
curatedBio: Verena was an Egyptian Christian maiden from Thebes who journeyed to the Roman province of Raetia (modern Switzerland) in the wake of the martyrdom of the Theban Legion under Saint Maurice. Settling as a solitary anchorite near Solothurn and later Zurzach along the Rhine, she devoted her life to unceasing prayer, nursing the diseased, and bathing lepers. Depicted in iconography carrying an earthen water pitcher and a double-sided hygiene comb, she converted numerous Alamannic pagan inhabitants through her tender charity and miraculous healings.
deathSummary: Saint Verena reposed peacefully in her hermitage at Zurzach around 344; venerated as a major patroness of Switzerland.

image.title: Saint Verena of Zurzach Sacred Icon

name: Saint Theodota of Bithynia
title: Holy Martyr Theodota of Bithynia
curatedBio: Theodota was an early Christian woman of Bithynia during the persecutions of the Roman emperors. Refusing to offer sacrifices to pagan gods or renounce her confession of Jesus Christ, she was arrested and brought before the imperial governor. Subjected to scourging, iron hooks, and imprisonment, she answered threats with joyful prayers, confessing Christ as the true Emperor and King of Heaven. Crowned with martyrdom by decapitation, her heroic steadfastness inspired numerous secret believers in Asia Minor.
deathSummary: Saint Theodota was beheaded for her faith in Bithynia in the early fourth century.

image.title: Saint Theodota of Bithynia Sacred Icon

name: Saint Phoebe the Deaconess
title: Saint Phoebe the Deaconess of Cenchreae
curatedBio: Phoebe was a faithful early Christian woman and deaconess (diakonos) of the church at Cenchreae, the eastern port of Corinth. Commended by the Apostle Paul in his Epistle to the Romans (Romans 16:1-2), she is lauded as a 'patroness of many and of myself also,' who generously used her personal wealth and prominent social standing to shelter and support traveling evangelists and the local poor. Entrusted by Paul with transporting his monumental Epistle to the Romans across the Mediterranean, she faithfully delivered the text to Rome.
deathSummary: Saint Phoebe reposed peacefully in the first century after serving as an indispensable pillar of the apostolic church.

image.title: Saint Phoebe the Deaconess Sacred Icon

name: Saint Rosalia of Palermo
title: Saint Rosalia of Palermo, La Santuzza, Solitary of Monte Pellegrino
curatedBio: Rosalia Sinibaldi was born into Sicilian Norman nobility, descended from Emperor Charlemagne. Escaping court life and an arranged marriage at the royal court of King Roger II of Sicily, she was guided by the Virgin Mary to embrace solitary eremitic life. Rosalia spent her remaining years in continuous contemplation, prayer, and penance in a secluded cavern on Monte Pellegrino near Palermo. In 1624, during a catastrophic plague epidemic, her relics were miraculously revealed in the cave; when carried in solemn procession, the plague ceased immediately.
deathSummary: Saint Rosalia reposed peacefully in her cave on Monte Pellegrino around 1166; venerated as primary patroness of Palermo.

image.title: Saint Rosalia of Palermo Sacred Icon

name: Saint Teresa of Calcutta
title: Saint Mother Teresa of Calcutta, Mother to the Poorest of the Poor
curatedBio: Anjezë Gonxhe Bojaxhiu was born to an Albanian family in Skopje. Entering the Sisters of Loreto in Ireland, she was sent to teach in Calcutta, India. On September 10, 1946, while traveling by train to Darjeeling, she experienced a 'call within a call' to leave the cloister and live among the poorest destitute in the slums. In 1950, she founded the Missionaries of Charity, wearing simple blue-bordered white cotton saris to nurse dying destitute, lepers, and abandoned infants, radiating Christ's thirst for souls.
deathSummary: Saint Teresa of Calcutta reposed peacefully in Calcutta on September 5, 1997; canonized by Pope Francis in 2016.

image.title: Saint Teresa of Calcutta Sacred Icon

name: Saint Bega of Cumberland
title: Saint Bega of Cumberland, Irish Virgin and Hermitess
curatedBio: Bega was an Irish royal maiden of the seventh century celebrated for her virginal purity and ardent devotion to Christ. Fleeing across the Irish Sea in an open boat to escape a forced marriage arranged with a pagan Norwegian prince, she received a mysterious bracelet marked with the holy cross as a token of her heavenly betrothal. Washing ashore on the rugged coast of Cumberland (modern Cumbria), she lived as an anchorite recluse in deep solitude, later founding a religious settlement at Saint Bees.
deathSummary: Saint Bega reposed peacefully in Cumberland around 660; her holy bracelet became one of northern England's most venerated relics.

image.title: Saint Bega of Cumberland Sacred Icon

name: Saint Regina of Alise
title: Holy Virgin Martyr Regina (Reine) of Alise
curatedBio: Regina was a Christian maiden of Alise-Sainte-Reine in Burgundy, born to a pagan father who disowned her when she was baptized into the faith. Living as a shepherdess tending sheep in rural pastures, her radiant virtue and beauty caught the attention of the Roman proconsul Olybrius. When Olybrius demanded her hand in marriage and demanded that she sacrifice to Roman idols, Regina steadfastly refused, proclaiming her singular betrothal to Christ. Subjected to iron whips, pincers, and torches, she was crowned with martyrdom by decapitation.
deathSummary: Saint Regina was beheaded in Alise-Sainte-Reine around 251 under Emperor Decius.

image.title: Saint Regina of Alise Sacred Icon

name: Nativity of the Theotokos
title: The Nativity of Our Most Holy Lady the Mother of God
curatedBio: The Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary marks the dawn of universal salvation, born to the righteous and long-barren Joachim and Anna in Nazareth. Enduring decades of societal reproach due to childlessness, the elderly couple had redoubled their prayers, fasting, and almsgiving, vowing to dedicate any child to the service of God. An archangel appeared separately to both Joachim and Anna, announcing that they would bring forth a daughter through whom all nations would be blessed. Her birth initiates the fulfillment of the divine promises.
deathSummary: Commemoration of the miraculous birth of the Holy Mother of God; celebrated throughout the Christian world on September 8.

image.title: Nativity of the Theotokos Sacred Icon

name: Saint Gorgonia of Nazianzus
title: Righteous Gorgonia, Sister of Saint Gregory the Theologian
curatedBio: Gorgonia was the daughter of Saint Gregory the Elder and Saint Nonna of Nazianzus, and elder sister to Saint Gregory the Theologian. Renowned for modesty, temperance, and exceptional hospitality, she lived in marriage with Vitalian, an official in Pisidia, successfully leading her husband and children to holy baptism. When stricken with a severe malady and trampling injury from runaway horses, she went into church at night, pressed her head against the altar steps, and was instantaneously healed. Saint Gregory preached her funeral panegyric praising her as the crown of women.
deathSummary: Saint Gorgonia reposed peacefully in Pisidia around 372 surrounded by her family; eulogized by Saint Gregory the Theologian.

image.title: Saint Gorgonia of Nazianzus Sacred Icon

name: Saint Pulcheria Augusta
title: Holy Empress Pulcheria, Guardian of Orthodoxy
curatedBio: Aelia Pulcheria was born into the Byzantine imperial family, daughter of Emperor Arcadius. At age fifteen she took a perpetual vow of virginity, transforming the imperial palace in Constantinople into a house of prayer, ascetic study, and charity. Serving as regent for her younger brother Theodosius II, she defended orthodox Christian doctrine against Nestorianism and Monophysitism. In 451, Pulcheria and her consort Emperor Marcian convoked the Fourth Ecumenical Council at Chalcedon, which definitively defined the two inseparable natures of Jesus Christ.
deathSummary: Saint Pulcheria reposed peacefully in Constantinople in 453, bequeathing all her vast private fortune to the destitute.

image.title: Saint Pulcheria Augusta Sacred Icon

name: Saint Theodora of Alexandria
title: Venerable Theodora the Penitent of Alexandria
curatedBio: Theodora was a beautiful married Christian woman of Alexandria in the fifth century. Deceived into committing adultery on a feast day, she was overwhelmed by remorse. She cut off her hair, donned male monastic garments, and fled to the Enaton monastery near Alexandria under the name Theodore. For years she labored in extreme austerity, humility, and silence. When falsely accused by a local girl of fathering a child, Theodora accepted the disgrace without defending herself, caring for the infant outside the monastery gates until her holy passing revealed her true identity.
deathSummary: Saint Theodora reposed in peace around 491; her identity was uncovered upon preparing her body for burial.

image.title: Saint Theodora of Alexandria Sacred Icon

name: Saint Martha of Alexandria
title: Saint Martha, Penitent of Alexandria
curatedBio: Martha was a notorious courtesan in the imperial metropolis of Alexandria renowned for worldly indulgence and seductive charm. Deeply convicted during a sermon on repentance, she threw herself weeping before the church doors, imploring the mercy of God. Withdrawing entirely from society, she entered an ascetic community in the Egyptian desert. Martha lived thirty-five years of severe tears, fasting, and contemplative prayer, transforming her former worldly passions into an incandescent love for Christ and receiving the grace of holy miracles.
deathSummary: Saint Martha reposed peacefully in the Egyptian desert in the fourth century.

image.title: Saint Martha of Alexandria Sacred Icon

name: Saint Ketevan of Kakheti
title: Holy Great Martyr Ketevan, Queen of Kakheti
curatedBio: Ketevan was the pious queen of Kakheti in eastern Georgia. When Shah Abbas I of Persia invaded the Georgian kingdom, Ketevan gave herself up as a hostage to protect her people from annihilation. Shah Abbas held her under house arrest in Shiraz for ten years, attempting by threats and bribes to force her to renounce Christ and enter his harem. Ketevan refused with majestic disdain. Enraged, the Shah ordered her subjected to agonizing torture: red-hot iron cauldrons, copper pincers, and iron nails, through which Ketevan surrendered her soul praying for Georgia.
mannerOfDeath: Tortured with red-hot iron tongs and cauldron
deathSummary: Saint Ketevan was martyred in Shiraz, Persia, on September 13, 1624; parts of her relics were saved by Augustinian friars.

image.title: Saint Ketevan of Kakheti Sacred Icon

name: Saint Placilla the Empress
title: Righteous Empress Aelia Flaccilla (Placilla), Servant of the Poor
curatedBio: Aelia Flaccilla was born into aristocratic Spanish nobility and became the Empress consort of Roman Emperor Theodosius the Great. Renowned throughout the Roman Empire for her profound humility, personal austerity, and fervent defense of the Nicene Creed against Arianism, she personally visited the public hospitals of Constantinople. There, Placilla washed the sores of lepers, dressed wounds, cooked broth for the bedridden, and spoon-fed paralyzed citizens with her own hands, affirming that while imperial gold belongs to the throne, physical service belongs to Christ.
deathSummary: Saint Placilla reposed peacefully in Thrace in 386; eulogized by Saint Gregory of Nyssa.

image.title: Saint Placilla the Empress Sacred Icon

name: Saint Melitina of Marcianopolis
title: Holy Martyr Melitina of Marcianopolis
curatedBio: Melitina was a fervent Christian maiden of Marcianopolis in Thrace during the persecutions under Roman Emperor Antoninus Pius in the mid-second century. Denounced for converting pagan citizens and publicly refusing to worship imperial idols, she was dragged before the governor Antiochus. Enduring horrific tortures with serene patience, she was cast into prison before being led outside the city and beheaded by the executioner. An aristocratic Christian woman named Saint Akyline secretly recovered Melitina's holy relics to convey them to Macedonia.
deathSummary: Saint Melitina was beheaded in Marcianopolis around 160 under Emperor Antoninus Pius.

image.title: Saint Melitina of Marcianopolis Sacred Icon

name: Saint Euphemia the Great Martyr
title: Holy Great Martyr Euphemia the All-Praised of Chalcedon
curatedBio: Euphemia was born to aristocratic parents in Chalcedon during the Diocletian persecution. Refusing to attend the pagan festival of Ares, she and forty-nine fellow Christians were seized and tortured. Thrown to wild bears and lions, the beasts merely licked her feet; she died from a minor bear wound while offering thanksgiving to God. In 451, during the Fourth Ecumenical Council of Chalcedon, the Orthodox and Monophysite statements of faith were sealed inside her shrine; when reopened days later, the Orthodox Tome rested in her right hand while the Monophysite tome lay under her feet.
mannerOfDeath: Mauled by wild beasts in the arena
deathSummary: Saint Euphemia was martyred in Chalcedon around 304; commemorated especially for the miraculous defense of the Council of Chalcedon.

image.title: Saint Euphemia the Great Martyr Sacred Icon

name: Saint Hildegard of Bingen
title: Saint Hildegard of Bingen, Doctor of the Church, The Sibyl of the Rhine
curatedBio: Hildegard was born in Bermersheim vor der Höhe, Germany, the tenth child of noble parents, and was enclosed as an anchoress at Disibodenberg alongside Jutta of Sponheim. Elected magistra, she later founded Rupertsberg and Eibingen abbeys near Bingen. A visionary mystic, theologian, polymath, naturalist, composer, and poet, she recorded her luminous illuminations in Scivias, Liber Vitae Meritorum, and De Operatione Dei. Her letters admonished popes and emperors, and her sacred musical compositions, including Ordo Virtutum, remain foundational to Western liturgical chant.
deathSummary: Saint Hildegard reposed peacefully at Rupertsberg Abbey on September 17, 1179; proclaimed a Doctor of the Church in 2012.

image.title: Saint Hildegard of Bingen Sacred Icon

name: Saint Richardis of Alsace
title: Saint Richardis, Holy Roman Empress and Abbess of Andlau
curatedBio: Richardis was an Alsatian noblewoman, daughter of Erchanger, Count of the Nordgau. In 862 she married Carolingian Emperor Charles the Fat and was crowned Holy Roman Empress by Pope John VIII in Rome in 881. Renowned for profound personal piety and care for the poor, she was falsely accused of adultery by her husband's ministers in 887. Submitting to trial by ordeal in a shirt of fire, she walked unharmed through blazing flames. Leaving the imperial court, she founded Andlau Abbey, living as an exemplary abbess until her repose.
deathSummary: Saint Richardis reposed peacefully at Andlau Abbey on September 18, 896; canonized by Pope Leo IX in 1049.

image.title: Saint Richardis of Alsace Sacred Icon

name: Saint Susanna of Eleutheropolis
title: Holy Virgin Martyr Susanna of Eleutheropolis
curatedBio: Susanna was a Christian maiden of Eleutheropolis in Palestine during the persecutions under Emperor Maximian Galerius in the early fourth century. Refusing to sacrifice to pagan idols or surrender her consecrated virginity to the local governor Alexander, Susanna publicly confessed her undying love for Christ. Stripped of clothing, scourged with rods, and racked with iron claws, she stood unbroken in prayer. She was cast into a blazing furnace, surrendering her spirit to God without a single cry of agony.
deathSummary: Saint Susanna was martyred inside a blazing furnace in Eleutheropolis around 304 under Maximian.

image.title: Saint Susanna of Eleutheropolis Sacred Icon

name: Saint Fausta of Cyzicus
title: Holy Virgin Martyr Fausta of Cyzicus and her Companions
curatedBio: Fausta was an orphan maiden of Cyzicus in Asia Minor during the reign of Emperor Maximian around 305. At age thirteen, she was dragged before the eighty-year-old pagan priest Evilasius for refusing to offer sacrifice to imperial deities. Strung up and tortured with hot iron needles, Fausta demonstrated such supernatural patience and heavenly peace that Evilasius himself repented and accepted Christ. When the proconsul Maximus arrived, he ordered both Fausta and Evilasius thrown into a boiling cauldron of pitch, receiving the martyr's crown together.
deathSummary: Saint Fausta was martyred inside a cauldron of boiling pitch in Cyzicus around 305.

image.title: Saint Fausta of Cyzicus Sacred Icon

name: Saint Maura of Troyes
title: Saint Maura of Troyes, Consecrated Virgin of Champagne
curatedBio: Maura was born in Troyes in Champagne in the ninth century. Converted to deep Christian asceticism at age twenty-three following the death of her father, she led her mother and brother Saint Eutropius, Bishop of Troyes, into lives of profound sanctity. Maura remained in her family home as an enclosed consecrated virgin, spending her nights in tears and vigils, weaving altar cloths for churches, and supplying the poor and monasteries of Champagne with bread, wine, and wax. Saint Prudentius of Troyes wrote an account of her extraordinary miracles.
deathSummary: Saint Maura reposed peacefully in Troyes on September 21, 850, at the age of thirty; eulogized by Saint Prudentius.

image.title: Saint Maura of Troyes Sacred Icon

name: Saint Irais of Alexandria
title: Holy Virgin Martyr Irais (Rhais) of Alexandria
curatedBio: Irais was a Christian maiden of Alexandria in Egypt during the severe persecution under Emperor Septimius Severus around 202. While drawing water at a public well on the bank of the river, she observed a boat moored to the shore containing Christian priests, deacons, men, and women bound in heavy chains and destined for execution in Antinoöpolis. Moved with ardent love for Christ and burning compassion for the confessors, Irais dropped her water jar, boarded the ship, and boldly proclaimed herself a Christian. She was condemned alongside them and beheaded first.
deathSummary: Saint Irais was beheaded for her spontaneous confession of Christ in Antinoöpolis around 202.

image.title: Saint Irais of Alexandria Sacred Icon

name: Righteous Elizabeth
title: Righteous Elizabeth, Mother of Saint John the Baptist
curatedBio: Elizabeth was a descendant of the priestly lineage of Aaron and the righteous wife of the priest Zechariah. Both lived blameless before God, keeping all commandments, but endured the sorrow of barrenness into elderly age. In their old age, Archangel Gabriel announced to Zechariah in the Temple that Elizabeth would bear a son to be named John, who would prepare the way for the Messiah. When visited by her kinswoman Mary, the infant leaped in Elizabeth's womb, and she proclaimed, 'Blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb!'
deathSummary: Righteous Elizabeth fled into the wilderness with the infant John to escape Herod's slaughter of the innocents, reposing peacefully in Christ.

image.title: Righteous Elizabeth Sacred Icon

name: Saint Thecla of Iconium
title: Holy Protomartyr and Equal to the Apostles Thecla of Iconium
curatedBio: Thecla was an aristocratic maiden of Iconium who heard the Apostle Paul preaching from the window of his neighboring house and resolved to consecrate her virginity to Christ, breaking her betrothal to the nobleman Thamyris. Denounced and condemned to the pyre, torrential rains miraculously extinguished the flames. Rejoining Paul and traveling to Antioch, she was cast before wild lionesses and savage bulls, which bowed submissively and defended her against male beasts. Receiving baptism in the arena pool, she lived as an anchorite teacher in Seleucia until age ninety.
mannerOfDeath: Peaceful departure after miraculous survivals of martyrdom
deathSummary: Saint Thecla reposed peacefully in Seleucia at age ninety; venerated universally as the Protomartyr among Women.

image.title: Saint Thecla of Iconium Sacred Icon

name: Saint Euphrosyne of Alexandria
title: Venerable Mother Euphrosyne of Alexandria
curatedBio: Euphrosyne was the only daughter of Paphnutius, a wealthy magistrate of Alexandria. Desiring a life of undivided monastic contemplation rather than an arranged secular marriage, she cut her hair, disguised herself in men's clothing under the name Smaragdus, and entered a men's monastery outside the city. The abbot placed the monk Smaragdus in an isolated cell for thirty-eight years of unceasing prayer, where her father Paphnutius unwittingly visited her for spiritual counsel during his grief. Only on her deathbed did Euphrosyne reveal her identity to her weeping father.
deathSummary: Saint Euphrosyne reposed peacefully in her cell around 470; her father Paphnutius distributed his goods and inhabited her cell until his death.

image.title: Saint Euphrosyne of Alexandria Sacred Icon

name: Saint Justina of Antioch
title: Holy Virgin Martyr Justina of Antioch
curatedBio: Justina was a Christian maiden of Antioch who turned pagan magician Cyprian to Christ when his demonic spells failed against her sign of the cross and pure prayer. Repenting of the occult, Cyprian burned his grimoires and was baptized, later becoming Bishop of Antioch. During the Diocletian persecution, both Justina and Bishop Cyprian were arrested and brought to Damascus before the proconsul. Enduring scourging and boiling pitch, they remained unharmed. They were transported to Nicomedia and beheaded by the banks of the River Gallus.
deathSummary: Saint Justina was beheaded alongside Saint Cyprian in Nicomedia around 304 under Diocletian.

image.title: Saint Justina of Antioch Sacred Icon

name: Saint Epicharis of Rome
title: Holy Martyr Epicharis of Rome
curatedBio: Epicharis was a Roman Christian woman who suffered for her faith during the severe persecution under Emperor Diocletian around 298. Denounced to the prefect Caesar for confessing Jesus Christ and refusing pagan idolatry, she was suspended from a wooden post and torn with iron hooks. When ordered to recant, she declared her joy at suffering for Christ. As the executioners prepared to inflict further barbarities, Epicharis offered a final prayer of commendation to her Savior and was beheaded by the sword.
deathSummary: Saint Epicharis was beheaded in Rome around 298 after enduring the rack and iron combs.

image.title: Saint Epicharis of Rome Sacred Icon

name: Saint Eustochium of Bethlehem
title: Saint Eustochium, Virgin and Desert Mother of Bethlehem
curatedBio: Eustochium Julia was the daughter of Saint Paula and a Roman patrician senator. Following the early death of her father, Eustochium made a perpetual vow of virginity, becoming the recipient of Saint Jerome's celebrated treatise Letter 22 on the preservation of virginity. In 385, she accompanied her mother and Jerome to the Holy Land, establishing four monastic communities in Bethlehem near the Church of the Nativity. Fluent in Latin, Greek, and Hebrew, Eustochium copied biblical manuscripts and assisted Jerome in translating the Vulgate Bible.
deathSummary: Saint Eustochium reposed peacefully in Bethlehem in 419; buried near the Grotto of the Nativity beside Saint Paula.

image.title: Saint Eustochium of Bethlehem Sacred Icon

name: Saint Rhipsime of Armenia
title: Holy Virgin Martyr Rhipsime, Proto-Martyr of Armenia
curatedBio: Rhipsime was a noble Roman Christian maiden residing in a convent under the guidance of Abbess Gaiana. When Emperor Diocletian sought her as his bride for her extraordinary beauty, the entire community of thirty-five virgins fled the empire to Vagharshapat, the ancient royal capital of Armenia. Discovering their refuge, the pagan Armenian King Tiridates III ordered Rhipsime brought to his palace. When she fiercely resisted the king's advances and refused to worship pagan gods, Tiridates ordered her tongue cut out, her body torn with sharp stones, and her limbs dismembered.
deathSummary: Saint Rhipsime was martyred in Vagharshapat around 301; her martyrdom directly precipitated the conversion of Armenia under Saint Gregory the Illuminator.

image.title: Saint Rhipsime of Armenia Sacred Icon

name: Saint Sophia and Daughters
title: Holy Martyrs Sophia and her Daughters Faith, Hope, and Charity
curatedBio: Sophia was a devout Christian widow of Rome who named her three young daughters Pistis (Faith, age 12), Elpis (Hope, age 10), and Agape (Love, age 9) after the cardinal theological virtues. Denounced during the reign of Emperor Hadrian around 137, the young sisters were interrogated by the emperor himself. When they adamantly refused to sacrifice to Artemis, Hadrian ordered each child tortured and decapitated before their mother's eyes. Sophia encouraged them to persevere for Christ; after burying their severed bodies outside Rome, she prayed at their tomb and surrendered her soul to God.
mannerOfDeath: Decapitation of daughters; mother reposed in grief upon their tomb
deathSummary: Saint Sophia and her three daughters were martyred in Rome around 137 under Emperor Hadrian.

image.title: Saint Sophia and Daughters Sacred Icon

name: Saint Thérèse of Lisieux
title: Saint Thérèse of the Child Jesus and the Holy Face, Doctor of the Church
curatedBio: Marie-Françoise-Thérèse Martin was born in Alençon, France. Entering the Discalced Carmelite convent at Lisieux at age fifteen by personal dispensation of Pope Leo XIII, she formulated her spiritual 'Little Way'—a path of radical spiritual childhood, interior confidence, and unconditional surrender to God's merciful love in the simplest daily actions. Her posthumously published spiritual autobiography, Story of a Soul, swept the world with immense spiritual fire. In 1997, Pope John Paul II declared her the youngest Doctor of the Church.
deathSummary: Saint Thérèse reposed peacefully in the Carmel of Lisieux on September 30, 1897; feast celebrated universally on October 1.

image.title: Saint Thérèse of Lisieux Sacred Icon

name: Saint Justina of Padua
title: Holy Virgin Martyr Justina of Padua
curatedBio: Justina was born to a noble patrician family of Padua in northern Italy, baptized secretly by Saint Prosdocimus, the city's first bishop. When Emperor Maximian arrived in Padua to enforce the imperial edicts against Christians, Justina was seized crossing the Po River. Brought before the Emperor, she boldly confessed her unshakeable faith in Jesus Christ, refusing to offer pagan sacrifice or forfeit her consecrated virginity. Maximian ordered her run through with a military sword upon the bridge.
deathSummary: Saint Justina was executed with a sword in Padua around 304; the renowned Abbey of Santa Giustina enshrines her tomb.

image.title: Saint Justina of Padua Sacred Icon

name: Saint Mother Théodore Guérin
title: Saint Théodore Guérin, Foundress of the Sisters of Providence
curatedBio: Anne-Thérèse Guérin was born in Brittany, France, and joined the Sisters of Providence of Ruillé-sur-Loir. In 1840, in response to an urgent appeal from the Bishop of Vincennes, Indiana, Mother Théodore and five sister companions crossed the Atlantic to the dense untamed wilderness of Indiana. Enduring extreme poverty, harsh winters, fire, and clerical hostility, she established the Saint Mary-of-the-Woods motherhouse and opened Saint Mary-of-the-Woods College, the oldest Catholic liberal arts college for women in the United States.
deathSummary: Saint Théodore Guérin reposed peacefully in Indiana on May 14, 1856; canonized by Pope Benedict XVI on October 15, 2006, feast celebrated October 3.

image.title: Saint Mother Théodore Guérin Sacred Icon

name: Saint Aurea of Paris
title: Saint Aurea of Paris, Abbess of Saint Martial
curatedBio: Aurea was born to noble Syrian parents who settled in Gaul. Around 633, Saint Eligius (Éloi), chief counselor to Merovingian King Dagobert I, established the great nunnery of Saint Martial in the heart of Paris and invited Aurea to serve as its first abbess. She governed three hundred consecrated virgins under the austere combined Rule of Saint Columban and Saint Benedict. For over three decades, Aurea led her community with radiant humility, prayerful contemplation, and constant care for the destitute of Paris.
deathSummary: Saint Aurea reposed peacefully in Paris during the great plague of 666 alongside one hundred and sixty of her nuns.

image.title: Saint Aurea of Paris Sacred Icon

name: Saint Faustina Kowalska
title: Saint Maria Faustina Kowalska, Apostle and Secretary of Divine Mercy
curatedBio: Helena Kowalska was born into a poor peasant family in Głogowiec, Poland. Entering the Congregation of the Sisters of Our Lady of Mercy in Warsaw at age twenty, Sister Faustina labored as a humble cook, gardener, and gatekeeper. Beginning in 1931 in Płock, she received extraordinary mystical apparitions of Jesus Christ, who revealed Himself with red and pale rays radiating from His Sacred Heart and commanded her to propagate the devotion to Divine Mercy and write her Diary, Divine Mercy in My Soul.
deathSummary: Saint Faustina reposed peacefully in Kraków-Łagiewniki on October 5, 1938; canonized as the first saint of the third millennium in 2000.

image.title: Saint Faustina Kowalska Sacred Icon

name: Saint Faith of Conques
title: Holy Virgin Martyr Faith (Sainte Foy) of Conques
curatedBio: Faith (Foy) was a noble Gallo-Roman Christian maiden of Agen in Aquitaine. During the fierce persecutions under Roman governor Dacian around 303, Faith, aged twelve, was denounced for confessing Christ. Refusing to offer sacrifice to Diana, she proclaimed that she had served Christ from her infancy and would not abandon Him for wooden idols. Dacian ordered her bound to a red-hot iron bed of coals and beaten. Unshaken by the flames, she was finally crowned with martyrdom by the sword.
mannerOfDeath: Roasted on a gridiron, then beheaded
deathSummary: Saint Faith was beheaded in Agen around 303; in the ninth century her relics were translated to the Abbey of Sainte-Foy in Conques.

image.title: Saint Faith of Conques Sacred Icon

name: Saint Osyth of Chich
title: Holy Virgin Martyr Osyth (Ositha) of Chich
curatedBio: Osyth was an Anglo-Saxon royal maiden, daughter of King Frithuwald of Surrey and niece to Saint Edith of Wilton. Educated in a convent, she desired to consecrate her virginity to Christ but was compelled into marriage with King Sighere of the East Saxons. When a wild white hart lured the king from the wedding banquet, Osyth fled to Bishop Acca and took the veil with her husband's subsequent consent. She established a monastery at Chich (modern St Osyth) in Essex until Danish Viking marauders raided the abbey and beheaded her.
deathSummary: Saint Osyth was beheaded by Danish Vikings at Chich around 700; she is venerated as a cephalophore martyr.

image.title: Saint Osyth of Chich Sacred Icon

name: Saint Pelagia the Penitent
title: Righteous Pelagia the Penitent of Antioch
curatedBio: Pelagia was a renowned and wealthy mime-actress, dancer, and courtesan of Antioch named Margarita for her shimmering pearls. While passing before the cathedral in ostentatious luxury, Saint Nonnus, Bishop of Edessa, was moved to tears by how she adorned her body compared to the soul's adornment for God. Penetrated with profound compunction after hearing Nonnus preach the next day, Pelagia fell at his feet, received baptism, gave all her riches to the destitute, and fled in male pilgrim attire to the Mount of Olives in Jerusalem to live in unceasing prayer.
deathSummary: Saint Pelagia reposed peacefully in her cell on the Mount of Olives around 457; revered across East and West.

image.title: Saint Pelagia the Penitent Sacred Icon

name: Saint Publia the Confessor
title: Saint Publia the Confessor, Deaconess of Antioch
curatedBio: Publia was a noble Christian woman of Antioch who, after being widowed, devoted her life to the Church and was ordained a deaconess. Gathering a community of consecrated virgins and widows in her home, she guided them in perpetual psalmody, prayer, and charity. When the apostate Emperor Julian passed by her house on his Persian campaign in 362, Publia and her virgins began chanting Psalm 115: 'The idols of the heathen are silver and gold, the work of men's hands.' Enraged, Julian had Publia dragged out and savagely beaten, but she endured the blows with serene joy.
mannerOfDeath: Natural causes (reposed after the fall of Julian)
deathSummary: Saint Publia reposed peacefully in Antioch in the late fourth century after fearlessly confronting Julian the Apostate.

image.title: Saint Publia the Confessor Sacred Icon

name: Saint Eulampia of Nicomedia
title: Holy Virgin Martyr Eulampia and her Brother Eulampius
curatedBio: Eulampia lived in Nicomedia during the cruel persecution instituted by Emperor Maximian around 303. Her brother Eulampius was arrested after mocking an imperial edict that demanded the death of Christians. Eulampius was strung up and torn with iron hooks. Witnessing her brother's steadfast fortitude from the crowd, Eulampia broke through the guards, embraced Eulampius, and publicly proclaimed herself a Christian. Cast together into a boiling cauldron of pitch, the flames were miraculously extinguished. Eulampius was then beheaded, while Eulampia yielded her spirit before the sword struck.
deathSummary: Saint Eulampia surrendered her soul to Christ in Nicomedia around 303 alongside her brother Saint Eulampius.

image.title: Saint Eulampia of Nicomedia Sacred Icon

name: Saint Ethelburga of Barking
title: Saint Ethelburga of Barking, Abbess and Wonderworker
curatedBio: Ethelburga was an Anglo-Saxon royal maiden, sister of Saint Erkenwald, Bishop of London. Around 666, Erkenwald founded Barking Abbey in Essex as a double monastery of monks and nuns, appointing Ethelburga as its founding abbess. Celebrated by Saint Bede the Venerable in his Ecclesiastical History for her sublime administrative wisdom, angelic gentleness, and prophetic visions, Ethelburga led her sisters through the devastating pestilence of 664, comforting the dying with miraculous revelations of heavenly light descending upon the abbey cemetery.
deathSummary: Saint Ethelburga reposed peacefully at Barking Abbey around 675; eulogized by Saint Bede.

image.title: Saint Ethelburga of Barking Sacred Icon

name: Saint Domnina of Anazarbus
title: Holy Martyr Domnina of Anazarbus
curatedBio: Domnina was a courageous Christian maiden of Anazarbus in Cilicia during the reign of Emperor Diocletian around 304. Arrested by order of governor Lysias for refusing to offer incense to Roman idols, she was stretched out upon the ground and severely beaten with rods. Lysias then ordered red-hot iron rods placed upon her joints and feet. Throughout her horrific torments, Domnina offered prayers of thanksgiving to Christ, refusing to compromise. Thrown back into prison, she surrendered her soul peacefully into the hands of the Lord.
mannerOfDeath: Tortured with rods and hot iron, died in prison
deathSummary: Saint Domnina died of her injuries in prison in Anazarbus around 304 under Diocletian.

image.title: Saint Domnina of Anazarbus Sacred Icon

name: Saint Parascheva the Younger
title: Venerable Mother Parascheva the Younger, Protectress of the Balkans
curatedBio: Parascheva (Petka) was born to wealthy Christian parents in Epibates on the Sea of Marmara in the eleventh century. Giving away her fine garments to the poor, she left Constantinople after her parents' death, journeying to Jerusalem and then entering the Jordan desert to live an ascetic life of prayer and fasting. Guided by an angel in her old age to return to her homeland, she returned to Epibates, reposing in obscurity as a stranger. Her incorrupt and fragrance-exuding relics in Iași, Romania, draw hundreds of thousands of pilgrims annually.
deathSummary: Saint Parascheva reposed peacefully in Epibates in the eleventh century; her holy relics are enshrined in the Metropolitan Cathedral of Iași.

image.title: Saint Parascheva the Younger Sacred Icon

name: Saint Fortunata of Caesarea
title: Holy Virgin Martyr Fortunata of Caesarea and her Brothers
curatedBio: Fortunata was a Christian maiden of Caesarea in Palestine during the persecutions under Emperor Diocletian around 303. Denounced alongside her brothers Carpophorus, Eristeus, and Hermogenes, Fortunata refused to deny Christ or offer sacrifice to the pagan gods. Subjected to cruel scourging and the rack, she was threatened with wild beasts in the arena, but the lions refused to touch her. Condemned to death by sword, Fortunata died with joyful serenity, her relics subsequently translated to Naples in Campania.
deathSummary: Saint Fortunata was martyred in Caesarea around 303; her relics are venerated in Naples and Baucina, Sicily.

image.title: Saint Fortunata of Caesarea Sacred Icon

name: Saint Teresa of Ávila
title: Saint Teresa of Jesus (of Ávila), Doctor of the Church, Reformer of Carmel
curatedBio: Teresa Sánchez de Cepeda y Ahumada was born in Ávila, Spain. Entering the Carmelite Monastery of the Incarnation, she experienced profound interior conversion after decades of lukewarmness, receiving extraordinary mystical raptures and the transverberation of her heart. With Saint John of the Cross, she spearheaded the Discalced Carmelite reform, traveling relentlessly across Spain to establish seventeen reformed cloisters founded on contemplative silence, strict enclosure, and sisterly poverty. Her masterpieces The Interior Castle and The Way of Perfection are immortal mystical classics.
deathSummary: Saint Teresa of Ávila reposed peacefully in Alba de Tormes on October 4/15, 1582; declared the first female Doctor of the Church in 1970.

image.title: Saint Teresa of Ávila Sacred Icon

name: Saint Margaret Mary Alacoque
title: Saint Margaret Mary Alacoque, Apostle of the Sacred Heart
curatedBio: Margaret Mary was born in L'Hautecour, Burgundy, and entered the Order of the Visitation at Paray-le-Monial in 1671. Between 1673 and 1675, she was favored with momentous apparitions of Jesus Christ, who revealed His Sacred Heart burning with flaming love for mankind, encircled with thorns, and surmounted by a cross. Instructed to institute the Feast of the Sacred Heart and First Friday Communions of reparation, she persevered through initial skepticism and mockery with the spiritual support of Saint Claude de la Colombière.
deathSummary: Saint Margaret Mary reposed peacefully in Paray-le-Monial on October 17, 1690, at age forty-three; celebrated on October 16.

image.title: Saint Margaret Mary Alacoque Sacred Icon

name: Saint Hedwig of Silesia
title: Saint Hedwig of Silesia, Duchess of Poland and Foundress
curatedBio: Hedwig was born in Andechs Castle, Bavaria, daughter of the Duke of Merania. Married at age twelve to Henry I the Bearded, Duke of Silesia, she bore seven children and used her royal status to protect the poor, establish hospitals for lepers, and found the Cistercian nunnery of Trebnitz. Following her husband's death in 1238, Hedwig entered Trebnitz Abbey as a nun, living in extreme austerity, walking barefoot through Silesian snows, and dedicating her grief after the death of her son Henry II at the Battle of Legnica to the passion of Christ.
deathSummary: Saint Hedwig reposed peacefully at Trebnitz Abbey on October 15, 1243; canonized by Pope Clement IV in 1267, celebrated on October 16/17.

image.title: Saint Hedwig of Silesia Sacred Icon

name: Saint Gwen of Brittany
title: Saint Gwen (Blanche) of Brittany, Mother of Saint Winwaloe
curatedBio: Gwen (meaning 'The White' or 'Blessed') was an early medieval Breton noblewoman, daughter of Prince Emyr Llydaw of Wales. Fleeing Anglo-Saxon invaders across the English Channel to Armorica (Brittany), she married Fragan, a Breton prince. Gwen was the mother of renowned Celtic saints: Winwaloe (founder of Landévennec Abbey), Guethenoc, Jacut, and Creirwy. Iconography portrays her with three breasts (Gwen Teir Bronn), symbolizing her miraculous nourishment of three future saints simultaneously, radiating maternal charity throughout the early Celtic church.
deathSummary: Saint Gwen reposed peacefully in Brittany in the sixth century; venerated throughout Brittany, Cornwall, and Wales.

image.title: Saint Gwen of Brittany Sacred Icon

name: Saint Laura of Córdoba
title: Holy Virgin Martyr Laura of Córdoba
curatedBio: Laura was a Spanish Christian woman born into Cordoban nobility during the Islamic Emirate of Córdoba in Andalusia. After the death of her husband, she entered the convent of Santa María de Cuteclara, later becoming its abbess. During the intense Moorish persecutions under Emir Muhammad I, Laura was denounced by Muslim authorities for being an apostate and public confessor of the Christian faith. Brought before the Islamic court, she refused to renounce Christ or embrace Islam; she was condemned to death by being submerged into a cauldron of boiling molten lead.
deathSummary: Saint Laura was martyred in Córdoba on October 19, 864; commemorated among the Forty-Eight Martyrs of Córdoba.

image.title: Saint Laura of Córdoba Sacred Icon

name: Saint Matrona of Chios
title: Venerable Mother Matrona of Chios, Wonderworker
curatedBio: Matrona was born in the village of Volissos on the Greek Aegean island of Chios in the fifteenth century, named Maria by her pious parents. Rejecting secular marriage proposals, she distributed all her inheritance to the poor and established a women's monastic community in the ruined fortress of Chios. Matrona lived an angelic life of rigorous fasting, night vigils, and radiant spiritual humility, receiving the gift of miraculous healings and spiritual discernment. Her monastery became a sanctuary of solace for Greek islanders during the Genoese and Ottoman occupations.
deathSummary: Saint Matrona reposed peacefully in Chios around 1462; venerated as the principal patron saint of Chios.

image.title: Saint Matrona of Chios Sacred Icon

name: Saint Ursula of Cologne
title: Holy Virgin Martyr Ursula and the Eleven Thousand Virgins of Cologne
curatedBio: Ursula was a Romano-British princess who, seeking to preserve her virginal dedication to Christ while negotiating an arranged marriage to a pagan prince, embarked on a grand maritime pilgrimage across Europe accompanied by a host of noble maiden companions. Traveling up the Rhine to Rome to pray at the tombs of the Apostles, they returned toward Cologne. There, the city was besieged by barbarian Huns. When Ursula and her companions refused to yield their chastity or deny Christ, the Hun chieftain shot Ursula with a barrage of arrows while her maidens were slaughtered.
deathSummary: Saint Ursula and her holy companions were martyred in Cologne around 383; the Basilica of Saint Ursula in Cologne stands upon their cemetery.

image.title: Saint Ursula of Cologne Sacred Icon

name: Saints Nunilo and Alodia
title: Holy Virgin Martyrs Nunilo and Alodia of Huesca
curatedBio: Nunilo and Alodia were two teenage sisters born in Adahuesca near Huesca in Moorish-ruled Spain to a Muslim father and Christian mother. Following their father's death, their mother raised them in the Christian faith. When she remarried an intolerant Muslim official during the anti-Christian decrees of Emir Abd ar-Rahman II of Córdoba, their stepfather denounced them to the governor of Alquézar. Interrogated and promised wealthy marriages if they renounced Christ, the sisters declared their eternal betrothal to Jesus; they were beheaded in the public square.
deathSummary: Saints Nunilo and Alodia were beheaded in Huesca on October 22, 851; their relics are preserved in Leyre Monastery, Navarre.

image.title: Saints Nunilo and Alodia Sacred Icon

name: Saint Oda of Aquitaine
title: Saint Oda of Aquitaine, Recluse and Widow of Brabant
curatedBio: Oda was a noble princess of Aquitaine who married Duke Boggis of Aquitaine in the early medieval period. Renowned for maternal charity and immense almsgiving, she devoted herself entirely to the Church upon being widowed. Leaving southern France, she journeyed on pilgrimage to the shrine of Saint Lambert in Liège. Guided to the wilderness near Sint-Oedenrode in the Netherlands, she built a solitary hermit's cell, living in austere contemplation, curing sick villagers of eye ailments, and preaching peace to the local population.
deathSummary: Saint Oda reposed peacefully in Sint-Oedenrode around 726; venerated as the patroness of Brabant and the blind.

image.title: Saint Oda of Aquitaine Sacred Icon

name: Saint Claudia Procula
title: Righteous Claudia Procula, Wife of Pontius Pilate
curatedBio: Claudia Procula was the noble Roman wife of Pontius Pilate, the Roman prefect of Judea. During the trial of Jesus Christ before Pilate's judgment seat in Jerusalem, Claudia sent an urgent message to her husband recorded in the Gospel of Matthew (Matthew 27:19): 'Have nothing to do with that just man, for I have suffered many things this day in a dream because of him.' Early Christian tradition recounts that she embraced faith in Christ after His Resurrection, becoming an ardent disciple and confessor who suffered for the Christian faith.
deathSummary: Saint Claudia Procula reposed peacefully in the first century as a faithful Christian confessor; feast celebrated in Eastern traditions on October 27 / October 24.

image.title: Saint Claudia Procula Sacred Icon

name: Saint Tabitha the Merciful
title: Saint Tabitha (Dorcas) of Joppa, Disciple Raised by Saint Peter
curatedBio: Tabitha (translated in Greek as Dorcas, meaning Gazelle) was a beloved disciple residing in the coastal port of Joppa, celebrated in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 9:36-42) as a woman 'full of good works and almsdeeds which she did.' When she fell sick and died, the weeping local widows sent for Saint Peter from nearby Lydda. Displaying the tunics and cloaks that Tabitha had sewn for the destitute, they mourned her loss. Peter knelt in prayer, turned to the body, and proclaimed, 'Tabitha, arise!' She opened her eyes, restoring joy to the entire Christian community.
mannerOfDeath: Natural causes (reposed at an advanced old age)
deathSummary: Saint Tabitha lived out her second life in holiness and endless almsgiving in Joppa, reposing in peace in the first century.

image.title: Saint Tabitha the Merciful Sacred Icon

name: Saint Daria of Rome
title: Holy Martyr Daria and her Husband Saint Chrysanthus
curatedBio: Daria was an Athenian priestess of Minerva who married the Roman patrician Christian Chrysanthus with the intent of drawing him back to pagan polytheism. Instead, Chrysanthus converted Daria to faith in Jesus Christ; both agreed to live in virginal matrimony, converting hundreds of Roman youths to Christ. During the reign of Emperor Numerian around 283, the couple was denounced and cast into prison. After tortures failed to shake their fortitude, they were led to a sandpit on the Via Salaria and buried alive beneath mounds of stones and sand.
deathSummary: Saint Daria was martyred by being buried alive on the Via Salaria in Rome around 283; celebrated on October 25/26 and March 19.

image.title: Saint Daria of Rome Sacred Icon

name: Saint Capitolina of Cappadocia
title: Holy Martyr Capitolina of Cappadocia and her Servant Eroteis
curatedBio: Capitolina was an aristocratic Christian maiden of Cappadocia during the persecutions of Emperor Diocletian around 304. Possessing immense familial wealth, she distributed her entire patrimony to the impoverished and freed all her slaves. Brought before the Roman governor Firmilian for refusing to offer sacrifice to pagan gods, Capitolina proclaimed that her singular treasure was Jesus Christ. She was thrown into a dungeon and beheaded. Her faithful servant Eroteis, moved by her mistress's heroism, rebuked the governor and was beaten with clubs before being beheaded.
deathSummary: Saint Capitolina was beheaded in Cappadocia around 304 under Diocletian.

image.title: Saint Capitolina of Cappadocia Sacred Icon

name: Saint Anastasia the Roman
title: Holy Virgin Martyr Anastasia the Roman (The Elder)
curatedBio: Anastasia was an orphan maiden of Rome raised from age three in a convent under the holy guidance of Abbess Sophia.
